title: China's Religious Crackdown: Trump to Raise Pastor Ezra Jin's Release with Xi at Beijing Summit
previewText: President Donald Trump has pledged to raise the release of Pastor Jin Mingri (金明日), known in English as Ezra Jin, with Chinese President Xi Jinping during his visit to Beijing beginning May 13. The

blocks.text: President Donald Trump has pledged to raise the release of Pastor Jin Mingri (金明日), known in English as Ezra Jin, with Chinese President Xi Jinping during his visit to Beijing beginning May 13. The pastor's family in Washington, D.C. is praying for a miracle.
A Rally at the White House on the Eve of the Beijing Visit

Speaking to reporters at the White House on May 11, President Trump said that during his May 13–15 visit to Beijing, he would press for the release of Hong Kong democracy advocate Jimmy Lai together with Pastor Jin.
Following a rally that day in front of the White House by the families of Chinese political prisoners, Jin's daughter Grace Jin Drexel, a U.S. Senate staffer, said:

My father, Pastor Ezra Jin, has been detained for more than 200 days today. With this trip, this upcoming summit, we hope and pray that my father will be able to rejoin his family members in the U.S. as soon as possible. We are praying for a miracle. 
── Grace Jin Drexel
The Founding of Zion Church

Jin is the founder of Zion Church (锡安教会), one of the largest underground churches in China. A student in Beijing at the time of the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre, he encountered Christianity in its aftermath. 

After serving for more than a decade in the government-sanctioned Three-Self Patriotic Movement, Jin founded Zion Church in 2007. The church grew into a network spanning more than forty cities, reaching approximately ten thousand people nationwide.

A church that does not place God as its ultimate leader is not a church that glorifies God. The state church, in its very system, is saying that the party has to come before God.
── Pastor Jin Mingri
A Bond Formed Under Surveillance

Grace held U.S. citizenship but lived in Beijing with her family. During the 2018 crackdown by Chinese authorities, the entire family was placed under an exit ban, leaving Grace, a U.S. citizen, unable to leave China.

Her husband, Bill Drexel, was an American graduate student in 2018 researching the Chinese government's surveillance of religious minorities when he attended a Zion Church service and met Grace. As they spoke, he came to understand that Grace was a target of the government.

In January 2020, Chinese authorities suddenly allowed Grace to leave. The reason remains unknown to the family. She moved to the United States, married Bill, and now lives in Washington, D.C. with their two children. Pastor Jin was never permitted to leave China and could not attend his daughter's wedding or meet his two grandchildren.
2018: The First Shutdown

The turning point came in early 2018, when revised "Regulations on Religious Affairs" made all religious activities outside government-sanctioned channels effectively illegal. Zion Church's worship space was shut down that year after Pastor Jin refused to allow facial recognition cameras to be installed inside the sanctuary.
2021: The Drugging at Dinner
In 2021, Pastor Jin had returned to Beijing when government officials invited him to dinner. He told his seminary students beforehand: "If I don't check back in in an hour, come and get me."

We later found out that the government officials drugged him at that dinner. When the seminarians came to look for him, he was slurring his words, very distraught, visibly disoriented. We have no idea what they were planning to do with him in that state.
Grace Jin Drexel said. The family has feared for Pastor Jin's safety ever since.
October 10, 2025: Nationwide Coordinated Raids

On October 10, 2025, Chinese authorities detained approximately thirty Christian leaders in coordinated raids across multiple cities. Senator Ted Cruz (R-Texas) called the operation "the largest nationwide crackdown in over four decades against a Christian house church in China." Eighteen people, including Pastor Jin, remain in custody, facing charges including subversion of state power and "illegal dissemination of information online."

On the morning of October 10, I woke up to a text from my dad about the arrest of another pastor, Pastor Wang Lin. Shortly after, my mom called saying she had not been able to reach my dad or anyone around him for many hours. Zion Church has a pastor in the U.S. who led a Zoom call with all the church leaders in China. In real time, we heard people say, "I have the police right outside my door right now," and then they just quit Zoom, and that person disappeared. ── Grace Jin Drexel
Harsh Conditions in Detention

The family has learned of Pastor Jin's situation in fragments through his lawyers. Jin has severe diabetes, but Chinese authorities have not permitted him to take his own medication. 

According to family testimony, he sleeps on a cold concrete bench in his cell, without a blanket or access to a Bible. Lead defense lawyer Zhang Kai had his law license revoked in January, and six other lawyers handling the case were given six-month suspensions.

Senator Cruz described Jin's treatment: "He is kept in terrible conditions, freezing cold, with snow and rain in his prison cell. He doesn't have a blanket. They are targeting specifically Christians for persecution."
Surveillance That Reaches Across the Pacific
Pastor Jin's family has testified that, even while living in the United States, they have been subjected to transnational surveillance and intimidation by the Chinese government.

A week after the family began speaking out publicly, Drexel's mother received a threatening phone call from someone impersonating a U.S. federal agent, falsely claiming she was under investigation for money laundering and pressuring her to return to China.
Months later, her tires were slashed while the car was parked inside her garage. Drexel herself has been followed and watched in Washington, D.C.

Senator Cruz, addressing this pattern, said: "China has a long pattern of abusing, in particular, the rights of Chinese Americans in the United States. The Department of Justice, the FBI, we need to be fighting back.”
A Global Call for Release

Pastor Jin's case is only one example of the broader religious crackdown in China. According to the 2025 USCIRF Annual Report, of more than 2,300 individuals detained or imprisoned worldwide for their faith, China holds the highest number at 810.

In the U.S. Senate, Senator Cruz and Senator Chris Coons (D-Delaware) passed a bipartisan resolution calling for the pastor's release. Secretary of State Marco Rubio issued a statement of condemnation immediately after the arrests.

More than 200 days of detention without trial. A cell with no medication, no blanket, no Bible. A defense lawyer stripped of his license. A family separated from a U.S. citizen daughter and her two grandchildren. The substance of the charge is that Pastor Jin shared biblical teaching online, an act that should be protected as a fundamental right.

The reality is China imprisons a lot of people for unconscionable reasons. We are fully aware that the likelihood of getting Grace's dad out, or any of those with him, is extremely low. It would be a miracle. We believe in a God of miracles, so we are hoping for that actively. ── Bill Drexel

It's not just about my dad's story. It's about the story of so many of these Christians who have been suffering for their faith for all these years. I'm asking for a miracle for my dad to be out of prison.── Grace Jin Drexel
The time remaining before President Trump meets with President Xi is short.
The world must look this reality in the eye, and the day must come, as soon as possible, when Pastor Jin and all those detained with him are immediately released.

title: Makers and Takers: The Invisible Line That Divides a Country
previewText:
Watch American politics for a while and the same pattern keeps coming back. Inside every country there are people who make things of value. There are also people who receive what others have made.
The

blocks.text: Watch American politics for a while and the same pattern keeps coming back. Inside every country there are people who make things of value. There are also people who receive what others have made.
The line between them is not drawn by income or by the kind of job a person holds. What draws it is where a person places the responsibility for their own results.
Defining the two groups
Makers.

They start businesses, hire people, and pay taxes. When something fails, they carry the loss themselves. Employees belong here too. Anyone who owns the results of their own work and raises their income by getting better at it stands on this side. What they share is a simple sense that their life improves by as much as they produce.
Takers.
They choose to draw from the system as their main way of getting by.

One point should not be misread here. A person who receives support because life got hard does not become a taker by doing so. Illness, job loss, and disaster reach everyone. Someone who takes help, recovers, and goes back to work is a maker.
The problem is the posture that treats support as a way of life instead of a stage to pass through.
The difference shows up in character first
Before this difference appears as a political opinion, it appears in personality.
How they feel about time.

Makers can hold off on what they want now in order to get something bigger later. Saving money, learning a skill, and building trust all take years before they pay off. Takers put a high value on the smaller gain they can have today.
Where they place the cause.

Do you see your situation as the result of your own choices, or as the result of your surroundings? People who choose the first answer believe that changing their behavior changes the outcome, so they change their behavior. People who choose the second believe nothing changes until the surroundings change, so they make demands of whoever can change them, which means the government.
How they take a loss.
Makers see profit as the payment for accepting the chance of a loss. Takers see the loss itself as unfair and expect someone else to cover it.
Where the right and the left split
By this point the link to political sides becomes clear.

The right, meaning conservatives, cares about personal responsibility, long time horizons, and protecting what has already been built. The left, meaning liberals and socialists, cares about closing gaps in outcomes, helping people quickly, and looking at the system rather than the person for the cause.
What separates the two is how they see human beings and how far ahead they look.
The same pattern shows up in other countries
Japan. Here the line runs between generations.

Pension and medi @cal benefits go mostly to older people, while the cost falls on those still working. Every election brings talk of cash payments and subsidies, and the question of who pays gets pushed back. Government debt is now well above twice the size of the economy. That bill is being handed to a generation that cannot vote yet.
South Korea. The same force is at work.

Cash payments for young people, more hiring in the public sector, and the sharp rise in the minimum wage carried out under the banner of income led growth. That last policy has been criticized for cutting jobs at small shops and small factories. Experts still disagree about the results. The thinking behind it is easy to follow. Move the money around first, and production will catch up later.
The behavior looks alike too.

In Korea, the number of young people who spend years preparing for civil service exams is talked about as a social problem. In Japan, a stable employer stays at the top of the list of places graduates want to work. In both countries, the share of young people who want to start a business is low by developed country standards.

This does not happen because people are lazy. In a society where the loss from failure falls on one person and no path back is built into the system, playing it safe is the correct call. People are responding honestly to the incentives the system gave them.
There is also a shared foundation. The population is shrinking.
When the number of people on the making side falls while the demands of the receiving side are locked into law, the math stops working.
The real danger comes when takers write the policy
For a politician, promising benefits is the cheapest way to buy votes. The money gets paid later and the votes come in now.

Repeat that trade enough times and more than half of all voters end up receiving more than they pay. Once a society reaches that point, any politician who says the system needs fixing loses the election. From the moment repair becomes politically impossible, decline stops being a choice and becomes the route the country is already on.
What Venezuela and Cuba showed

Venezuela went down that road. Oil money paid for larger handouts, and price controls and nationalization pushed the people who made things out of the country. Once the producers were gone, what remained was a state with nothing left to hand out. The economy shrank sharply over about ten years and millions of people left.

Cuba gave up the source of its growth in order to deliver equality. After the 1959 revolution, most companies and farmland were nationalized, and the room to decide anything on the producing side disappeared with them.

Sixty years later, the result shows up in the numbers. GDP in 2024 was more than 10 percent below its 2018 level, and blackouts lasting over twenty hours a day hit region after region. In 2024 alone, more than 250,000 people left, most of them of working age.
The Cuban government explains this as the result of US sanctions. Among researchers, the mainstream view points to the structure itself, a state that never let go of production.
Why people believe promises that sound too good
A sweet political promise is built the same way as an ad for a pill that melts the weight away.
There are three reasons.

First, people cannot sit through the long stretch between effort and result. Changing your body takes months. Not many are willing to take on the dull work of watching what they eat and exercising every day.

Second, the ad cuts out the hard part and shows only the result. Political promises do the same. The funding, the other choices being given up, and the side effects that show up after the program is locked in all stay off screen.

Third, the side making the promise loses nothing. The pill becomes profit for the company the moment it sells. The politician has already gotten what he wanted the moment he wins. When the promise fails, the one who pays for it is always the one who believed it.
Five questions to test a promise
Who pays, and when? A policy that gives no answer is hiding one that would not go over well.
How long until it works? When only the short term results get talked about, the long term cost is hidden somewhere.
Has it been tried anywhere? If it has, what happened?
Does the side promising it lose anything if it fails? A forecast from someone with nothing at stake is advertising.
Can it be undone? Almost no country has managed to shrink a benefit program on its own.
Conclusion
A country has to make before it can hand out. This is not a matter of belief. It is a matter of arithmetic.
So one test is enough for judging a policy. Does it add to the number of people standing on the making side, or take away from it?
Politics that cannot answer that question will wear a country down, no matter how good the words sound at the start.

title: If This Is an “Equal Paradise,” Why Do People Flee?
previewText:
North Korean defectors and what communism looks like after decades in full control
— A record of people whose words, families, and inner lives were taken by the state
 
North Korea still advertises

blocks.text: North Korean defectors and what communism looks like after decades in full control
— A record of people whose words, families, and inner lives were taken by the state

North Korea still advertises itself as a kind and equal country. Guided tours show monuments and smiling faces. But the people who live there keep leaving, even at the risk of being shot. If the poster were true, why would so few want to move in—and why would so many want to get out? A short visit is not the same as a life. Imagine staying.

A woman in Pyongyang, given the name Ji-yeon, went next door with water. No one answered. When the authorities opened the house, they found a family of three dead inside. The BBC reported this in 2023.

It happened in the capital, not in some remote village. A state that claims to care for everyone still let neighbors starve in silence. The reason is not only a lack of food. Speak too loudly, and your own family can be punished too. So people go quiet. Sometimes they go quiet to protect the people they love.
The first sentence written at school

The first sentence a North Korean child writes at school is not their own name, and not a letter to their mother. It is “Thank you, dear General.” In the morning they say the same words before a portrait.

Once a week, in a session called “life review,” they must name their own faults and then the faults of a classmate. In a notebook a defector brought to South Korea, a child wrote that they had failed to follow the teachings—and then criticized a friend for wanting to go home early because the house was far away.
Children want to be praised. They also want to be kind to their friends. That natural wish is turned in another direction from the start.

To doubt is not an opinion. It is a crime. The words of Kim Il-sung, Kim Jong-il, and Kim Jong-un are placed first in daily life. If you believe children should be free to think and free to be friends, picture this classroom. Before speaking of an ideal, sit in that child’s seat.
Only those who stop thinking remain

Song Hee-suk (a pseudonym), who survived the famine of the 1990s, lost her husband, her son, and her mother-in-law to hunger—and still did not blame the system. She believed it was because “America had the country surrounded,” and she took the blame herself. Until she reached China, it did not occur to her that the state might be at fault. You cannot live, she said, unless you stop thinking.

A person can be broken not only by a blow. They can also be broken by being taught to blame the wrong one. When someone who has lost a family cannot question the state, it is not because they are cold. It is because, on top of that grief, they were taught, “You are the one at fault.”
Whose is the family?

Neighbors are grouped into watch units of about twenty to fifty households, called inminban. In 2025 a woman still inside the country said officials come into the home every other day. There are cases of people being investigated simply for carrying in thirty kilograms of rice. There is also the story of a family expelled from Pyongyang after a grandfather, over drinks, said the equipment in a coal mine was dangerous. A friend’s father vanishes. No one is told why.

A home is meant to be a place where you can breathe. When the state walks that far inside, people stop trusting the neighbor. When trust dies, help has nowhere to go.
In 2023 a fisherman, Kim Il-hyok, fled across the sea with nine members of his family. A worker who married a farm worker was required to move to the countryside.

Falsifying class status meant the risk of a labor prison. Birth and marriage decide even where you may live. Trying to protect a family can become a crime. Can a country where you cannot choose, with the person you love, where you will live still be called an ideal?
Why can a song from outside be punishable by death?

Spreading South Korean dramas or K-pop can bring not only a labor sentence but the death penalty. A UN special rapporteur noted that about 45 percent of the population is malnourished—yet the government is extremely afraid of South Korean culture. One defector said that watching Naruto was what first made them want to leave. Another saw a person who prayed publicly killed as a case of “superstition.”

People do not touch a song from outside only because they want to do something wrong. They touch it because they glimpse a small light: another kind of life might exist. That light is what the system fears most.

Once you know the outside, you can ask, “Is this really paradise?” 
So songs are sealed off, words are sealed off, screens are sealed off. Missiles are called a national treasure, and people’s stomachs come later. When rations stopped, unofficial markets kept people alive. It was not the stated ideology that saved them. It was the trade that was supposed to be forbidden that saved a neighbor’s dinner. What do we do with that fact?
Born in a camp, a child who was sold

Shin Dong-hyuk was born in a prison camp and, as a child, watched his mother and brother executed in public. When prisoners grew too weak, they were sent home on “sick leave,” and they died there. Former prisoners say this was a way to keep the number of deaths inside the camp from looking too high.
In 2025, Kim Eun-ju testified at the United Nations: at eleven her father starved to death; in China she was sold for less than three hundred dollars. Her sister suffered the same violence.

North Korea’s ambassador called them “human scum.”
A society that calls those who fled scum is not protecting people. It is protecting the face of the system. Still, when these women give their names and speak, it is not only for revenge. It is also a plea: do not forget the people still inside.
Why people leave, and why they do not come in

Coming near the river is enough to be punished. In the first half of 2026, only 59 women and 4 men entered South Korea as defectors. Even so, Kim Il-hyok’s family—nine people, including a woman who was pregnant—crossed the sea at night. His wife said they went “from a dark sea to a sea of freedom.” If you think of a parent stepping into that water, what is there is not an ideology. It is the wish to keep a child alive.

Imagine living there, not a short visit. Not a guided walk through a building. Days when you cannot speak to the world. A job assigned to you. No honest talk with a neighbor. Having to teach your child to criticize a friend. Watching a song from outside, and knowing your family could be pulled under. Would you want to live in a country on those terms? Coming to look and going home is not the same as staying.
A country people line up to enter and a country people leave even if they may be shot are not the same “equality.” The voices of defectors are a record of that difference, written on the body.

Scripture says,
“You will know the truth, and the truth will set you free.” (John 8:32)
In North Korea, both truth and freedom have been taken away. Knowledge is what remains, and that is where people begin to leave the lie.
If you say socialism or communism is good, first imagine living there yourself.
What kind of society should human beings live in?

title: Communism and Socialism: What the Words Mean, and Why Reality Diverged
previewText:
Marx’s idea, and the stage theory that came later
 
In the nineteenth century, Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels did not draw a strict line between “socialism” and “communism.” What they cared about was

blocks.text: Marx’s idea, and the stage theory that came later

In the nineteenth century, Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels did not draw a strict line between “socialism” and “communism.” What they cared about was this: factories, land, and machines, the means of production, should not be privately owned. Society should own them. 

The end point was a society with no classes and no state, where each person works according to ability and receives according to need.

Even the “dictatorship of the proletariat” in the middle was meant as a transition. The working class as a whole would hold down the old ruling class. It was not a design for a permanent one-party rule by professional revolutionaries.
Marx wrote little about how to build a state in practice.
The two-stage theory that later became common is mainly a Lenin-era reading. Drawing on Marx’s Critique of the Gotha Programme (1875), the usual textbook split looks like this.
Marx’s definition
First phase of the society after capitalism: the means of production are held in common. Goods are distributed according to work. Differences in ability still show up as differences in income.
Higher phase: after productive power is high enough, classes disappear. Goods go according to need.
Marx did not call the first phase “socialism” and the higher phase “communism.”
Lenin’s definition, and what came after
Socialism (lower stage): Marx’s first phase, renamed. Later writers added that the state remains in this stage, and they folded Marx’s separate idea of the dictatorship of the proletariat into it.
The Soviet Union said it was building this. China still says it is only in the primary stage of socialism, not a finished socialist society.
Communism (higher stage): Marx’s higher phase, renamed. Later writers added that the state withers away and money exchange ends. No country has ever reached it.

In everyday speech, socialism often means welfare and redistribution, and communism often means one-party planned economies. In the theory, the core questions are how complete equality is, and whether the state, classes, and private ownership remain or vanish.
What history actually produced was not the ideal, but Leninist dictatorship
Marx’s end point was never reached.

The people who built states were Lenin and those after him. A small vanguard party, democratic centralism inside the party, a secret police, and the crushing of opposition: that is where “the dictatorship of a class” became “the dictatorship of a party.” Stalin completed that party dictatorship. The state did not fade. It grew.

So the regimes later called communist states were not Marx’s destination. They froze a transition that was supposed to be temporary. They called themselves socialist states. The system was a party standing above the state. China belongs to this line.
What China says officially

The Chinese Communist Party’s constitution still names communism as its highest ideal and final goal. At the same time it says China is in the “primary stage of socialism,” that this stage will last a long time, and that markets and private firms are allowed in order to develop productive forces.
It calls this “socialism with Chinese characteristics” and a “socialist market economy.”

Under Xi Jinping, communism is still restated as the highest ideal, but the near-term goals are basic socialist modernization by 2035 and a “great modern socialist country” by mid-century. “Common prosperity” is also a slogan, with the repeated caveat that it does not mean uniform equality.
China itself admits it is not communist yet, and that even its socialism is immature.
It still does not meet Marx’s ideal

The “primary stage” label cannot hide what is missing.
Private firms and privately owned homes are back, and so are many billionaires. Official Chinese figures still put the private sector above 60 percent of GDP.

In 2025, disposable income per person was about 103,778 yuan in the top group and about 10,150 yuan in the bottom group, a gap of about ten times. Extreme poverty fell, but through growth that let some get rich first, not through a classless order. What remains is a deep economic divide.

The state is stronger, not fading.
Party rule is in the constitution, and elections cannot change who holds power. Churches, mosques, and temples that will not submit to the Party are restricted, raided, or driven underground.
Under Mao, political campaigns and the Great Leap Forward killed tens of millions. That record is the opposite of a state that was supposed to wither away.

Deng let some get rich first and output rose, but the result looks like capitalism under the Party. The Soviet Union kept the plan and fell. China used the market and survived. Neither ended classes or the state. That path is Lenin’s party dictatorship, not Marx’s communism.
What people call “socialism” or “communism” in the United States and South Korea
Neither country has nationalized the economy or abolished elections. Private firms and private property remain. That does not make the direction harmless.
In the United States, Democratic Socialists already sit in Congress and run major city halls, and they use the word without apology.
They want the state to seize the commanding heights of health care, housing, energy, and industry, and to tax private wealth to fund that control.

Their platform also aims to abolish the Senate and fold the presidency and the courts under Congress. That is not full one-party rule yet. It is a plan to trap more of the economy and more political power inside the state, a trade that elsewhere raised costs and made government almost impossible to remove.

In South Korea the claim covers more than welfare. It includes rewriting the justice system, laws that favor the governing camp, tighter speech rules, and state pressure on religious groups treated as political problems.
Those now in office are using the legislature and the executive to change the courts, the press, and the churches that are supposed to limit power.

This is not Marx’s classless society. It is the older pattern: promise fairness, weaken the checks, leave more power in fewer hands. That is how the Soviet Union moved toward dictatorship, even though these countries still start from elections and markets.
Conclusion
For Marx, socialism was a transition: shared ownership of production, pay according to work. Communism was the end he wrote down: no state, no classes, no money, and goods according to need.
No government that took power in that name arrived there. Lenin built a party dictatorship. Stalin and the Chinese Communist Party made that “temporary” stage permanent.
China still calls itself the primary stage of socialism, while it keeps private capital, billionaires, and a stronger party-state. It meets neither of Marx’s tests.

In South Korea and the United States the same words do not mean shared property or the end of the state. Those in office, or those bidding for office, are trying to pull courts, law, speech, and religion under political control. The United States and South Korea are not one-party states. The risk is still the same pattern: weaker checks, more power in fewer hands.
People who praise the slogan often skip what followed it: dictatorship, famine, political killing, and the policing of faith and speech.

title: Two Political Prosecutions, Two Postures: Rev. Sun Myung Moon Then, Dr. Hak Ja Han Now
previewText:
Forty-four years separate the two criminal cases that have most tested the Unification movement against state power. In 1981 the U.S. government indicted Rev. Sun Myung Moon.
On August 31, 2026, the

blocks.text: Forty-four years separate the two criminal cases that have most tested the Unification movement against state power. In 1981 the U.S. government indicted Rev. Sun Myung Moon.

On August 31, 2026, the Seoul Central District Court handed down a first-instance verdict against his widow, Dr. Hak Ja Han, and sentenced her to two years in prison. The charges differ. So does the answer the movement has given.
1981: they did not stay silent

They did not stay silent, and they did not accept the charges. From the day of the indictment they treated it as an attack on the church itself and ran an organized public, legal, and interfaith campaign.
Immediate reaction, October 1981.

Rev. Moon was indicted on October 15, 1981, on tax-fraud and conspiracy counts involving interest and stock the government said was his personal income. Church officials immediately called the indictment "wholly without merit," a "religious witch hunt," and harassment of a minority religion. U.S. church president Mose Durst said it had "no merit and no substance whatsoever." Rev. Moon's lawyer said the same.
Rev. Moon flew back from Korea to face arraignment rather than stay abroad.

On October 22 he pleaded not guilty. The same day the church staged a large, planned rally across from the courthouse in Foley Square. More than 5,000 supporters sang patriotic songs; Rev. Moon spoke and framed the case as racial and religious bigotry: he would not be there, he said, if his skin were white and his religion Presbyterian.
Durst called him "the most moral man in America." The speech was later reprinted as a full-page New York Times advertisement.
Legal and public posture.

They posted large bail bonds through church-related entities, surrendered Rev. Moon's passport with a limited exception for a Korea trip, and fought the case in court as a matter of whether funds in his name were church assets held in trust rather than personal income.

After conviction in May 1982 they continued to insist he would be "fully vindicated" and described him as "the most abused and misunderstood religious leader of the 20th century." They appealed through the courts; the Supreme Court declined review in 1984.
PR and coalition campaign, especially 1984 to 1985, while he was in prison.
This was not a quiet legal defense.

The U.S. church mailed booklets, letters, and videotapes to roughly 300,000 Christian leaders and collected petitions. They hired outside help, including a PR firm and high-profile legal names such as Laurence Tribe in later stages, and built a coalition that included Jerry Falwell, Joseph Lowery, Harvey Cox, Eugene McCarthy, elements of the ACLU, and others who cast the case as a religious-liberty threat.

Newspaper ads compared the tax issues to those of other public figures. After Rev. Moon's release in August 1985, clergy and civil-rights figures held events calling the prosecution persecution and asking for a pardon.
Summary of actions.

Public denial and persecution framing from day one. Mass rally at arraignment and paid newspaper ads. Full criminal defense and appeals. Nationwide mailing and petition drive to clergy. Interfaith and political coalition work, and later professional PR and lobbying around the conviction and imprisonment.

They never treated the indictment as something to accept quietly. They contested the facts in court and contested the motive in public, arguing that holding church money in the founder's name was comparable to practices in other religions and that the case was selective. The government, and the jury, disagreed; the church's public line did not change.
2026: a first-instance verdict, and a quieter answer
Dr. Han is not guilty of the crimes attributed to her.

She has denied authorizing or participating in any unlawful activity throughout. August 31 was a first-instance ruling, not a final one. Her legal representatives have said they will appeal, and the organization has stated that it cannot accept the ruling.

The movement's public voice, however, has been softer than the record of 1981 would suggest. When the arrest warrant was issued in September 2025, the church said it humbly accepted the court's decision and apologized for causing concern. On the day of the verdict it said it deeply apologizes for causing "big concerns and disappointment to the people," and only then said it would appeal. Apology preceded defense. In 1982 there was no apology at all.
What is actually at issue

The other difference lies in the structure of the case. What is at issue is conduct in which a church executive's private interest was involved (though not every executive charged in this case acted out of private interest). The person who committed the wrongdoing was that executive.
The question, therefore, narrows to a single point: did Dr. Han know, and was she briefed and did she approve?

What was offered on that point was the testimony of the executive who committed the wrongdoing. No core physical evidence establishing it was presented in court. Prosecutors sought thirteen years; the sentence was two. That gap says something quiet about where the proof stood.

So the questions are not the same as in 1981. 
Then, the issue was whether funds in the founder's name were his or the church's, a question that treated leader and institution as one. Now, the issue is what a leader could have known about a subordinate's acts, a question that pulls the two apart. Different questions call for different courtroom strategies.
But a difference in legal strategy is not the same as a difference in posture. And the posture is plainly different.

Dr. Han has walked the world as the Mother of Peace and has given her life to the work of world peace. That person has now been convicted without core physical evidence. This is not the problem of one spiritual leader.
In 1981, clergy of other faiths did not treat Rev. Moon's prosecution as someone else's affair.

They felt that they could be next, and that is why people of incompatible theologies stood on the same platform. Jerry Falwell and figures associated with the ACLU on the same side was not something any other issue could have produced. What joined them was not sympathy for the Unification Church. It was the imagination to see that when one faith is targeted, the next target is your own.

Dr. Han is not the only religious leader in Korea currently answering to prosecutors, and the pattern of who is being investigated has not gone unnoticed by believers outside her church. This is the moment for the religious world to speak with one voice. This is the moment to stand with her.
In 1981 the movement understood that a case fought only in the courtroom is a case half fought. The appeal ahead will test whether that understanding still holds.

title: Former U.S. Ambassador Says Dr. Hak Ja Han Verdict Reflects a "Weaponized" Justice System
previewText: Randy Evans, former U.S. Ambassador to Luxembourg, told Family Federation USA president Damian Dunkley that South Korea's prosecution of the church's leader follows a pattern of politically driven

blocks.text: Randy Evans, former U.S. Ambassador to Luxembourg, told Family Federation USA president Damian Dunkley that South Korea's prosecution of the church's leader follows a pattern of politically driven enforcement that has already reached American citizens.
The Verdict

A Seoul court sentenced Dr. Hak Ja Han, the 83-year-old leader of the Family Federation for World Peace and Unification, to two years in prison on August 31 over political funding and bribery allegations tied to influence-seeking with the administration of former President Yoon Suk Yeol. Prosecutors had sought 13 years.

Days before the ruling, Evans, now a visiting professor of law at Ave Maria School of Law in Naples, Florida, recorded an extended interview with Dunkley arguing that the case rested on association rather than evidence.
"Since President Lee took office in South Korea, we have seen a steady weaponization of the government to attack what he perceives to be political enemies."
It Started Before the Family Federation

Evans argued the sequence matters. The first target, he said, was a conservative Protestant pastor, Son Hyun-bo, prosecuted under South Korea's election law for remarks delivered in a sermon and later released with a suspended sentence.

Once that succeeded, Evans said, the approach spread: anyone affiliated with a church who opposed the government could be accused, indicted, convicted, and imprisoned. He described it as an effort to divide faith communities and remove them one at a time.
The Raids

Authorities conducted repeated search-and-seizure operations against the church, its institutions, and Dr. Hak Ja Han's residence, including a July 2025 operation involving more than 1,000 officers. Evans said he was in Korea during one raid.
Asked by Dunkley whether U.S. judges would approve warrants to search the same premises two or three times, Evans said no, citing First Amendment protections.

"Long ago the prosecutions here crossed a very clear boundary.
But that's when it became so obvious what was happening."
Guilt by Association

A former chief of staff received eight months, suspended for two years. Dr. Hak Ja Han faced a demand of 13 years. Dunkley asked why the spiritual leader would draw the heavier penalty when prosecutors had not shown direct involvement.

"Guilty by association. They haven't been able to prove she had anything to do with any of this stuff directly. Why would the leader of a global movement get more time than the pastor of a local church? If the person making that decision is worried about relative political power, is that not enough proof itself?"
Evans put the underlying charge in plainer terms, saying the church backed a candidate who lost and was being accused of picking the wrong horse in the last race.

He also rejected the principle of holding a faith leader responsible for the conduct of members, noting that Christ had Judas but was not crucified for Judas's sins. Pressed on what the prosecution was ultimately about, Evans said the charges would disappear if Dr. Hak Ja Han withdrew from public life and endorsed the government.

"They'd leave her alone tomorrow if she just quit. This isn't about what
she's done. This is about who she is."
Where Power Comes From

Evans framed the dispute as a disagreement about the origin of rights, contrasting a system in which liberties come from God and cannot be removed with one in which the state is the source of authority.

"What he's done is to weaponize the government in a way to say: the state
has the power to prevent you from worshiping in the way you want to
worship."

He pointed to Japan as evidence that advanced democracies are not exempt. Courts there ordered the dissolution of the Unification Church, and Evans described the consequences in concrete terms: churches padlocked, hymnals seized, cemeteries taken.

"Imagine any of us having the remains of our fathers and our mothers and
our sisters and our ancestors seized by the government and put up for
public sale."

He said the objection he most often hears is that such things happen only in countries without established legal protections. His answer was that Japan and South Korea are advanced democracies and treaty allies of the United States.
An American Ambassador Indicted

Dunkley raised the risk of speaking publicly at all, noting he was not supposed to be discussing the subject. Evans agreed the risks were serious, citing Morse Tan, a former U.S. ambassador-at-large who had his passport withheld and was indicted in South Korea on defamation charges.
"If they're willing to take the passport and arrest and indict a former United States ambassador, I don't want to diminish the threat."
Members of Congress have written to South Korea's ambassador in Washington raising concerns about freedom of expression and due process in Tan's case.
Isolation and Faith
Dr. Hak Ja Han has been transferred repeatedly between a detention center and hospital for treatment of a heart condition, injuries from a fall, and glaucoma.
Evans said confinement serves a purpose beyond punishment: separating a leader from her family, friends, and fellow believers in the belief that isolation will break her faith.
"Locking an 83-year-old grandmother in a detention facility that results in her being repeatedly hospitalized is cruel. But they're not going to win. They nailed Christ to a cross and they lost."

Asked what members should do if the sentence proved harsh, Evans offered three things: pray, stay publicly engaged, and reject apathy, which he called the condition that allows churches to be dissolved.
On the prospect of dissolution proceedings against the Family Federation itself, he was direct.
"I defy any power on planet Earth to dissolve or eliminate the church. It's not going to happen."
Dunkley closed by inviting members to a prayer gathering in Las Vegas on August 30, timed to the August 31 first-instance verdict against Dr. Han in Seoul.
The venue is the International Peace Education Center, a facility he said was purchased and built by Rev. Sun Myung Moon and Dr. Hak Ja Han for the purpose of gathering to pray for world peace.

Dunkley said participants would move outside the building to pray under the open sky, and framed the gathering as directed not only at her case but at religious freedom broadly. It marked the closing day of a period of daily prayer and fasting that members had observed worldwide in the weeks leading up to the verdict.

title: South Korean media publishes portions of the ruling on Dr. Hak Ja Han
previewText: Sisa Journal, a South Korean outlet, has published an article quoting portions of the first-instance ruling handed down by the judges on August 31 in the case concerning Unification Church Dr. Hak Ja

blocks.text:
Sisa Journal, a South Korean outlet, has published an article quoting portions of the first-instance ruling handed down by the judges on August 31 in the case concerning Unification Church Dr. Hak Ja Han.   

The following is an English translation of the original Korean-language article.


"Church-state collusion": Unification Church leader Han Hak-ja sentenced to 2 years in prison; her "right-hand man" chief of staff gets a suspended sentence
By Kim Hyun-ji (metaxy@sisajournal.com) | Sisa Journal | 2026.08.31

Named as the apex of the illegal 100 million won political funds and luxury-goods lobbying allegations
 "They committed the offenses in expectation of state support for the Unification Church and expanded political influence"

Han Hak-ja, leader of the Unification Church, who was indicted and detained as the central figure in the church-state collusion allegations surrounding the Yoon Suk-yeol government, was sentenced to two years in prison at first instance.

On the afternoon of the 31st, the Seoul Central District Court's Criminal Division 27 (presiding judge Woo In-sung) sentenced Han to one year in prison on charges of violating the Political Funds Act, and one year in prison on charges of violating the Act on the Aggravated Punishment of Specific Economic Crimes (embezzlement).

The court sentenced Jung Won-ju, Han's former chief of staff and the so-called "shadow power broker," who was indicted alongside her, to eight months in prison suspended for two years on the Political Funds Act charge, and eight months in prison suspended for two years on the charges of violating the Improper Solicitation and Graft Act and embezzlement.

Yoon Young-ho, the former Unification Church headquarters director whose testimony triggered the investigation, was sentenced to six months in prison. Yoon's spouse, identified only by the surname Lee, was sentenced to six months in prison suspended for one year.

Han is accused of conspiring with Jung and Yoon around January 2022, before the 20th presidential election, to deliver 100 million won (roughly $72,000) in political funds to Kwon Seong-dong, a former People Power Party lawmaker aligned with Yoon Suk-yeol, and of donating 144 million won (roughly $104,000) in Unification Church organizational funds to People Power Party lawmakers and others around March and April of that year, in violation of the Political Funds Act.

Han, the others, and Lee are also accused of passing an expensive necklace and a Chanel bag to First Lady Kim Keon-hee around July 2022 through the shaman known as "Geonjin beopsa," Jeon Seong-bae, while soliciting favors on matters pending before the church, in violation of the Improper Solicitation and Graft Act. They are further accused of embezzling Unification Church funds to purchase the high-value items.
Han and Jung were also accused of instructing Yoon to destroy evidence after receiving information in October 2022 about an investigation into overseas casino gambling in Las Vegas.
"They saw it as a chance to expand the church on the strength of its financial power"

The court explained that according to the record, Yoon reported to Han with Jung present, and that Jung did not simply sit in on the meetings but expressed views on important matters, so a conspiracy among them regarding the 100 million won delivered to Kwon was established.

Most of the charges involving split donations to politicians were also found guilty. The court stated that after prior consultation among Han, Jung, and Yoon, Han made remarks at a special assembly supporting Yoon Suk-yeol, who was then a candidate, and that donations to the People Power Party were made immediately after receiving Han's approval. The court also found that the expensive necklace and other items were delivered to Kim Keon-hee with Han's approval for the purpose of obtaining support for Unification Church events.

The court said of Han and the others that they had viewed the situation as an opportunity to expand the church on the strength of its financial power, and had committed the offenses in the expectation that if a government led by a presidential candidate friendly to the Unification Church took office, they would receive state support for church-related policy and expanded political influence. Colluding with political forces in a manner unrelated to missionary work or education, the court said, was not a light offense. Regarding Han in particular, the court said that considering her status and role in the Unification Church and her attitude of shifting responsibility onto Yoon, a custodial sentence was unavoidable.

The court did, however, treat as mitigating factors the fact that Yoon appeared to have planned the offenses overall, and that Han acted for the purpose of expanding the church and its political influence rather than for personal gain. The court said there were aspects making it difficult to regard the policies the Unification Church pursued as improper in themselves, and that it had also taken into account Han's full repayment of the embezzled amount, the church's expressed wish that she not be punished, and her apparent efforts toward world peace as a religious leader.

Of Jung, the court said that despite holding a position involved in major decision-making, he had minimized his own role by characterizing himself as nothing more than an aide. The court added that it had considered that he did not lead the planning or execution of the offenses and was involved by carrying out Han's instructions and approved matters. Regarding Yoon and Lee, the former finance bureau director, the court said their culpability was not light, but that it had taken into account their cooperation in establishing the substantive truth despite tangible and intangible pressure from the Unification Church side.

The court dismissed the prosecution on the charges of instigating destruction of evidence and occupational embezzlement against Han and the others, on the grounds that those charges were unrelated to the scope of investigation authorized under the special counsel law.
Han Hak-ja: "I do not covet power with money"

The special counsel team led by Min Joong-ki, which investigated allegations involving Kim Keon-hee, asked the court at the closing hearing on the 10th of last month to sentence Han to 13 years in prison. It sought 10 years for Jung and three years and six months for Yoon, and three years for Lee. The special counsel team characterized the case as a serious crime that directly violated the constitutional principle of separation of religion and politics and damaged representative democracy.
Han's side argued that all of the offenses were personal deviations by Yoon. In her final statement, Han denied the charges outright, saying she does not covet power with money.

Yoon countered that Han had given instructions and granted approval. Yoon was separately indicted on charges of delivering money and goods to Kim Keon-hee and Kwon, and has had a sentence of one year and six months in prison confirmed by the Supreme Court. Kwon also had a sentence of two years in prison and forfeiture of 100 million won confirmed by the Supreme Court on the 16th of last month, a penalty that costs him his parliamentary seat.

Han is separately standing trial at first instance alongside Kim Keon-hee and others in connection with allegations that Unification Church members joined the People Power Party en masse in November 2022. The joint prosecution-police investigation headquarters, led by senior prosecutor Kim Tae-hoon, also announced on the 31st that it had detected additional charges including occupational embezzlement and had indicted Han without detention.

Han, who was indicted and detained last October, has been staying in a hospital after receiving a suspension of execution of her detention on grounds of deteriorating health. The suspension runs until 6 p.m. on September 2.

After the first-instance ruling, the Unification Church issued a statement saying it would use the occasion to further establish an emergency reform system covering overall church operations, and would comprehensively overhaul its decision-making structure, financial execution processes, internal checks and oversight systems, and its compliance review and record management systems for external activities. The church said it trusts the rule of law in the Republic of Korea and respects judicial procedure, while stating that it finds it impossible to accept the first-instance ruling's finding that Han Hak-ja instructed the conduct or approved it while aware of an unlawful purpose. It indicated it will appeal.

This article is an English translation of an article published in Sisa Journal. Credit belongs to Sisa Journal.

title: South Korea Wants the Power to Close and Control Churches
previewText:
An 83-year-old woman was wheeled into the Seoul Central District Court on Monday morning in hospital clothes and a mask, and left with a two-year prison sentence.
On August 31, 2026, the court

blocks.text: An 83-year-old woman was wheeled into the Seoul Central District Court on Monday morning in hospital clothes and a mask, and left with a two-year prison sentence.

On August 31, 2026, the court convicted Hak Ja Han — leader of the Family Federation for World Peace and Unification, long known as the Unification Church — on political funds and anti-graft counts arising from the 2022 election period.

The court found she was involved in the delivery of 100 million won, about $73,000, to then–People Power Party floor leader Kweon Seong-dong, and in the use of church money for luxury gifts to former first lady Kim Keon Hee.
Prosecutors had asked for thirteen years.

Sociologist Massimo Introvigne, editor-in-chief of Bitter Winter and founder of the Center for Studies on New Religions, noted that the donations and gifts cited in the decision total under $250,000, and that the case rests on the shifting testimony of a former executive expelled from the movement; his verdict on the ruling is unambiguous — "Mother Han is innocent and should have been acquitted."

Co-defendants drew far less: a former chief of staff eight months suspended for two years, former global headquarters head Yun Young-ho six months, a former finance director six months suspended for one year.
The Family Federation's U.S. affiliate said Han has consistently denied authorizing any unlawful act and that her lawyers will appeal.

Two separate legal objects — a special-counsel sentence and a wrap-up briefing — landed on the same morning. Treating them as one story is how a two-year term begins to feel like permission to close a church.
Because what is actually being built is not one verdict. It is three tools.
Tool One: The Pulpit

Article 85 of the Public Official Election Act bars campaigning inside religious organizations. The Constitutional Court upheld it in 2024. Introvigne's point is not that the statute is illegitimate — it is that the statute was traditionally applied with restraint, and that clergy who violated it were historically punished with small fines.

Pastor Son Hyun-bo of Busan's Segero Presbyterian Church, one of Korea's largest congregations, was arrested on September 8, 2025, and accused of election-law violations after telling his congregation that certain candidates carried an anti-Christian agenda.
He spent 143 days in detention before the Busan District Court's 6th Criminal Division, on January 30, 2026, sentenced him to six months suspended for one year and ordered his release.

On release he thanked Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Vice President J.D. Vance for raising his case, and said separation of church and state means the state cannot interfere with a church's worship and faith.9 He is appealing.

The escalation did not stop with his release. Segero's associate pastor Kim Bok-yeon is now being prosecuted under the same act for leading a prayer at a church gathering — the indictment citing his use of a microphone and prayer topics displayed on a screen.
That is the pattern the editor of this file should sit with: the law did not change. Its enforcement did.
Tool Two: The Membership Roll
Shincheonji is not the Family Federation. Its theology and its standing in Korea are different, and folding the two into one caption is precisely how a method becomes reusable.

Lee Man-hee, 95, Shincheonji's founder, was arrested on June 24, 2026, and indicted from detention on June 30 under Article 42 of the Political Parties Act, which forbids compelling anyone to join or leave a party against his own free will.

Investigators allege at least 56,472 members were enrolled in the People Power Party between 2021 and 2024 under innocuous cover names such as a "Pilates Project." The church denies the accusations and says it has about 200,000 followers.

If organized coercion is proved at trial, that is ordinary criminal law, and nothing in an honest account requires denying the possibility. Two things travel with the charge anyway. Lee has not been convicted. And on the day of the indictment, Justice Minister Jeong Seong-ho announced it on social media, wrote that strict punishment was inevitable, and closed the post by quoting Matthew 7:15 — "Beware of false prophets." Introvigne called that prejudging the outcome before trial.
On January 9, 2026, independent Rep. Choi Hyuk-jin and eleven lawmakers submitted Civil Code Amendment Bill No. 2215932, which Korean media promptly nicknamed the Church Dissolution Act.

Introvigne reports that Choi, announcing the bill, explicitly named the Unification Church and Shincheonji as the groups needing dissolution. The bill would let the government audit, suspend, and dissolve religious corporations and absorb their assets into public ownership. Korean reporting describes it the same way: permits revoked and assets seized where a religious body is judged to have interfered in politics and harmed the public interest in violation of election law.

And in Bitter Winter's reading of the draft text, the bill would allow dissolution where a representative or director has been sentenced to prison for repeated acts related to the organization. If that reading is right, August 31 is not an atmosphere. It is a trigger.
Tool Three: Existence

This is the one the verdict now sits beside. A leader can be guilty. A church is not the same object as a leader.  On December 9, 2025, President Lee Jae-myung told a Cabinet meeting that individuals are sanctioned when they commit crimes, and that likewise a corporation committing acts that violate the Constitution and the law should be dissolved.

Minister of Government Legislation Cho Won-cheol answered that dissolution of a religious body is not first a constitutional question but an application of Civil Act Article 38 — while stressing that such action requires clear confirmation of wrongdoing.

Article 38 is not a court process. A minister revokes the permit. Bitter Winter, reading the draft text of the pending Civil Code bill, reports that dissolution would be available where a representative or director has been sentenced to prison for repeated acts related to the organization — tying the power directly to a criminal sentence against a leader.
And the bill routes a dissolved religious corporation's assets into public ownership, not to creditors or successors.
Convict the leader; a ministry cancels the charter; the property goes to the state. On that path, no judge decides whether a church continues to exist.

That bill is real and pending. On January 9, 2026, independent Rep. Choi Hyuk-jin and eleven lawmakers submitted Civil Code Amendment Bill No. 2215932, which Korean media promptly nicknamed the Church Dissolution Act; Introvigne reports that Choi, announcing it, explicitly named the Unification Church and Shincheonji as the groups needing dissolution.

Korean reporting describes the same machinery: permits revoked and assets seized where a religious body is judged to have interfered in politics and harmed the public interest in violation of election law.
Why mainstream churches are not reassured

They can read a statute. Conservative Protestant leaders who belong to neither group under investigation protested at the National Assembly. The World Evangelical Alliance warned on June 1 that terms such as "political involvement" are undefined, that administrators could investigate, suspend and dissolve religious bodies and route their assets to the treasury, and that ICCPR standards require compelling justification, an independent judicial process, and strict proportionality.

The precedent Seoul cites cuts the other way. Korean officials have invoked Japan's dissolution of the Unification Church as a model — a decision four UN Special Rapporteurs criticized on October 3, 2025, warning that the "public welfare" concept it rested on is vague and open-ended and may permit restrictions exceeding what the ICCPR allows. Japan, at least, had to go to a court. Under Article 38, the first move in Korea would not.
What is firm, and what is not

A first-instance sentence of two years against Han, under appeal. Twenty-six billion won seized and 32 people indicted by a joint headquarters. Lee Man-hee indicted and detained, with no verdict. Son Hyun-bo sentenced to six months suspended, released, appealing. Bill 2215932 filed and pending. Dissolution of the Family Federation inside Korea: ordered as a subject of study by the President, ordered by no court.you're

South Korea can prosecute bribery. It can enforce an election code. It can charge coerced party enrollment. None of that requires a new power, and the criticism here is not that the statutes exist — it is that a law once enforced with fines is now enforced with cells, and that a Civil Code provision written for defunct foundations is being read as a licence to end churches.

A person can be convicted. A church is not a person, and a congregation is not a co-defendant. If the Republic of Korea wants the authority to decide which religions may continue to exist, that authority should be debated as itself, in the National Assembly, in daylight — not carried in on the atmosphere of a two-year sentence that never decided it.

title: 한국의 반신앙 광란극 이재명, '악랄한' 교회 - 압수수색으로 트럼프를 곤혹스럽게 하다
previewText:
월요일, 종교의 자유를 향한 끝없는 행진의 다음 단계가 세계평화통일가정연합의 공동 창설자이자 세계 총재인 한학자 총재에게 가해진다.
원문: 와싱턴 타임즈 │ 랜디 에번스│2026년 8월 26일
 
【OPINION】
이는

blocks.text: 월요일, 종교의 자유를 향한 끝없는 행진의 다음 단계가 세계평화통일가정연합의 공동 창설자이자 세계 총재인 한학자 총재에게 가해진다.
원문: 와싱턴 타임즈 │ 랜디 에번스│2026년 8월 26일
【OPINION】
이는 이재명 대통령이 국내 종교계에서 자신의 정적으로 간주하는 이들을 상대로 벌여온 조직적 박해의 또 하나의 이정표다.
이 대통령의 정적을 향한 보복은 한 총재나 가정연합에서 시작된 것이 아니며, 역사가 보여주듯 그녀의 유죄 판결로 끝나지도 않을 것이다. 그것은 한 총재와 가정연합을 훨씬 넘어, 이 대통령이 자신의 정치 권력을 위협한다고 여기는 모든 종교와 신앙에 미치고 있다.
이 대통령의 행보는 정치적 반대 세력, 특히 교회와 신앙인을 억누르기 위해 정부의 모든 권한을 동원할 의사가 있는지에 대한 어떠한 합리적 의심도 남기지 않는다.
일련의 사건의 시간 순서가 그 목적을 뒷받침한다.
이제 세계가 아는 바와 같이, 이 정부는 2025년 7월 가정연합을 포함한 한국 내 여러 교회에 대한 '수사관'과 압수수색으로 시작했으며, 부산 세계로교회(장로교)에 대한 수사도 계속되고 있다.
이 사안이 국제적으로 부각된 것은 트럼프 대통령이 2025년 8월 25일 이 대통령과의 회담 직전에 "교회에 대한 악랄한 압수수색"이라는 보도를 공개적으로 언급했을 때였다.
트럼프 대통령의 우려에도 불구하고, 이 정부는 9월 손현보 목사를 구속했다. 손 목사는 한 총재나 가정연합과 아무런 관련이 없다. 그는 세계로교회 담임목사이자 저명한 보수 기독교 활동가였다.
종교계의 어떠한 도전도 억누르려는 이 대통령의 집착을 고려하면 놀랄 일도 아니지만, 손 목사는 선거법 위반 혐의로 기소되었다. 이 기소는 교회 활동과 얽힌 정치적 발언을 문제 삼아 다른 종교 기관과 지도자들을 박해하는 이 정부의 본보기가 되었다.
손 목사는 결국 5개월간 구금된 끝에 집행유예 판결을 받았다.
이 대통령의 구상은 2025년 9월 터닝포인트USA의 찰리 커크가 한국을 방문하면서 검증대에 올랐다. 커크는 '빌드업 코리아 2025'라는 이틀간의 콘퍼런스에서 주요 연사로 나섰다.
커크는 기독교, 공산주의, 자유, 보수 정치, 그리고 자신이 한국에서 벌어지는 신앙에 대한 정치적 탄압이라고 본 사안에 대해 발언했다.
실제로 커크는 자신의 우려를 마코 루비오 국무장관에게 전달했고, 루비오 장관은 커크의 비극적인 암살 이후 추모식에서 그 내용을 세계에 전했다. "저는 지금 한국에 있습니다. 돌아가면 루비오 장관에게 전하고 싶은 우려가 많습니다."
이 대통령은 자신이 위협으로 여긴 신앙인과 교회를 향한 행동이 드러났음에도 흔들리지 않았다. 2025년 9월, 이 정부의 검찰은 당시 82세였던 가정연합 지도자 한 총재를 뇌물, 정치자금, 기타 선거 관련 혐의로 구속했다.
과거 통일교로 알려졌던 가정연합은 워싱턴타임스를 포함한 사업체들을 창설하고 운영해왔다.
2025년 7월부터 12월까지 한국 당국은 한 총재의 교단, 자택, 관련 기관을 상대로 최소 네 차례의 압수수색을 실시했다.
보도에 따르면 2025년 7월 작전에는 1,000명이 넘는 수사관이 투입되었고 약 15시간이 소요되었다.
아무런 제동 없이, 2025년 말까지 이 정부는 초점을 신앙인 개인에 대한 혐의에서 종교 기관 자체로 옮겨갔다. 이 대통령은 한국에서 종교적 반대 세력을 제거하려는 운동의 일환으로, 종교법인 처리와 관련해 일본을 포함한 외국의 제도를 검토하라고 정부 관계자들에게 지시하기까지 했다.
1월에 이르러 이 대통령의 정책은 단순한 기소를 넘어, 그가 "불법적 정치 관여"로 규정한 행위를 근거로 종교 단체를 해산시킬 명분을 만드는 쪽으로 무게가 옮겨갔다.
당연하게도 법원은 1월 손 목사에게 유죄를 선고했다. 형량은 징역 6개월, 집행유예 1년이었다.
다음으로 이 정부는 신천지예수교회 신자들의 조직적인 정당 가입 의혹에 대한 수사에 착수했다. 창설자 이만희 씨(95)는 6월에 체포되었다. 정부는 수만 명의 신자가 당내 정치에 영향을 미치기 위해 동원되었다고 주장했다.
그사이 이 대통령의 의도는 드러났다. 지난달 손 목사는 이 문제를 직접 워싱턴으로 가져가 백악관에서 트럼프 대통령과 만나 종교의 자유와 해산 관련 법안에 대한 우려를 전달했다. 이 정부는 아무것도 바꾸지 않았다.
월요일 한 총재의 선고를 앞두고, 이 정부는 입법 추진을 계속하고 있다. 그것은 손 목사나 한 총재 같은 종교 지도자의 구금, 기소, 유죄 판결에 그치지 않고, 궁극적으로는 이 대통령이 자신의 정치 권력에 위협이 된다고 판단하는 모든 종교 단체와 개인을 제거할 수 있게 하는 것이다.
찰리 커크가 옳았다.
한국이 형사법의 정당한 집행에서 정치적으로 미움받는 종교 단체에 대한 선별적 집행으로 넘어갔다는 데에는 거의 의문의 여지가 없다.
이러한 배경을 고려하면 한 총재의 판결과 그에 따른 형량에 놀랄 사람은 없을 것이다. 그것은 어떤 대가를 치르더라도 종교적 이견을 잠재우려는 정부의 꾸준한 행진의 또 한 걸음일 뿐이다.
한 총재와 가정연합에게 그 대가는 앞으로도 매우 현실적일 것이다. 그럼에도 정치 권력을 지키기 위해 강행되는 종교적 불관용이 신앙을 파괴한 적은 없다. 오히려 신앙을 더 강하게 만들 뿐이다. 그것은 언제나 진실이었고, 이번에도 그러할 것이다.
・랜디 에번스는 에이브 마리아 로스쿨 객원교수다. 제23대 주룩셈부르크 미국 대사를 지냈다.

title: 韓国の「反信仰」の狂騒曲ー李在明大統領、「悪質な」教会家宅捜索でトランプ氏を困惑させる
previewText:
月曜日、宗教の自由に対する終わりなき行進の次の一歩が、世界平和統一家庭連合の共同創設者であり世界会長である韓鶴子総裁に下される。

原文：ワシントンタイムズ │ランディ・エバンズ著 │ 2026年8月26日

blocks.text:
月曜日、宗教の自由に対する終わりなき行進の次の一歩が、世界平和統一家庭連合の共同創設者であり世界会長である韓鶴子総裁に下される。

原文：ワシントンタイムズ │ランディ・エバンズ著 │ 2026年8月26日
【OPINION】
これは、李在明大統領が国内の宗教界において自らの政敵と見なす人々に対して行ってきた組織的迫害の、また一つの節目である。
李氏の政敵に対する報復の追求は、韓総裁や家庭連合から始まったわけではなく、歴史が示す通り、彼女の有罪判決で終わるわけでもない。それは韓総裁と家庭連合をはるかに超え、李氏が自らの政治権力を脅かすと見なすあらゆる宗教と信仰に及んでいる。
李氏の行動は、政治的反対勢力、とりわけ教会や信仰者を抑え込むために政府の全権力を行使する意思があるかどうかについて、いかなる合理的疑いも残していない。
一連の出来事の時系列が、その目的を裏付けている。
すでに世界が知る通り、李政権は2025年7月、家庭連合を含む韓国内の多くの教会に対する「捜査官」と家宅捜索から始まり、釜山の世界路教会（長老派）への捜査も継続している。
この一件が国際的に可視化されたのは、トランプ大統領が2025年8月25日の李氏との会談の直前に、「教会への悪質な家宅捜索」に関する報道に公然と言及した時である。
トランプ氏の懸念にもかかわらず、李政権は9月にソン・ヒョンボ牧師を拘束した。ソン牧師は韓総裁や家庭連合とは関係がない。彼は世界路教会の主任牧師であり、著名な保守系キリスト教活動家であった。
宗教界からのいかなる挑戦も抑え込もうとする李氏の執着を考えれば当然のことだが、ソン牧師は公職選挙法違反で起訴された。この訴追は、教会活動と絡み合った政治的言論をめぐる違反容疑で他の宗教団体や指導者を迫害するための、李政権の雛形となった。
ソン牧師は最終的に5カ月間拘束された後、執行猶予付き判決を受けた。
李氏の計画は、2025年9月にターニング・ポイントUSAのチャーリー・カーク氏が訪韓した際、精査の目にさらされた。カーク氏は「Build Up Korea 2025」と題する2日間の会議で登壇者を務めた。
カーク氏はキリスト教、共産主義、自由、保守政治、そして自身が韓国における信仰への政治的弾圧と見なすものについて語った。
実際、カーク氏はその懸念をマルコ・ルビオ国務長官に伝えており、ルビオ氏はカーク氏の暗殺という悲劇の後の追悼式で、その内容を世界に向けて語った。「私は今韓国にいる。戻ったらルビオ長官に伝えたい懸念がたくさんある」
李氏は、自らが脅威と見なす信仰者や教会への行動が明るみに出ても動じなかった。2025年9月、李政権の検察は、当時82歳だった家庭連合指導者・韓総裁を、収賄、政治資金、その他の選挙関連の容疑で拘束した。
かつて統一教会として知られた家庭連合は、ワシントン・タイムズを含む事業体も創設・運営してきた。
2025年7月から12月にかけて、韓国当局は韓総裁の教団、住居、関連機関に対し少なくとも4回の捜索・押収を実施した。
報道によれば、2025年7月の作戦には1,000人を超える捜査員が動員され、約15時間に及んだ。
誰にも阻まれることなく、2025年末までに李政権は標的を信仰者個人への容疑から宗教団体そのものへと移した。李氏は韓国から宗教的反対勢力を一掃する運動の一環として、宗教法人への対処について日本を含む外国の制度を検討するよう政府当局者に指示するに至った。
1月には、李氏の政策は訴追にとどまらず、彼が「違法な政治関与」と見なすものを理由に宗教団体を解散させる根拠づくりへと比重を移していった。
当然のごとく、裁判所は1月にソン牧師に有罪判決を下した。量刑は懲役6カ月、執行猶予1年であった。
次に李政権は、新天地イエス教会の信者による組織的な政党入党をめぐる疑惑の捜査に着手した。創設者の李萬熙氏（95）は6月に逮捕された。政府は、数万人の信者が党内政治に影響を及ぼすために動員されたと主張した。
その間に、李氏の狙いは白日の下にさらされた。先月、ソン牧師はこの問題を直接ワシントンに持ち込み、ホワイトハウスでトランプ氏と会談して、宗教の自由と解散関連法案への懸念を訴えた。李政権は何も変えなかった。
月曜日に韓総裁の判決が言い渡されるのを前に、李政権は法整備の推進を続けている。それは、ソン牧師や韓総裁のような宗教指導者の拘束・訴追・有罪化にとどまらず、最終的には李氏が自らの政治権力への脅威と見なすあらゆる宗教団体や個人を排除することを可能にするものだ。
チャーリー・カークは正しかった。
韓国が刑事法の正当な執行から、政治的に疎まれた宗教団体への選別的執行へと移行したことは、ほとんど疑いの余地がない。
こうした背景を踏まえれば、韓総裁の判決とそれに伴う量刑に驚く者はいないはずだ。それは、いかなる代償を払っても宗教的異論を封じ込めようとする政府による、着実な行進の一歩にすぎない。

韓総裁と家庭連合にとって、その代償は今後も現実のものであり続けるだろう。それでもなお、政治権力を維持するために強行される宗教的不寛容が信仰を破壊したことはない。むしろ信仰を強めるだけである。それは常に真実であり、今回もそうなるだろう。

ランディ・エバンズはエイブ・マリア法科大学院客員教授。第23代駐ルクセンブルク大公国米国大使を務めた。

title: South Korea Detained a 95-Year-Old Religious Leader. The Heresy Label Silences Even Conservatives
previewText:
Signing up party members is a minor violation in South Korea. It is now grounds to hold an elderly man in custody before trial.
He arrived at the courthouse leaning on a cane, held up under both arms.

blocks.text: Signing up party members is a minor violation in South Korea. It is now grounds to hold an elderly man in custody before trial.
He arrived at the courthouse leaning on a cane, held up under both arms. Hours later, a Seoul judge sent him to a holding cell.

Lee Man-hee, born in 1931 and now 95, was taken into custody on June 24, 2026. The Seoul Central District Court issued an arrest warrant on suspicion of violating the Political Funds Act, citing a risk that he would destroy evidence.

Investigators allege he directed roughly 50,000 followers to register as dues-paying party members to influence the People Power Party's 2021 presidential primary and its 2024 general election nominations. Chosun Ilbo, citing legal sources, reported that 56,472 people were registered between July 2021 and January 2024.

Lee denied the allegations during questioning on June 4. Under Article 42 of the Political Funds Act, enrolling someone in a party carries a maximum penalty of two years in prison or a fine of up to 2 million won (about $1,300). The court rejected his petition for release on June 28.
What Shincheonji Actually Teaches
Lee founded Shincheonji Church of Jesus, the Temple of the Tabernacle of the Testimony, in 1984. The Korean name means "new heaven and new earth." The church claims roughly 200,000 members.
The central claim is not about divinity. It is about reading.

Lee is a man, not God. The church calls him the "Promised Pastor," the witness who saw the prophecies of Revelation come true and was sent to testify to what he saw. Twelve tribes, each sealed with 12,000 members, form the 144,000 of Revelation 7 and 14.
How the "Heresy" Label Gets Built

When mainstream Protestant denominations brand Shincheonji a heresy or a cult, the background is not purely theological. Reuters has noted that many mainstream Christian groups describe the church as a brainwashing sect.

The theological objection is real, and it is simple. For mainstream churches the Bible is finished and salvation through Jesus Christ is complete. Shincheonji treats Lee as the one who unlocks what Revelation actually means. Mainstream churches hear a living man adding himself to a closed book.

There is also a dispute over recruiting. Shincheonji members have been accused of joining other congregations without disclosing their affiliation. The church describes this as a way of avoiding persecution. Its critics call it infiltration. That argument has run for two decades and explains much of the hostility.
Three switches occur as that criticism turns into a campaign of social exclusion.

1. A difference in interpretation is treated as a social crime.
Orthodoxy and heresy are questions internal to each denomination. They are disputes over scripture. Mainstream churches take that difference and attach the labels "antisocial cult" and "brainwashing."

2. Blame for mainstream decline gets shifted.
Korea's traditional Protestant churches face sharp youth attrition and a run of scandals. Shincheonji, growing fast through intensive Bible study, became the most visible threat to that base. The heresy campaign carries an organizational and financial motive, conducted under the banner of protecting doctrine.
3. Forced deconversion gets legitimized.
The pastor convicted of abducting and confining believers to force them out of their faith talks down to Shincheonji.

Mainstream pastors operate "heresy counseling centers" that persuade families to bring believers to facilities and pressure them to renounce their faith. Some cases have involved abduction and confinement carried out through relatives. Positioning themselves as orthodox lets the operators recast that as a rescue.
Monarch Report takes no position on Shincheonji's theology. That question belongs to churches, and they are free to answer it. The state is not.
When the Heresy Verdict Enters Government

On June 30, South Korea's Minister of Justice posted about the case. Lee had been indicted and detained. Strict punishment matching his responsibility was unavoidable, the minister wrote. The post closed with Matthew 7:15: "Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep's clothing."
Two problems sit inside that post.

Lee has been indicted. He has not been tried. The minister sits atop the system prosecuting him, and called punishment unavoidable before a judge heard the evidence. That tells the court what answer is expected.
False prophet is a religious category. No criminal code contains it. Once a minister applies it to a named defendant, the state has stopped describing a crime and started describing a faith.
Shincheonji says the church cooperated fully with investigators, and calls the detention a physical punishment on a 95-year-old.
The Pattern Foreign Observers Now Name
Since January, a joint prosecution and police task force has been investigating suspected ties between politicians and religious groups, including Shincheonji and the Unification Church.

On August 7, 2026, five international organizations, Human Rights Without Frontiers, CAP Liberté de Conscience, FOREF, CESNUR, and Bitter Winter, held a press conference at the Seoul Foreign Correspondents' Club and signed a letter calling for Lee's immediate release.

CESNUR managing director Massimo Introvigne said South Korea had crossed a concerning line. He argued the UN Nelson Mandela Rules would call for house arrest rather than imprisonment for a 95-year-old accused of a nonviolent offense, and said the charges were stretched too far legally and conceptually.

Introvigne also applied what he calls the "Law model." Minorities are attacked in three stages: media-driven intolerance, then discrimination by courts and administrators, then persecution and violence.

He said the same selective use of election law has now reached Pastor Son Hyun-bo, 83-year-old Dr. Hak-ja Han of the Family Federation, and Lee Man-hee. He warned that forced deconversion has already produced cases in South Korea where believers were badly beaten or killed.
The Principle

If Lee coerced tens of thousands of citizens into registering with a political party, that is a matter for the courts, decided on evidence, with the ordinary protections any 95-year-old defendant would receive.
Nothing in Revelation 7 is a crime.

Mainstream Protestants call a rival reading heresy to defend their own doctrine. That is a theological argument, settled inside churches. A democratic state has no authority to decide which reading of the Bible is orthodox and which is false.
That verdict belongs to churches. It does not belong to a courtroom. Borrowing a rival church's logic of theological exclusion as a pretext for police handcuffs cannot be permitted.

title: 「カルト」「洗脳」——かつて学者が悪意なく用いた言葉は、いまや国家権力の道具となるのか？
previewText: イタリアの宗教社会学者マッシモ・イントロヴィニェ氏は語る。「カルト」という言葉には犯罪学的な負荷がかかっており、「洗脳」はあらゆる証拠上の検証に耐えず、東京の解散命令は東アジアをはるかに越えて民主主義

blocks.text: イタリアの宗教社会学者マッシモ・イントロヴィニェ氏は語る。「カルト」という言葉には犯罪学的な負荷がかかっており、「洗脳」はあらゆる証拠上の検証に耐えず、東京の解散命令は東アジアをはるかに越えて民主主義諸国が警戒すべきものである、と。
かつて学者たちが悪意なく用いた言葉が、いまや国家権力の道具となっている。マッシモ・イントロヴィニェ氏は、統一教会の宗教二世信者が立ち上げた宗教の自由をテーマとするYouTubeチャンネル「The 12 Gates」でのインタビューで、そう論じた。
変質した言葉
ウェーバーは近代社会学の礎を築いたドイツの社会学者で、『プロテスタンティズムの倫理と資本主義の精神』の著者。トレルチは同時代のプロテスタント神学者・宗教史家で、主著『キリスト教会・教派の社会教説』を残した。両者は宗教集団を「教会」「セクト」などに分類する類型論を築き、そこで用いられた用語のひとつが「カルト」だった。
ウェーバーとトレルチは「カルト」という語を、信仰を受け継いだのではなく成人してから自ら加わった人々から成る、若い宗教を指すために用いた。その典型例が使徒たちであり、この語は行状について何も含意しなかった。これに対しチェーザレ・ロンブローゾの流れをくむ犯罪学者たちは、重大犯罪の嫌疑がかかる集団を指してこの語を用い、20世紀半ばまでにその意味が優勢となった。
古い語義は今も抗弁として生き延びている。名誉毀損で訴えられた者は、ロンブローゾの意味で用いておきながら、ウェーバーへと退避するのである。
ヨーロッパが引いた
2022年12月に判断が示された「トンチェフほか対ブルガリア」事件で、欧州人権裁判所は、プロテスタント教会に近づかないよう家庭に警告するキャンペーンが信教の自由を侵害したと判示した。加盟46か国の政府はこれで通告を受けたことになる。少数派の信仰をカルトと呼ぶことは犯罪性を主張することであり、公的にそう呼ぶことは差別にあたる。
「洗脳」をめぐる証拠
その主張はなお立証されねばならないが、証拠は乏しい。「洗脳」という語が一般の語彙に入ったのは、朝鮮戦争における米兵捕虜をめぐる冷戦期の宣伝を通じてだった。アイリーン・バーカーの調査によれば、統一教会のセミナーに参加した数百人のうち入信したのは1～2パーセントで、その大半も3年以内に離れていた。
説得や影響力そのものは、社会のいたるところにある。広告は買わせようとし、企業は社員を組織の価値観に染め、軍隊は訓練で兵士の行動様式を作り替える。それらは誰も犯罪とは呼ばない。
「洗脳」という主張が成り立つには、通常の説得と、意思を奪う「洗脳」とを分ける境界線が存在し、それを示せなければならない。だが、その境界を実証した研究はこれまで存在しない。1990年の合衆国対フィッシュマン事件で、米国の裁判所も、洗脳理論は科学的な裏付けを欠くとして法廷での証拠採用を認めなかった。
とはいえ、これは宗教団体を法の外に置くものではない。強姦、児童虐待、テロは動機のいかんを問わず訴追の対象であり、組織的に犯罪を犯す集団が解散させられることは正当でありうる。ここでの異議はもっと狭い。すなわち、「カルトであること」自体を罪とすることへの異議である。
東京とソウル

なぜこの区別が重要なのか。
本来、国家がある団体に手を下すには、その団体が何をしたか、つまり具体的な犯罪を立証しなければならない。だが立証できないとき、国家は別の口実を探すことになる。そこで役立つのが「カルト」という言葉だ。この言葉を使えば、問いは「何をしたか」から「どういう団体か」へとすり替わる。行為ではなく性質を根拠に、団体を処分できるようになるのである。

日本はまさにそれを行った。
2025年3月25日に東京地方裁判所が解散を命じたとき、世界平和統一家庭連合は、民事上の根拠のみで解散させられた日本初の宗教法人となった。先例であるオウム真理教と明覚寺の解散は、いずれも刑事有罪判決を受けてのものだった。今回、有罪判決はない。命令を根拠づけたのは、組織そのものについて積み上げられた像であり、それは「カルト」という語が議論に与える形そのものだった。
韓国は別の経路——裁判所ではなく国会に提出された法案——で、これに比肩する地点に近づきつつある。機構は異なるが、方向は同じだ。両国において問われているのは、もはやその宗教団体が何について有罪とされたかではなく、それがどのような団体であるかなのである。
議論は家庭へと移る

入信の数字があまりに不利であるため、日本と韓国の批判者たちはいま、強制の所在を家庭に求め、信者の子どもたちに焦点を当てている。カトリックや福音派の家庭も同じことをしていると指摘されると、彼らは主張を撤回するのではなく、それらの家庭にまで主張を拡張する。日本の「宗教の信仰等に関係する児童虐待」への対応指針が、地獄について語ることから子どもの読むものを制限することまで、主流派キリスト教では当たり前の慣行にまで及んでいるのはそのためだ。
誰が元信者を代表するのか
教会を去った人がみな、その教会を批判するようになるわけではない。社会学者デイヴィッド・ブロムリーは、報道がほとんど気づいていない区別を指摘している。脱会者の大半は、静かに教会を離れ、良い面も悪い面もあったと受け止めて、そのまま自分の生活に戻っていく。ごく一部だけが「背教者」となる。彼らは去った後に仲間と組織を作り、その教団は有害だという主張を社会に向けて発信し続ける。
この後者は、カトリック教会を含めどの集団でも、脱会者のうち2～10パーセントにすぎない。ところが、本を出すのも、記者の電話に出るのもこの人たちである。だから報道機関は、残りの90パーセント以上の元信者に会うことがほとんどない。教団についての世間の像は、この少数派の証言だけで形づくられていく。

教団を離れることには確かに代償が伴う、とイントロヴィニェ氏も認める。人間関係を失い、住む場所や仕事を失うこともある。批判者はここに「洗脳」の証拠を見出す。抜けたくても抜けられない状態に置かれているのだから、留まっているのは本人の意思ではない、と。

だが同じ理屈は、結婚にも職場にも当てはまる。離婚すれば家庭も財産も失いかねず、会社を辞めれば収入を失う。それでも私たちは、結婚や雇用を人を縛る違法な仕組みだとは呼ばない。抜けるのに代償が伴うというだけでは、その集団を特別扱いする根拠にはならないのである

＊元信者と背教者に関するより詳細な分析については、マッシモ・イントロヴィニェ氏が編集長を務める Bitter Winter を参照。
 https://bitterwinter.org/nisei-are-second-generation-apostates-from-the-unification-church-reliable-1-who-are-the-apostates/
東アジアを越えて
この構図はアジアに限らない。ストラスブールで退けられた論法は、いま米国の法廷で使われはじめている。形は東京と同じで、犯罪の立証ではなく、宗教的な育ちが子どもに何を残すかという説明として現れる。ニューヨーク州のトゥエルブ・トライブズ共同体への強制捜査の後、検察官は、そこで育った子どもは将来の就職で不利になると主張した。日本と同じ理屈である。
5歳児を企業社会での競争に備えさせることも、同じく価値観の教え込みだとイントロヴィニェ氏は返す。両者を分けるのは証拠ではなく好みであり、裁判所がそれを選ぶことは、子育てそのものを裁くことにほかならない。
結局は言葉の問題に戻る。「カルト」が法的な範疇になれば、国家は子どもをどの信仰で育ててよいかを決める権限を得る。本来持たないはずの決して付与されたことのない権限だ。ヨーロッパはそれを手放し、東京とソウルは広げている。
