title: "Cult," "Brainwashing" — Words Scholars Once Used Without Malice Are Now Instruments Of State Power
previewText: Massimo Introvigne says the word carries a criminological charge, that "brainwashing" fails every evidentiary test, and that Tokyo's dissolution order should alarm democracies far beyond East Asia.

blocks.text: Massimo Introvigne says the word carries a criminological charge, that "brainwashing" fails every evidentiary test, and that Tokyo's dissolution order should alarm democracies far beyond East Asia.

A word scholars once used without malice is now an instrument of state power. That is the argument Massimo Introvigne, of Turin's Center for Studies on New Religions, put to The 12 Gates, a religious-freedom channel hosted by a second-generation Unification Church member.
A Word That Changed

Max Weber and Ernst Troeltsch used "cult" for a young religion whose members joined as adults rather than inheriting the faith. The apostles were the paradigm case, and the word implied nothing about conduct. Cesare Lombroso's criminologists used it instead for groups suspected of serious crime, and by mid-century that meaning had won out.
The older sense survives as a defence: anyone sued for defamation retreats to Weber while having meant Lombroso.
Europe Draws a Line

In Tonchev and Others v. Bulgaria, decided in December 2022, the European Court of Human Rights held that a campaign warning families away from Protestant churches violated religious freedom. Governments across forty-six member states are now on notice: to call a minority faith a cult alleges criminality, and officially to do so is discrimination.
The Brainwashing Evidence

The accusation must still be proved, and the evidence is poor. "Brainwashing" entered public vocabulary through Cold War messaging about American prisoners in Korea. Eileen Barker found that of hundreds attending Unification Church seminars, one or two percent joined, most leaving within three years.

Influence is real, in advertising, corporations and armies alike; what has never been shown is a break point where persuasion becomes something else. American courts said as much in United States v. Fishman in 1990.

None of which places religious organisations beyond the law. Rape, child abuse and terrorism remain prosecutable whatever the motive, and a systematically criminal group may properly be dissolved. The objection is narrower: to offences consisting in being a cult.
Tokyo and Seoul

That distinction matters because a state unable to prove a crime needs another ground for acting, and the cult category supplies one, converting a judgment about what a religion is into a reason to move against it.

Japan has done exactly that. When the Tokyo District Court ordered its dissolution on 25 March 2025, the Family Federation for World Peace and Unification became the country's first religious corporation dissolved on civil grounds alone. The earlier dissolutions of Aum Shinrikyo and Myokakuji followed criminal convictions. Here there were none. What justified the order was an accumulated picture of the organisation itself, the shape the word "cult" gives an argument.

Korea is reaching comparable ground by another route, a bill in the National Assembly rather than the courts. The mechanism differs; the direction is the same. In both countries the question is no longer what a religious body has been convicted of, but what kind of body it is.
The Argument Moves Home

With the recruitment figures so unhelpful to it, critics in Japan and Korea now locate the coercion in the family, focusing on the children of believers. Told that Catholic and evangelical households do the same, proponents extend the claim to them rather than retreat. Japan's guidance on religious abuse of children accordingly reaches practices ordinary in mainstream Christianity, from discussing hell to limiting what children read.
Who Speaks for Ex-Members

Not everyone who leaves becomes a critic, and the sociologist David Bromley drew the line most coverage misses. The ordinary leave-taker walks away, allows there was good and bad in it, and gets on with life. The apostate leaves and then organises, building a public account of the group as harmful.

The second category runs at two to ten percent of departures from any group, the Catholic Church included, but they write the books and take the reporter's call, so the press meets almost no one else.
Leaving can be costly, Introvigne concedes, but marriages and employers create the same dependency, and so general a condition cannot be legislated against.

*For a more detailed analysis of former believers and apostates, see Bitter Winter, where Massimo Introvigne serves as Editor-in-Chief.
 https://bitterwinter.org/nisei-are-second-generation-apostates-from-the-unification-church-reliable-1-who-are-the-apostates/
Beyond East Asia

The pattern is not an Asian one. The reasoning barred in Strasbourg now works through American courtrooms, arriving as it did in Tokyo: not as a charge of crime but as an account of what a religious upbringing does to a child. After a raid on a Twelve Tribes community in New York State, prosecutors argued the children raised there would be handicapped as adults in the labour market, the reasoning used in Japan.

Preparing a five-year-old to compete for a corporate career, Introvigne answers, transmits a value system just as surely. What separates them is not evidence but preference, and a court asked to choose is ruling on how families raise children.

Which returns the question to the word. Admitted as a legal category, "cult" hands the state a power it was never granted: to decide which beliefs a child may be raised in. Europe has begun withdrawing it. Tokyo and Seoul are extending it.

title: Beijing Freed Pastor Jin Mingri — and Proved Religion Is the Party's "Glass Jaw"
previewText:
On July 4, an underground church pastor who had spent nine months in Chinese detention walked free onto American soil.
Pastor Ezra Jin Mingri, founder of Beijing's Zion Church, arrived in Los Angeles

blocks.text: On July 4, an underground church pastor who had spent nine months in Chinese detention walked free onto American soil.

Pastor Ezra Jin Mingri, founder of Beijing's Zion Church, arrived in Los Angeles and reunited with his family shortly before Independence Day. His release did not come from a Chinese change of heart. It came after the President of the United States said his name to Xi Jinping.
What Beijing did

Jin was arrested on October 10, 2025, for practicing and sharing his faith and for his leadership as a pastor. He and 17 other Zion Church leaders were detained in what has been described as one of China's largest crackdowns on a single church in decades.

Authorities had already shut Zion's physical premises in 2018, but the church kept operating online, reaching thousands of worshippers — which is precisely why it was targeted. Jin had refused to register Zion with the state; he and nine other leaders were charged with "running illegal business operations."
That is the tell. A house church that would not submit to state control was prosecuted not for any crime of violence but for the administrative offense of existing outside the Party's reach.
The lever that worked
Here is what a democracy's leverage looks like when it is actually used.

At a May summit in China, President Trump raised Jin's case directly with Xi Jinping. 

Jin's family thanked the Trump administration for its leadership and said they believed his release could not have happened without that direct intervention. Jin's wife, Anna Liu, thanked Xi, Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and the 44 U.S. lawmakers who had signed a joint statement calling for his release.

Congress had built the pressure in the open. On May 13, 2026, the House passed H.Res.1259 by unanimous consent, a resolution urging the President to prioritize securing the release of Pastor Jin Mingri — along with Pastor Gao Quanfu and his wife Pang Yu, Dr. Gulshan Abbas, and Jimmy Lai — in his engagements with Xi Jinping. The Senate passed a companion resolution the same day.
Named. Prioritized. Pressed at the highest level. Released. That is the sequence, and it is not a coincidence.
The glass jaw

The lesson is one that religious-freedom advocates have argued for years: faith is the Chinese Communist Party's greatest weakness, not its afterthought. A regime that governs 1.4 billion people cannot tolerate ten thousand Christians logging on to worship — so it disappears their pastor and charges him as a swindler. Strength does not behave that way. Fear does.

That is why a single name, spoken by a president who chose to spend the capital, could pry open a cell that condemnation alone never would. The Party guards this pressure point precisely because it knows how exposed it is.
The crackdown has not ended
One release is not a victory, and Beijing has made sure no one mistakes it for one.
Freedom House welcomed Jin's freedom while stressing that other Zion Church leaders and members remain detained and that others still face serious criminal charges.

Anna Liu called for the release of the eight other Zion Church leaders still in custody. And within days of Jin's arrival in the United States, Chinese authorities denied bail to another detained Zion member, preacher Wu Qiuyu, held since October 2025 — an unmistakable signal that the campaign against the church continues.
Xi released the man Washington named. He kept the ones it did not.
What Washington should do
The takeaway for U.S. legislators is not sentimental. It is operational.

Naming works. The prisoners the United States lists, prioritizes, and raises at the summit table are the prisoners who come home. The ones left off the list stay in the cell. If a single resolution and one presidential ask freed Jin Mingri, then the eight Zion leaders still held, Pastor Gao Quanfu and Pang Yu, Dr. Gulshan Abbas, and Jimmy Lai are not beyond reach — they are simply waiting to be named with the same insistence.

A government that jails a pastor for worshiping online is not projecting confidence. It is protecting a glass jaw. The question for Washington is whether it will keep aiming there — case by case, name by name — until the cells are empty.
Which name goes on the list next?

title: A Torture Survivor Offered to Educate His Enemy's Children: Inside Moon's 1990 Walk Into the Kremlin
previewText:
The communists had tortured him. They had worked him near to death in a North Korean labor camp. Any man would have earned the right to hate them.
So when Sun Myung Moon walked into the Kremlin in

blocks.text: The communists had tortured him. They had worked him near to death in a North Korean labor camp. Any man would have earned the right to hate them.
So when Sun Myung Moon walked into the Kremlin in April 1990, the world expected a reckoning.
Instead, he offered to educate their children.

That is the paradox at the center of one of the Cold War's strangest meetings — and the clearest thing Moon ever did to prove he meant the word he had chosen decades earlier. Not anti-communism. Victory over communism: defeat the ideology, and save the person trapped inside it.
For twenty-two years that was theory pressed into speeches and newsprint. In Moscow it became an offer he could not take back.
The offer

In April 1990 Moon convened the Eleventh World Media Conference and a Summit Council for World Peace in Moscow — journalists, scholars, and former heads of state, assembled in the capital of the empire he had fought his whole adult life. On April 11 he met President Mikhail Gorbachev face to face, a meeting church accounts call historic given that Moon held no office and South Korea had no diplomatic relations with the USSR.

He did not lecture Gorbachev on the failures of Marx. He proposed bringing thousands of Soviet students and young leaders to the United States to see faith and free society for themselves. Church accounts put the figure at 3,000, and the program went forward.

The logic was consistent with everything he had preached: you do not liberate a nation by humiliating it. You liberate it by giving its young people something the old system could not — the direct experience of freedom, and a worldview centered on God rather than the state.

According to his movement's own telling, when hardline communists launched the August 1991 coup to reverse Gorbachev’s reforms and preserve the old centralized system, young Russians shaped by these programs — who had directly tasted freedom and a God-centered worldview — stood among those who defended reform in the streets.
Treat that claim as the movement's account, not settled history. The timeline around it, however, is not in dispute: just twenty months after Moon’s visit, the Soviet Union was gone.
Why it still matters
It is easy, in an age of permanent outrage, to treat opponents as enemies to be crushed. Moon's Moscow gambit rebukes that instinct — and it came from a man who had every reason to indulge it.

Nothing about his conviction softened. He had spent the 1970s warning that "godless communism" was the gravest threat of the age, and in 1982 he founded The Washington Times to press the case. What changed at the Kremlin was not the target but the method: confront the ideology, redeem the person.

A democracy that knows only how to defeat its adversaries, and never how to win them over, eventually forgets the difference between fighting evil and destroying people. Moon never confused the two. He opposed the system precisely because he refused to write off the human beings living inside it.
Thirty-six years later, with faith again under pressure and authoritarian power again on the march, the question he answered in that room is still the live one:
When you finally have your enemy in front of you — do you try to destroy him, or do you try to save him?

title: 13-Year Prison Sentence Sought and the Trial of Socrates: The Law Punishes Actions, Not Existence
previewText:
Original: World Daily (Korea), Written by Jeong Seong-su, Religious Affairs Specialist Reporter, July 12, 2026, [Religious Column]
On the 10th, the special prosecution team led by Min Joong-ki sought

blocks.text: Original: World Daily (Korea), Written by Jeong Seong-su, Religious Affairs Specialist Reporter, July 12, 2026, [Religious Column]

On the 10th, the special prosecution team led by Min Joong-ki sought a 13-year prison sentence for Dr. Hak Ja Han, President of the Family Federation for World Peace and Unification. This breaks down to 5 years for violations of the Political Fund Act and an additional 8 years for the other charges. It is an unusually heavy sentence rarely seen in our society. The shock was surely felt not only by Dr. Han herself, but by countless believers at home and abroad who are enduring with heavy hearts the harsh reality now facing their religious organization.

Coincidentally, the founder of the Family Federation, President Sun Myung Moon, also endured unjust imprisonment under a past communist regime. Though the times and systems differ, it is precisely when a religious leader stands in court that the judiciary must render judgment based on the strictest possible evidence and legal principles. This is also why the judiciary in a liberal democracy must be clearly distinguished from that of an authoritarian regime.

However, a requested sentence is nothing more than the prosecution’s hope — it is not the court’s verdict. The body that ultimately determines guilt or innocence and the sentence is the court. The judicial panel will comprehensively examine the prosecution’s arguments, the defense’s rebuttals, the submitted evidence, and all sentencing factors before reaching an independent judgment. This is a fundamental principle of South Korea’s criminal justice system.

In this case, the special prosecution repeatedly emphasized the seriousness of the matter using grandiose terms such as “collusion between politics and religion,” “undermining democracy,” “ultimate beneficiary,” and “final decision-maker.” Yet for a 13-year sentence to carry such weight, the evidence must be equally solid and detailed. The special prosecution offered plenty of flamboyant rhetoric, but the content disclosed at the sentencing hearing still failed to present sufficient direct evidence. For more than two years, the special prosecution and other investigative agencies have conducted sweeping investigations into the Family Federation, including multiple raids, account tracing, communication analysis, and questioning dozens of individuals. Nevertheless, objective evidence that Dr. Han directly ordered or conspired in the delivery of political funds or the provision of gifts to First Lady Kim Keon-hee has yet to emerge from the fog.

The special prosecution labeled Dr. Han the “final decision-maker” and “ultimate beneficiary” and sought to hold her accountable. This is a classic case of “comprehensive responsibility theory,” inferring criminality based solely on one’s position and circumstances within an organization. However, modern criminal law punishes specific criminal “acts”; it does not condemn a person’s “status” or “existence” itself. The logic that holds a leader responsible merely for the outcomes of actions taken by subordinates is merely a modern variation of pre-modern guilt-by-association or strict liability. When concrete proof of specific acts is lacking, those in power routinely resort to grand narratives and symbols to inflate the sentence.

The trial of Socrates in 399 BC — widely regarded as one of history’s most infamous cases of judicial murder — was exactly this. The accuser Meletus could not specifically prove whom Socrates had harmed or which law he had broken. Instead, he imposed a vast and vague frame: “corrupting the youth and not believing in the gods of Athens.” It was purely on the circumstantial charge that Socrates the giant’s “existence” and his influence on society were uncomfortable that the excessive sentence of death was imposed.

The special prosecution’s sentencing request in this case similarly evokes the Socrates trial the moment it relies more on symbols and status than on concrete actions. When direct evidence linking actual criminal conduct is insufficient, investigative agencies attack the defendant’s position using abstract grand discourses such as “political-religious collusion” or “undermining democracy.” The French Reign of Terror’s “Law of Suspects,” which permitted punishment based merely on circumstances and speech without concrete acts, operated on the same principle. A judiciary that convicts on the basis of “given the position and circumstances, one cannot but be a criminal” without sufficient evidence easily becomes the sword of dictatorship disguised as democracy. In the history of justice, whenever “suspicion” outpaces “proof,” a dark chapter of judicial abuse is invariably written.

Evaluations of Dr. Han will continue to be divided. Some will remember her as a religious leader who guided an era, while others will view her as a target of criticism. The trajectory of her life — traveling across the world for decades, convening numerous international conferences on interfaith harmony, global peace, family values, and peace on the Korean Peninsula as a chosen nation, and engaging with world leaders — remains an undeniable historical fact. Whatever conclusion the court reaches, it must be grounded in evidence and legal principles.

In her final statement at the sentencing hearing, Dr. Han declared, “I have lived my entire life serving Heaven for the sake of humanity’s peace and the realization of one family,” and “I have never sought power with money.” She also expressed deep apology for the current outcome caused by those she trusted and entrusted, while affirming her resolve to continue walking the path toward a world of peace.
This article is an English translation of a piece originally published by World Daily (Korea). All credits and copyrights belong to World Daily.

title: Nation God Raised" at 250: Blessing & Hope from Rev. Moon & Dr. Han for America
previewText:
In the darkest winter of the Revolutionary War, at Valley Forge, George Washington is said to have knelt in the snow and asked God for help.
The story has endured for generations. Turning to God in a

blocks.text: In the darkest winter of the Revolutionary War, at Valley Forge, George Washington is said to have knelt in the snow and asked God for help.

The story has endured for generations. Turning to God in a time of crisis is one of this country's oldest habits. Washington declared days of prayer, Lincoln called the nation to prayer and repentance during the Civil War, and Dr. King spoke of God's justice.

Now, 250 years later, on July 4, 2026, America marks its 250th birthday. Even as the world's most powerful nation, it faces deep division, broken families, and moral confusion, while beyond its borders, forces that reject God are growing stronger.
It is in exactly such a time that words spoken half a century ago are being read again — not merely as an old speech, but as a timely message of blessing and responsibility coming true today.
The Couple Who Loved God Deeply

The message came from Rev. Sun Myung Moon (1920–2012) and his wife, Dr. Hak Ja Han, who together founded the Unification movement in Korea. What makes their words carry such weight is not abstract theory, but a life forged in love for God and firsthand knowledge of suffering.

Rev. Moon was imprisoned by the communist regime in North Korea as a young man and endured over two years of torture and forced labor in a prison camp. Dr. Han was also born in the North; at the age of five, she fled south with her family in the middle of the night after her mother and grandmother were taken by communist authorities.
Having witnessed what happens when a system denies God, the couple chose a different path.

Married in 1960, they dedicated their lives to realizing God’s will out of deep love for Him. Their mission became the restoration of true families and a world of peace. In 1971, they moved the center of their work to America, which Rev. Moon called “God’s last bulwark.”
Rev. Moon called this country "God's last fortress."
In 1976, America's 200th year, Rev. Moon spoke at two huge rallies in the United States (the year before, he had drawn about 1.2 million people to Yoido Plaza in his home country of Korea).

On September 18, the roughly 300,000 people who gathered at the Washington Monument made up the largest religious rally the capital had ever seen. The first thing Rev. Moon said was that God had been at work in the birth of this nation.
"I am certain that the United States of America was truly created by God."

Why could he say this? According to Rev. Moon, there were two kinds of people among the nation's founders. One kind came seeking wealth; the other came seeking God and freedom. And it was the people who put God first, he said, who built this country.

"The only reason the first settlers came to North America was God. Because they came seeking God, they found not only God but also freedom and wealth. But the people who went to South America seeking gold found neither gold, nor God, nor freedom."

Rev. Moon also saw God's hand in America's own history. At Valley Forge during the Revolutionary War, Washington asked God for help and defeated the British army that many had thought could not be beaten. In a very short time, the world's strongest nation was born. Hard work alone cannot explain this, Rev. Moon said: "If God had not been the main partner, today's America could never have come into being."

The greatest enemy threatening this nation of God, Rev. Moon warned, was communism, which denies God. Seeing the Cold War as a struggle between God and those against God, Rev. Moon called America "God's last fortress" and argued that the free world must one day set the communist world free.
"Godless communism is the worst of all. This is not America's problem alone. It is a problem for people of faith, and a problem for God himself."
Blessing comes with responsibility, Rev. Moon taught. But at the root of his words was not scolding — it was a deep love for America.

"I came to America because this is the country God has chosen. Even if America turns away from God, God will not give up on this nation. God's will is to make America a model of a faithful nation that other countries can follow. To save the world, America must lead the way."
The Warning Came True
These words carry weight because much of what he said came true.

Back in 1972, Rev. Moon predicted that communism, which began in 1917, would fall apart by the late 1980s — around its seventieth year. At the time, almost no one in the West expected the Soviet bloc to end. Yet in 1989 the Berlin Wall fell, and in 1991 the Soviet Union broke apart.
The problems he named at home — broken families, moral confusion, and young people who have lost their way — are now worries shared across the political left and right.
Carrying the Call Forward
After the passing of Rev. Sun Myung Moon, Dr. Han took over the movement he had built.

She calls America a special nation with the responsibility to lead the countries of the world. But her message is not some far-off ideal. The place to begin rebuilding society, she says, is the home closest to us.
"A family that is not built on God carries conflict within it and will break apart in time. And a nation made up of such families will also fall into decline."

When husband and wife are joined by real love and raise their children with care, the health of each single family supports the stability of the whole nation. This is what Dr. Han has taught again and again.
Dr. Han continues to share this conviction wherever she goes:
"I have lived my whole life to bring the dream of our Creator, the Heavenly Parent, to life on this earth."

The same call — "return to God" — now rings out from the center of American politics as well. In his January 2025 inaugural address, President Trump spoke of surviving an assassin's bullet the year before and said, "I was saved by God to make America great again."

He went on: "We will not forget our country, we will not forget our Constitution, and we will not forget our God." Turning to God in times of crisis is not only America's oldest tradition; it is something people, and this nation, need in order to keep standing.
The Choice at 250
Why did God bless this nation?
The founders who put God first were given, along with God, both freedom and wealth — that, Rev. Moon taught, is America. But the blessing was not for this country alone.

God raised America as a model for the world to follow, placed it at the head of the free world, and gave it a mission: to rise above the forces that deny God and build "one world under God." The blessing was given for that purpose.

From many places where freedom and faith are under threat, people still look to the last fortress. Now, while forces that challenge God remain, can America rise again as "God's last fortress," rebuild the family, and offer hope to the world?
For a country that has turned back to God in every time of crisis over these 250 years, this is not decoration for an anniversary year — it is a choice that cannot be avoided.
God Bless America — so that its true blessing may be won back.

title: 신천지와 통일교: 한국 법무부 장관, “거짓 선지자”에 “엄벌”을 약속하다
previewText:
고령 종교 지도자들이 구속된 가운데, 정치인은 복음서를 인용해 “이단”을 비난하고 일본에서 일어난 일을 환영하고 있다.

원문 : Bitter Winter 마시모 인트로비네 | 2026년 7월 2일
 
한국의 법무부 장관

blocks.text:
고령 종교 지도자들이 구속된 가운데, 정치인은 복음서를 인용해 “이단”을 비난하고 일본에서 일어난 일을 환영하고 있다.

원문 : Bitter Winter 마시모 인트로비네 | 2026년 7월 2일
한국의 법무부 장관 정성호가 많은 사람들이 우려하던 바를 확인하는 이례적인 Facebook 게시물을 올렸다. 신천지 이만희 총회장(95세)은 폭력과 도주 우려가 전혀 없는 혐의로 구금되어 있다. 해당 혐의는 종교와 국가의 분리 원칙을 위반했다는 것이다.
장관은 이렇게 썼다. “특정 정당에 5만 명이 넘는 신도를 강제 등록한 혐의를 받는 신천지 이만희 총회장이 기소되었고 구금되었다. 대선 경선, 지방선거, 당 지도부 선거 등 주요 정치 행사 기간 동안 대규모 당원 등록을 통해 정당과 국민의 정치적 의사를 왜곡하고 헌법상 종교와 국가의 분리 원칙을 위반했다는 것이다.”
이 발언은 95세 노인이 정치 참여 관련 혐의로 감옥에 있다는 사실을 확인시켜준다. 이는 민주주의 국가에서 모든 시민에게 주어진 권리다. 어떻게 “강제적으로” 공동 신도를 정당에 등록시켰다는 것인지 제대로 설명되지 않았다.
장관은 계속해서 “종교 단체는 내적 평화와 영적 위안을 위한 신앙 공동체이지, 권력을 추구하는 정치 집단이 아니다”라고 밝혔다. 이 문장은 신자들을 영적 영역에 가두고 공적 생활에 참여할 권리를 부정하는 종교관을 드러낸다.
장관은 또 “국가가 세속 영역에 머물고 종교가 영적 영역에 머무를 때에만 민주주의와 공동체의 평화가 유지될 수 있다”고 썼다. 그러나 민주주의는 시민들이 — 종교 공동체에 속한 사람들을 포함해 — 자유롭게 의견을 표현하고, 정당에 가입하고, 투표할 때 유지된다. 장관의 발언은 이 원칙에 대한 직접적인 도전이다.

그는 일본 대법원이 통일교에 대한 최종 해산 명령을 내렸다고 언급하며, “신도들에게 대규모 금전 요구와 여당과의 밀접한 유대” 문제를 들었다. 

그러나 이는 사실이 아니다. 해산 판결문에는 여당과의 관계가 언급되지 않았다. 법무부 장관이 언론 서사를 사법 문서와 혼동하는 것은 매우 우려스러운 일이다.
장관은 이만희 총회장으로 돌아가며 “이 사건 역시 중대한 범죄이며, 그 책임에 상응하는 엄중한 형사처벌은 불가피하다”고 밝혔다. 법무부 장관이 진행 중인 수사에 대해 미리 “엄벌이 불가피하다”고 선언하는 것은 사법 시스템의 신뢰성을 훼손하는 행위다.
장관은 게시물을 마태복음 7장 15절을 인용하며 마무리했다. “거짓 선지자들을 조심하라. 그들은 양의 옷을 입고 너희에게 오지만 속은 탐욕스러운 이리다.”
정 장관은 독실한 장로교 신자로 알려져 있다. 그의 교회에는 많은 선량한 기독교인과 의로운 사람들이 있지만, 동시에 신천지 등 다른 종교 단체 신도들을 강제로 탈퇴시키는 ‘강제 탈회 상담(deprogramming)’을 하는 목사들도 포함되어 있다. 이러한 행위에는 신천지 신도들을 납치해 신앙을 포기하도록 강요하는 것이 포함된다.
장관이 공식적인 자리에서 성경을 인용한 것은, 자신이 주장하는 선을 스스로 넘는 행위이다. 그는 다른 사람들이 종교와 정치를 혼합한다고 비난하면서, 정작 자신은 종교를 이용하고 있다.
통일교 지도자 한학자 총재(83세) 역시 수개월째 한국에서 구속되어 있으며 현재 감시하에 병원에 입원해 있다.
95세 노인과 83세 여성이 가혹한 조건에 처해 있는 상황은 많은 의문을 불러일으킨다. 정부는 이들이 재판을 받을 때까지 살아남지 못하기를 바라는 것인가.
종교 운동은 수세기 동안 박해를 견뎌왔다. 제국, 독재, 정치적 폭풍을 이겨냈다. 이번에도 살아남을 것이다. 정부와 정당은 오르내리지만, 교회는 지속된다.

본 기사는 국제적 종교 자유 전문가이자 Bitter Winter 편집장인 
마시모 인트로비네가 기고한 논설을 번역한 것입니다.
크레딧은 Bitter Winter에 귀속됩니다.

title: 新天地と統一教会：韓国の法務大臣が「偽預言者」に対する「厳罰」を約束
previewText:
高齢の宗教指導者たちが拘束され続ける中、政治家は福音書を引用して「異端」を非難し、日本で起きたことを称賛する。

原文：Bitter Winter マッシモ・イントロヴィーニェ 著 | 2026年7月2日 |

blocks.text:
高齢の宗教指導者たちが拘束され続ける中、政治家は福音書を引用して「異端」を非難し、日本で起きたことを称賛する。

原文：Bitter Winter マッシモ・イントロヴィーニェ 著 | 2026年7月2日 |
韓国の法務大臣、鄭聖鎬（チョン・ソンホ）は、異例のFacebook投稿を公開し、多くの人が懸念していたことを確認した。新天地（Shincheonji）の李萬熙（イ・マンへ）会長（95歳）は、暴力とは無関係で逃亡の恐れもない容疑で拘束されている。容疑は、宗教と国家の分離原則の違反とされる。大臣は次のように書いている。
「新天地のイ・マンへ会長は、特定の政党に5万人以上の信者を強制的に登録したとして起訴され、拘束された。容疑の内容は、大統領予備選、地方選挙、党指導部選挙などの主要政治イベント中に大規模な党員登録を行い、政治政党と市民の政治的意思を歪曲し、憲法上の宗教と国家の分離原則に違反したというものだ。」
これらの言葉は、95歳の男性が政治参加に関する罪で投獄されていることを確認する。民主主義国家では、この権利はすべての市民に属する。彼がどのように信者たちを「強制的に」政党に登録させたのか、説明はほとんどなされていない。

大臣は続ける。「宗教団体は、内面的な平和と精神的な慰めのための信仰の共同体であり、権力を求める政治集団ではない。」

この文は、信者を精神的な領域に閉じ込め、公的生活への参加権を否定する宗教観を露呈している。民主主義は、宗教共同体に属する市民を含むすべての市民が意見を表明し、政党に参加し、投票できるという考えの上に成り立っている。大臣の発言は、この原則に対する直接的な挑戦である。

大臣はさらに、「国家が世俗の領域にとどまり、宗教が精神的な領域にとどまる時こそ、民主主義と共同体内の平和が維持される」と書いている。

民主主義は、市民が自由に話し、投票し、参加できる時に維持される。これには宗教的な市民も含まれる。大臣の投稿は、政治権力が憲法原則の言葉を使って宗教共同体を沈黙させる方法を示している。それは、正義がイデオロギーに取って代わられることを示している。国家と宗教の境界が、抑圧を正当化するために利用されることを示している。

彼はこう付け加える。「わずか1週間前、日本の最高裁判所も、信者に対する大規模な金銭要求や与党との密接な関係などの問題で、統一教会に対する最終的な解散命令を出した。」

これは不正確である。解散決定は与党との関係に触れていない。法務大臣がメディアの語りを司法文書と混同しているのは憂慮すべきことだ。韓国では、指導者が有罪判決を受けた宗教、または「政治に干渉する」宗教を迅速に解散させることを認める法案が審議中である。この文脈で、大臣による日本決定の誤解釈は不気味な響きを持つ。
大臣は、会長に戻りながら「同様に」と統一教会を指してこう書く。「この事件も同様に重大な犯罪であり、その責任に応じた厳しい刑事罰は避けられない。」法務大臣は公平性を保証すべき存在である。進行中の捜査について予断を述べてはならない。裁判が行われる前に「厳罰は避けられない」と宣言することは、司法制度の信頼性を損なう。

大臣は投稿を、マタイによる福音書7章15節を太字で引用して締めくくる。「偽預言者に注意せよ。彼らは羊の衣を着てあなたがたのところに来るが、内側は貪欲な狼である。」

彼は、自分が嫌う宗教運動の指導者たちを描写するためにこの聖句を公式Facebookアカウントで使用した。

チョン氏は敬虔な長老派クリスチャンとして知られる。彼の教会には多くの善良なクリスチャンと正しい人々がいるが、新天地や他の団体から脱会させるための「脱会カウンセリング」（deprogramming）を行う牧師も含まれる。

これらの実践には、新天地などのメンバーを誘拐し、信仰を棄てるよう強制することが含まれる。大臣が公式の場で聖書を引用することは、彼自身が守ると主張する境界線を越える行為である。彼は他者が宗教と政治を混同していると非難しながら、自分は宗教を呼び起こしている。
統一教会の指導者、韓鶴子総裁（83歳）は、数ヶ月間韓国で拘束されており、現在は監視下の病院に入院している。彼女も政治干渉の容疑を受けている。

高齢の宗教指導者の拘束は疑問を呼ぶ。95歳の男性と83歳の女性が過酷な状況に置かれる時、政府は彼らが裁判を見るまで生きていないことを望んでいるのではないかと疑いたくなる。宗教運動は何世紀にもわたり迫害に耐えてきた。それらは帝国、独裁政権、政治的嵐を生き延びてきた。この時期も生き延びるだろう。政府と政党は興亡するが、教会は存続する。

―――――

title: 家庭連合を解散させたのは本当に「法」だけだったのか——多数派感情と韓国起源への歴史的偏見を問う
previewText: 6月22日、日本の最高裁判所は世界平和統一家庭連合（旧統一教会）に対する解散命令を最終確定た。これを受け、韓国『世界日報』の宗教専門記者・鄭聖洙（チョン・ソンス）氏は6月25日、鋭い論考を発表した。

blocks.text:
6月22日、日本の最高裁判所は世界平和統一家庭連合（旧統一教会）に対する解散命令を最終確定た。これを受け、韓国『世界日報』の宗教専門記者・鄭聖洙（チョン・ソンス）氏は6月25日、鋭い論考を発表した。

タイトルは「日本は何を解散させたのか」。
単なる判決報道を超え、宗教の自由という民主主義の根幹が試されているのではないか、という根本的な問いを投げかける内容だ。

メディアで「高額献金」「被害者」「政治家との癒着」といった単語ばかりが目立つ中、この記事はそうした一面的報道を超えた歴史的・文化的背景や、今回の判決が今後どのような意味を持つのかを丁寧に考察している。

以下は原文記事の日本語訳である。  

原文：世界日報 鄭聖洙（チョン・ソンス）宗教専門記者│2026年6月25日

去る22日、日本の最高裁判所は、世界平和統一家庭連合（旧統一教会）に対する東京高等裁判所の解散命令決定を最終的に確定した。判決の報せに接した瞬間、憂慮を隠せなかった。多数の感情が宗教の自由という基本権よりも優先されるとき、民主主義は危険な試練の場に立たされる。法的判断は尊重されなければならないが、すべての判決が歴史的な正当性を保証するわけではない。司法部の決定は当時の法律を反映するに過ぎず、歴史は、その決定が自由を拡大したのか、それとも偏見に屈したのかを冷徹に問い直すからである。

今回の判決を見て、一つの疑問が頭から離れない。日本裁判所は、教団の長期間にわたる献金関連の民事上の違法行為を解散命令の根拠として提示した。しかし、違法行為への責任追及と宗教法人解散という最も強力な制裁の間には、果たして十分な比例性があったのかは依然として議論の対象である。加えて今回の決定は、教団幹部の重大な刑事犯罪ではなく、民事上の違法行為を根拠とした日本憲政史上初の宗教法人解散事例である点で、少なからぬ論争を残している。

すべての事件の発端は、2022年の安倍晋三元首相暗殺事件だった。犯人は母親の高額献金で家庭が破綻したとして、個人的な恨みを犯行動機として明らかにした。もちろん被害者たちの声には耳を傾けるべきであり、違法行為があれば法的責任を負うのが当然である。しかし、個人の犯罪と宗教団体全体の存立とは本質的に異なる事案である。安倍元首相を暗殺したのは犯人個人であり、教団ではない。それにもかかわらず、メディアの刺激的な特集報道と政界の線引き、世論の急激な悪化が連動し、今日の解散命令局面をもたらした。個人の犯罪が宗教団体全体の責任へと拡大されたという批判が出る理由である。

民主主義社会で最も危険な瞬間は、大衆の怒りが法律を圧倒するときである。日本を宗教の自由が保障された先進民主国家と思うことが多いが、歴史の裏面を覗いてみれば全く異なる感情が流れている。

外部から流入した宗教や異質な信仰に対する日本社会の警戒心は、想像以上に深く古い。

すでに16世紀末から多数のカトリック信者が処刑され、潜伏キリシタンたちは数百年にわたり信仰を隠したまま息を潜めて生きなければならなかった。日本統治時代に在日朝鮮人が民族的アイデンティティを守るために守ってきた信仰や民族宗教も、日本社会で決して歓迎されることはなかった。さらに明治維新以降は国家神道体制を構築し、天皇中心の宗教秩序を全国民に強要し、宗教と国家権力が結託した強力な同質性文化を形成した。

今回の統一教会に向けられた敵対感情も、このような歴史・文化的文脈から自由ではない。特に日本社会において統一教会は、宗教的な拒否感に加え、韓国で始まった宗教であるという二重の烙印を負っていた。

しかし、日本国内の家庭連合信者たちが社会に貢献してきた厳然たる歴史的事実も存在する。

1970年代、日本社会がイデオロギー対立と共産主義拡大論争の中にあった時期、一部の信者たちは命を賭して「勝共」運動に参加し、当時の社会運動地形の中で一つの市民的対応勢力として機能した。

また、日韓関係が今よりはるかに冷却していた時期、日本信者たちが大挙して国際合同結婚に参加し、韓国人配偶者と出会い、民間レベルの日韓交流と和解の接点を広げることに一定の役割を果たしたという点も、しばしば言及される。少なくとも一つの宗教団体を、歴史的な功罪を分離せずに単一のイメージに還元するのは危険である。

国際社会で懸念の声が出る理由もここにある。米国務省は『国際宗教自由報告書』を通じて、日本政府の家庭連合解散命令請求を「既存の慣行から逸脱した措置（deviation from the norm）」と明記した。刑事犯罪ではなく民事上の違法行為を根拠に宗教法人解散を推進した初の事例だという指摘である。これは国際社会がこの事案を国内問題を超えて、普遍的宗教自由の観点から厳しく注視していることを示している。

民主主義国家において宗教の自由は、多数が支持する宗教だけのための権利ではない。むしろ、社会的非難の中心に立たされた宗教であるほど、より厳格な原則の中で法の保護を受けなければならない。大衆の好感を得る宗教だけが自由を享受できるならば、それは自由ではなく「特権」に過ぎない。

判決により法人は解散されても、信仰まで消えることはない。ローマ帝国の迫害の中でも初期キリスト教は生き残り、ソ連と中国の弾圧の中でも信念は消されなかった。法人は国家がなくすことはできるが、人間内面の信念は決して解散させることはできない。

日本の家庭連合は行政的に大きな試練を経験するだろうが、信仰共同体の本質までは消滅しないだろう。当代の法的正当性を認められた判決が、後世の歴史の法廷で覆された事例は数えきれない。日本の最高裁判所の今回の決定も、遠からぬ未来に厳しい歴史的評価を受けることになるだろう。

解散されたのが果たして一つの宗教法人だけだったのか、それとも民主主義を支える宗教自由の一部までもだったのかについての歴史的評価は、今まさに始まったばかりである。

---  

本記事は韓国『世界日報』に掲載された韓国語記事の日本語訳です。

title: Family Federation Dissolution Confirmed: Japan's Supreme Court Avoided All Constitutional Debate
previewText: Japan's Supreme Court, which is meant to be the final protector of the constitution, confirmed the dissolution of a religious group without ever discussing that constitution. It is the first case in

blocks.text: Japan's Supreme Court, which is meant to be the final protector of the constitution, confirmed the dissolution of a religious group without ever discussing that constitution. It is the first case in Japan where a religious corporation was dissolved not over a criminal offense, but over a civil-law dispute alone.

The group is the Family Federation for World Peace and Unification (the Unification Church). Former chairman Tanaka Tomihiro and Imamura, a former Legal Affairs Bureau official, went through the ruling on the YouTube program "No Filter."

On June 22, 2026, Japan's Supreme Court rejected the appeal of the Family Federation  and confirmed the order to dissolve it. Japan's Ministry of Education filed for the dissolution in October 2023. After that, the district court and the high court both upheld it, and after more than two and a half years, the Supreme Court reached its conclusion.
An Overview of the Supreme Court Decision
The decision held two surprises.

The first is that the Supreme Court, which is supposed to handle the constitution, avoided discussing the constitution. The second is that even a "settlement," which is meant to bring a dispute to a peaceful close, was treated as evidence of wrongdoing.

On top of that, the decision was very short: the actual ruling was a single line, and the whole document was only four pages. Former chairman Tanaka Tomihiro says, "It was so short that I could guess what was inside before I even read it."

Although this kind of case is normally handled by five judges, the name of one judge, Okino Masami, was missing from the decision. She was the judge the Family Federation had asked to have removed, because of critical remarks she had made in the past. Tanaka suspects that "the inconvenient part was quietly taken out."
Avoiding the Constitutional Debate

Japan's Supreme Court is called "the guardian of the constitution," the court that makes the final check on whether a law or a ruling breaks the constitution. The "special appeal" the group used is also a procedure that is allowed only when the reason is a violation of the constitution. So the group knocked on that last door, saying, "This dissolution order breaks the constitution." Several constitutional scholars and lawyers had submitted written opinions pointing out constitutional violations.
But the decision did not answer those constitutional questions head-on.

For example, the group had argued, "Deciding to dissolve us without ever holding an oral hearing (a session to hear each side's case) violates our right to a trial." This too is a constitutional argument. In response, the decision treated the dissolution order not as a normal trial where the two sides argue in court, but as a "non-contentious case" that the court handles as routine business, and brushed it aside, saying "so no oral hearing is needed" and "this is an administrative action."

Then, at the end of the decision, the other constitutional arguments the group had laid out were all dismissed together as "in substance, merely claims of a violation of ordinary law." This means, "That is not a constitutional issue, just a matter of ordinary law," and once it is treated that way, a special appeal can no longer get through.
Tanaka spoke with clear surprise.

"That is exactly why we filed a special appeal on the grounds of a constitutional violation, but they rejected all of it. They put a lid on the constitutional debate completely. If that is so, what is the point of having a Supreme Court at all?"
The Grounds for the Ruling
The reason for the dissolution is Article 81(1)(i) of Japan's Religious Corporations Act.

What matters is that this "violation of law" was found to include not only criminal acts but also a "wrongful act" under civil law, an act that breaks the law and harms people. The group has not had a single criminal case. It was dissolved over a civil-law dispute alone.

The district court found that, from 1973 to 2022, believers had kept asking for donations in ways that amounted to wrongful acts and had harmed many people, and the Supreme Court took this as it stood. But Imamura questions that end date, "until 2022." The last civil case fought in court was around 2014. If you ask which act, and when, counted as a violation after that, almost no one can answer.

Even so, the ruling said the violations continued until 2022. What is more, even cases that had been closed by "settlement" in the past may have been counted as evidence of a violation. A settlement, which is supposed to be an agreement to end a dispute peacefully, was turned into "evidence of having done something wrong."

The group also had a way to challenge the fact-finding itself. On the same day as the special appeal, it had filed another objection called a "permitted appeal," which can point out not only constitutional problems but also faulty fact-finding and violations of law. But this objection was decided not by the Supreme Court, but by the high court itself, the very court that had made those findings, and it was thrown out the same day, on March 31.
The door to question the constitution was closed at the Supreme Court, and the door to question the fact-finding was closed at the high court. For the group, both doors to fight were shut.
What happens to believers' "freedom of faith"?
The decision said that the impact on both freedom of religious activity and freedom of association would be "only an indirect, practical effect."

Even if the group loses its buildings, faith itself is not banned; even if it is no longer a religious corporation, it can keep going as an ordinary group, so the impact is "indirect." That is the reasoning. But Tanaka pushes back: there is no way that losing places of worship and the centers of their activity is "indirect" for believers.
The decision itself also admits, at one point, how serious the problem is.

Once the dissolution is final, places of worship and other property will be sold off, and this could get in the way of believers' religious life. So the decision says it "must carefully examine whether the constitution allows going this far."

Yet the Supreme Court did not carry out that examination itself. If it is truly a problem, then Parliament has no choice but to rewrite the law. And the court left that big homework behind and stepped away from it.
Concerns for the Future
What this decision leaves behind is not just the fate of the Family Federation.

Tanaka points out that religion has a weakness it cannot avoid. While faith burns strong, things are fine, but once it cools, some people later come to feel they were "deceived" and sue the group. This is not unusual in the world of religion. In other words, no religious group can be completely free of civil disputes.

On top of this, the new decision weighs heavily. As noted earlier, even the fact of a settlement was treated as evidence of a violation. Now that the peaceful way out has been shut, religious groups will come to feel it is safer to avoid settlements and fight every dispute to the end in court.

From now on, the dissolution of a religious corporation may also move forward through a closed, non-public process. Together with a new law passed in recent years that limits aggressive fundraising for donations, the organizations and places that support faith will walk a narrower road than before.

Believers could not even argue their case fully in court. And the conclusion that finally came was a thin one of only four pages, and it felt careless. The Japanese media, which kept reporting on the whole uproar for a long time, also turned its attention away once the trial closed, and there is hardly any reporting that digs into what such a decision actually says. The worry remains that, among people who see only this decision, prejudice against people of faith will spread even further.

The conflict surrounding the Family Federation has continued for many decades. Without knowing that long background and what each believer is really like, one cannot speak about this group. Even if a dissolution order is handed down, it is a procedure that removes legal status, and it is not a reason to brand believers as a criminal group, as antisocial, or as a cult.

title: U.S. Ambassador Barred From S. Korea Warns of Political Crisis: "Lee Jae-myung Must Step Down”
previewText: Morse Tan, who is under a travel ban and being investigated for defamation, gave a live-streamed interview on June 17, 2026, speaking in detail about the breakdown of the rule of law in South Korea

blocks.text: Morse Tan, who is under a travel ban and being investigated for defamation, gave a live-streamed interview on June 17, 2026, speaking in detail about the breakdown of the rule of law in South Korea and allegations of election fraud.
A Former U.S. Ambassador Stuck in Seoul

Morse Tan @MorseHTan served as the U.S. Ambassador-at-Large for Global Criminal Justice under President Donald Trump's first administration. The role involves investigating mass killings and large-scale human rights abuses around the world and reporting findings to the president. He currently teaches at Liberty University in Virginia.

South Korean police opened a defamation investigation against Tan and applied for a travel ban after he said at a press conference at the National Press Club in Washington, D.C., in June 2025, that President Lee Jae-myung had been involved in a serious crime as a teenager and sent to a juvenile detention center. 

Tan had come to South Korea to personally check whether the June 3, 2026, local elections had been conducted fairly. He remains in Seoul today.

In December 2025, a Seoul appeals court ruled that similar statements made by attorney Kang Yong-seok on YouTube were "enough to make ordinary voters believe that President Lee had been to a juvenile detention center," and sentenced him to one year in prison, suspended for two years.
"I Have Evidence. My Confidence Has Not Wavered."
When host Lee Young-don asked about the defamation investigation, Tan did not back down from his claims about Lee's alleged time in a juvenile detention center.

"I looked at the various evidence and concluded there was enough to support what I said. My view has not changed since the press conference in Washington, D.C. If anything, my confidence has grown stronger. They do not try to prove otherwise. Because they cannot."

When asked about being called "far-right" and a "conspiracy theorist" by those aligned with President Lee, Tan replied, "That is a joke. If the mainstream of Korea is far-right, then I guess that is what it is."
Three Lawyers and Outreach to the U.S.
Tan said he is fighting back on several fronts at the same time.
"I have good lawyers representing me. At the same time, I am reaching out directly to people in the U.S. government and working with U.S. media."

He also revealed that former Prime Minister Hwang Kyo-ahn @hkyoahn  has traveled to the United States and briefed Mike Lindell, a conservative businessman and close ally of President Trump, on Tan's situation. "The message has reached the highest levels of the U.S. government directly," Tan said.

In response to Tan's travel ban, a U.S. State Department spokesperson told the conservative outlet Daily Caller News Foundation, "The Trump Administration has no higher priority than the safety and security of Americans."
The spokesperson also said the department "takes seriously any concerns that U.S. citizens are subject to exit bans without a fair and transparent process to resolve them."
South Korea's Legal System — "Like a North Korean Courtroom"
Drawing on his years of research and investigation into international criminal justice and human rights, Tan shared his view of South Korea's legal system.

"The rule of law in Korea has broken down on a large scale. The legislature, the courts, and the prosecution have all come under political influence. Among them, people who have studied the North Korean way of doing things have come to make up a large number. In North Korean courts, only the words that the Kim Jong-un regime orders to be announced are announced. The same thing is starting to happen in South Korea."

Host Lee Young-don added his own view, saying, "The National Assembly is now made up mostly of lawmakers who won their seats through fraudulent elections, and that is connected to the courts and the government, causing the whole country to break down."
Election Fraud Allegations — "A Third-Grader Could See the Problem"
Tan has consistently claimed that South Korean elections have been rigged, starting with the June 2025 presidential election.

"Last year, my international election observation team put together a report. You can find it at election-fraud.com. At 140 polling stations, the number of actual ballots cast and the number reported by the National Election Commission differed by nine to fifteen percent. The math simply does not add up. A third-grader could see that something is wrong."

Lee Young-don also pointed to the gap between early votes and votes cast on election day. "In past elections, the difference was around eight to ten percent. This time it was even wider. That kind of gap is not normal."

South Korea's election authorities, the Lee Jae-myung administration, and major media outlets dismiss these claims as conspiracy theories. Tan pushed back, calling that "gaslighting" — a term for when someone tries to make another person doubt what they can clearly see is true.
Warnings of Communization, Military Collapse, and Rebellion
Lee Young-don summarized Tan's views on the biggest dangers facing South Korea.

"South Korea is moving quickly toward communization and dictatorship. The rule of law is breaking down, and the most basic human rights are being destroyed. If North Korea swallows South Korea, it would have the same effect as China taking over the entire Korean Peninsula."

On the destruction of the military system, Tan himself said, "Generals and colonels are being removed one after another, and the military academy system is being dismantled. This is an act of rebellion."
Tan noted that as someone who has investigated authoritarian regimes around the world in his former role, he recognized this as a familiar pattern.
Two Messages to the Police
Tan sent two different messages to South Korean police.

The first was a criticism of their failure to investigate the allegations against Lee Jae-myung. Tan said that the more seriously the allegations are investigated, the more facts damaging to Lee will come out, and that is precisely why the investigation is not being done.

"The police know. They know that investigating this will cause problems. The more they come at me, the stronger I become. The police just follow orders from above. It is wrong, but it is not funny. The police are being gaslit."

The second was a direct appeal to officers on the streets of Seoul, where protests have been ongoing. He said in English, "These are your neighbors, these are your friends, these are your family members. Do not harm them."
"Lee Jae-myung Must Step Down"
In the middle of talking about election fraud and the breakdown of the justice system, Tan stated his view of President Lee Jae-myung directly in English.
"I think Lee Jae-myung needs to step down."

He also called for the National Assembly to be dissolved and for a new, legitimate election to be held. "Lee Jae-myung is not the rightful president of South Korea. The National Assembly should be made up of people truly chosen by the people."
The U.S.-Korea Alliance and His Vision for the Future
Tan was also clear about where he stands on the U.S.-South Korea alliance.
"The alliance must be strengthened, not destroyed. China and North Korea are actively working to tear it apart, and the Lee Jae-myung administration is helping them do it."
At the end of the interview, Tan praised the South Korean people for the many ways they continue to resist through music, art, social media, and public protests.

"The Korean people are doing so well. More and more people are waking up and raising their voices. Even in this situation, God is at work. I know that God loves South Korea. Let us keep fighting together for truth and justice."

Tan said he hopes to play a role in Korean reunification and in strengthening the U.S.-South Korea alliance in the future, whether through a position in the Trump administration or through independent work.
Since early June, he has been unable to return to his family in America or go back to his job there. Even so, he believes this is God's will, and he continues to work for South Korea.

title: Seoul Court Sentences Yoon Suk-yeol to 30 Years — "Who Is Really the One Aiding the Enemy?"
previewText:
A former South Korean president has been sentenced to 30 years in prison for responding militarily to North Korea. The question that follows is unavoidable: who does a verdict like this serve?
 
The

blocks.text: A former South Korean president has been sentenced to 30 years in prison for responding militarily to North Korea. The question that follows is unavoidable: who does a verdict like this serve?
The Verdict and the Shape of the Prosecution

On June 12, the Seoul Central District Court sentenced former President Yoon Suk-yeol to 30 years in prison on charges of general treason (일반이적) and abuse of power. It is the first time in South Korean history that a former president has been convicted on enemy-aiding charges.
The case began in July 2025, when Democratic Party of Korea lawmaker Park Seon-won filed a complaint with the special prosecutor.
Defence attorney Kim Gye-ri explained the core problem with the indictment:
"Enemy instigation requires proof of collusion with a foreign enemy. The special prosecution could not establish that. So the charge they used instead was general treason."

General treason is a charge that can be applied when a person damages their own country's military interests — without any need to prove collusion with the enemy. The defence also noted that the lawmaker who filed the complaint, Park Seon-won, has a prior record of violations under the National Security Act.
Yoon filed an appeal on the day of sentencing.
The Defence's Arguments at Trial

Throughout the proceedings, Yoon consistently denied both ordering the drone operation in advance and approving it after the fact. He rejected the special prosecution's claim connecting the operation to the martial law declaration as fabrication.
In his final statement, Yoon maintained that the operation was "a legitimate military response to North Korea's trash balloon provocations" and pleaded not guilty.

The defence team issued a statement in the same vein: "The drone-based leaflet operation directed at North Korea was a legitimate response to the 7,000 trash balloons North Korea sent into our country. We strongly protest a prosecution that calls this enemy-aiding."

The defence also argued that the court's interpretation — that a military response to North Korean provocation constitutes aiding the enemy — has no basis in legal logic. The court rejected all of these arguments.
North Korea's Trash Balloons — A Provocation Left Unexamined
Behind the defence's claim of legitimate response lies a pattern of repeated North Korean provocation.
From spring 2024 onward, North Korea sent large numbers of balloons carrying trash, excrement, and hazardous materials across the border into South Korea.

Thousands of balloons entered South Korean territory, with some landing at various locations across Seoul. Multiple vehicles were reported damaged in separate incidents. Analysis of the waste found inside the balloons confirmed the presence of parasites including roundworms, traced to human excrement.

North Korea justified the campaign. Kim Yo-jong, vice director of the Korean Workers' Party, described the trash balloons in an official statement as "gifts of sincerity" and framed them as retaliation for South Korea's refusal to stop anti-North Korea leaflet operations across the border.

The court characterised the drone operation as "a psychological warfare operation designed to provoke a North Korean military reaction." The documented reality of North Korea's own provocations received virtually no consideration in the verdict.
The Security Foundations Dismantled Under Moon and Lee
The defence's question — who is really the one aiding the enemy — points to a specific chain of policy decisions made by two successive administrations.

The Moon Jae-in administration stripped the National Intelligence Service of its counter-espionage authority in 2020. The core function responsible for detecting and prosecuting North Korean and foreign intelligence operations was effectively neutralised. Under the stated goal of improving inter-Korean relations, South Korea's intelligence and surveillance capabilities directed at the North retreated broadly.

The Lee Jae-myung administration disbanded the Defence Counterintelligence Command — the military body dedicated to investigating espionage and enemy-aiding activity within the armed forces. Its dissolution left a direct gap in the military's internal security. The same administration also effectively dismantled the Drone Operations Command.

The defence's position is that this successive dismantling of security infrastructure is the true act of enemy-aiding — and that what Yoon and his co-defendants did was a legitimate attempt at national defence against that very crisis.
A Verdict Delivered as Security Collapses — and a Media That Looked Away
At the post-verdict press conference, Kim Gye-ri put the question directly.

"North Korea has entered the Russia-Ukraine war and expanded its drone warfare capabilities. In the middle of all this, we disbanded the Drone Operations Command. Does that not seem strange? Who is it that is actually aiding the enemy?"

The side that attempted a military response — while counter-espionage functions were being stripped, the counterintelligence command was being disbanded, and drone capabilities were being eliminated — is the side that was convicted of enemy-aiding. It is why the defence described the ruling as "an act of self-harm against national security by the judiciary."
Kim closed with a direct appeal to the public.
"Whether the president engineered this case is not for the judiciary to decide. Citizens, please make that judgment yourselves."
Most major South Korean media outlets reported the verdict largely as established fact.

The documented reality of the trash balloon campaign and the dismantling of security infrastructure received little examination. The defence's arguments were reduced to brief rebuttals appended at the end of reports. The entire trial was conducted behind closed doors, and the evidentiary record was never made public — yet reporting that followed the prosecution's account without scrutiny dominated the coverage.
A press whose core function is to hold power to account gave little sign of doing so.
The Appeal
At the press conference immediately following the verdict, the defence team declared that "if these unjust proceedings continue, history will demand a reckoning."

Attorney Bae Ui-cheol described the ruling as "an act of self-harm against national security that has bound the hands and feet of the soldiers and officials who work for this country's defence" and "an act of tyranny by a judiciary that sides with North Korea."

The 30-year sentence is the second-heaviest handed down across the eight criminal proceedings against Yoon, behind the life imprisonment term imposed in the separate insurrection case in February 2026. Yoon is currently contesting that ruling before the Seoul High Court.

title: 旧統一教会：解散後の粛清_学校における監視と強制的なカウンセリング
previewText:
新たな学校向け手順が教育者に対し、旧統一教会家庭の子どもたちを特定・監視するよう指示しており、プライバシー侵害への懸念が高まっている。

原文：Bitter Winter │ パトリシア・デュバル著 │ 2026年6月4日

blocks.text:
新たな学校向け手順が教育者に対し、旧統一教会家庭の子どもたちを特定・監視するよう指示しており、プライバシー侵害への懸念が高まっている。

原文：Bitter Winter │ パトリシア・デュバル著 │ 2026年6月4日
カルト問題に関する心理カウンセリングの手引き
文部科学省――宗教問題を所管し、統一教会の解散を申請した省庁――の担当者に奨励される形で、日本臨床心理士会は学校カウンセラーおよび臨床心理士向けの冊子を作成した。この「手引き」は反カルト文献およびマインドコントロール理論への言及のみを根拠としている。

冊子には以下の指示が記されている。
「3. 丁寧に話を聞き、配慮をもって具体的な内容を引き出す。子どもの生活状況や家庭環境を詳細に把握することが必要です。その際、子どもができるだけ具体的な状況を話せるよう促すことが重要です。たとえば、日曜日にどのような場所へ連れて行かれるか、親にどのようなことを言われているかを尋ねることで、宗教的な要因が関係しているかどうかを明らかにすることができます。その後、該当する子どもが特定された場合には、学校管理職と連携してカウンセリングを組織する。」
この指示それ自体が、信教の自由に関する権利――自らの宗教的帰属を明かすことを強制されない権利を含む――の侵害に当たる。このことは、自由権規約委員会の一般的意見第22号において明確に示されている。「第18条2項および第17条に従い、何人も自らの思想または宗教もしくは信念への帰属を明らかにすることを強制されない。」
自由権規約（ICCPR）第17条は「何人も、その私生活、家族、住居もしくは通信に対して恣意的にもしくは不法に干渉され、または名誉もしくは信用を不法に攻撃されない」と定め、第18条2項は「何人も、自ら選択する宗教もしくは信念を持ちまたは採用する自由を侵害するおそれのある強制を受けない」と定めている。
子どもの宗教的帰属に関する情報収集を学校カウンセラーや職員に指示し、その上でカウンセリングを課すという手順は、子どものプライバシーの権利と信教の自由の双方を侵害するものである。

明らかな問題が報告されていない状況においても、学校職員は子どもたちに家族の宗教的慣行について情報を提供するよう促し、また親への批判を表明させるよう奨励されている。

「同時に、子どもは親について話すことをためらう場合があります。否定的なことを言いたくない、あるいは話題を避けようとすることもあります。そのため、子どもが困難や苦労を感じた状況を尋ねる際には、プレッシャーをかけず、子どものペースで話せるよう、状況を一つ一つ丁寧に確認していくことが重要です。」
その上で、「宗教的背景に関連した困難を抱えている疑いがある生徒については、学校管理職に報告・検討する」よう指示されている。

この目的のため、子どもたちは宗教的帰属を学校全体で共有することに同意するよう求められる。

「情報共有に先立ち、生徒の同意を得ることが重要な考慮事項です。生徒が難色を示した場合、カウンセラーは情報共有が生徒の安全と福祉を確保するためであることを丁寧に説明し、懸念が解消されるまで継続的な対話を通じて理解を求める必要があります。同意が得られた後は、学校全体として組織的・体系的に対応することが重要です。学校管理職のもと、カウンセラー、担任、学年主任、養護教諭、スクールソーシャルワーカーなど関係職員が連携し、事実情報を丁寧に整理・確認する。」

続いて手引きは、「カウンセラーがよく陥る不適切な対応」を取り上げている。不適切な対応の第一として挙げられているのは、「親や家族とよく話し合ってみましょう」というものである。

その説明は示唆的だ。「子どもは、家族と十分に話し合うことが難しいことを十分に理解しています。それは単に親が頑固であったり、言葉による虐待があるためではなく、親の考えが宗教的確信に基づいているため変わりにくいのです。さらに、子どもは日常生活の中で、自分の意見が親の望みと異なる場合には受け入れてもらえないという経験を繰り返しています。そのため、単に『家族と話し合いなさい』と助言することは、子どもの現実を把握できていない可能性があります。」
子どもへの指示は明確である。学校で自分の親の宗教的帰属について話されていることを、親に伝えてはならない、というものだ。
2025年6月にジュネーブの国連での証言において、二世信者の母親である西芳子氏は、自分の息子がテレビの報道を見て学校で説明を受けてから、母親に口を利かなくなったと述べた。息子は、両親が犯罪組織に属していると信じ込むようになった。この母親は、学校での説明について話さないよう子どもたちに言い聞かせられており、親が質問しても答えてもらえないため、何が起きているか知ることができないと述べた。

同氏はこう語った。「私の人生で最も辛い瞬間の一つは、14歳の息子とのものでした。ある日、歯医者に行った際、テレビが私たちの教会を『犯罪的』と報じているのを見て帰宅した息子は動揺していました。彼は私に尋ねました。『僕たちは何か悪いことをしたの？』私はいいえと答え、説明しようとしました。しかし学校やメディアで憎悪にさらされ続けた息子はこう言いました。『この教会をやめないなら、連絡を絶つ。愛していると言うけれど、どうして自分の子どもをそんな危険にさらせるの？』息子の恐怖は本物でした。仲間外れにされることへの恐怖。友人を失うことへの恐怖。教育や就職の機会を奪われることへの恐怖。かつて優しかった息子は今、自分の家族を恐れ、妄想と羞恥心の中で生きています。この政策は社会を守っているのではありません。平和な市民を犯罪者として烙印を押し、数万もの命と家族を壊しているのです。」
子どもたちが親に対抗させられた後、学校チームは一時的な保護措置を含む引き離しの検討に入る。生徒に対して「親や他の信者のいる環境から離れた一時的な居場所」が提案される。「計画によれば、生活再建への道を歩む支援として、そのような居場所を提供する」とされている。
世界平和統一家庭連合の信仰は家族的価値観を根幹とし、信者の多くが愛情と敬意の中で大家族を育んでいる。日本政府の計画はこうした信仰に基づく家族を解体することを目的とし、実際にその崩壊を招いている。日本の公立学校で実施されているこの政策は、旧統一教会二世信者数千人への烙印を結果としてもたらしており、この点に関するあらゆる国際人権基準に反するものである。
結論
この状況は、日本における良心と信仰の自由にとって極めて深刻である。
私たちは、国連人権機関に対し、すべての人の信教の自由、平和的集会の自由、および表現の自由を守る義務について、日本当局に改めて想起させるよう、謹んで要請する。

パトリシア・デュバルは、パリ弁護士会所属の弁護士。ソルボンヌ大学で公法の修士号を取得し、国際法を専門とする。

title: 「アメリカよ、神に立ち返れ！」—かつて退廃の密林と呼ばれたNYで描かれた刷新のビジョン
previewText: 「アメリカは神に選ばれた国である——しかし今日、彼らは神から離れてしまった。」50年前、アメリカ建国200周年に際し、文鮮明総裁はこのメッセージを携えて全米を巡った。

blocks.text: 「アメリカは神に選ばれた国である——しかし今日、彼らは神から離れてしまった。」50年前、アメリカ建国200周年に際し、文鮮明総裁はこのメッセージを携えて全米を巡った。
その旅は二つの大群衆の前で頂点に達した——ヤンキースタジアムに集まった4万人と、ワシントンD.C.に集まった30万人である。
そして今日、トランプ大統領は建国250周年を「神への再献身」として記念しようとしている。文総裁があの群衆の前で語った言葉は色褪せていない。それは今こそ、かつてないほど必要とされている。
「神に選ばれた国」
文総裁のスピーチは一つの信念から始まった——神がアメリカを導いて建国させたという確信である。
1976年6月1日、統一教会（現・家庭連合）は建国200周年を記念して「God Bless America Festival」を開催した。
集会は文鮮明・韓鶴子総裁が主導した。なぜ韓国人の指導者が、アメリカ市民でもないのに、国家的な祝典を主導するのか？文総裁は、アメリカ合衆国が神によって構想された国であるという確固たる信念によると語った。神を求めてこの地にやって来た人々が、神を中心とした国家を築いた、と彼は説明した。
わずか200年の間に、神はこの国を地上で最も強大な国へと育て上げた。しかし祝福には責任が伴い、その責任を手放した国は祝福をも失う、と彼は言った。
集会前夜——ほうきを手に、動き出す街

ヤンキースタジアムの集会は突発的なものではなかった。
1972年に文・韓総裁がアメリカに来てから四年間、全米で積み重ねてきた活動の大きな節目だった。
準備は街頭から始まった。信徒たちは「God Bless America」と書かれたユニフォームを着てほうきを持ち、自らの手でニューヨークの街を掃き清めた。
当時、アメリカ統一教会の会長を務めていたニール・サロネンは後にその光景を振り返った。もし誰もが自分の家の前の道路を掃除すれば、街の問題はなくなる——しかし各自が自分の役割を果たし、他の人も同じようにするという信頼が必要だ、と。それは言葉ではなく行動で示された信念だった。
サロネンの二歳になる娘も小さなユニフォームを着て列に加わった。間もなくその光景は新聞に掲載され、街中の話題となった。
集会が近づくにつれ、興奮は街全体に広がった。文総裁の姿を一目見ようと人々がチケットを求め、支持の署名は数十万件にまで膨れ上がった。
十人のオペレーターが朝から深夜まで鳴り止まない電話に対応した。マンハッタンの街頭には文総裁の顔を掲げたポスターが並び、新聞には全面広告が掲載され、ラジオとテレビが集会の告知を流し続けた。
信徒たちは地下鉄の駅や街角に立ち、チラシを配りながら通行人に6月1日の夜のことを伝えた。街は様々なイベントや集まりで満ち、ウォール街では数千人が集まる集会も開かれた。
そうしたイベントや集まりが機運を盛り上げる中、アメリカ経済の中心地であるウォール街でも、フェスティバルの知らせを街の核心部へと伝えるための最大規模の集まりが開かれた。
そしてすべての活動を貫いていたのは一つの信念——6月1日の夜、国全体が目覚めるという確信だった。
嵐の中の奇跡
その夜、物語は災難から始まった。
プログラムが始まる直前、スタジアムに嵐が襲いかかった。時速約100キロの強風が新しく設置された装飾を吹き飛ばした。気象予報士は竜巻を警告し、激しい雨が降り注いだ。集会は中止寸前にまで追い込まれた。
しかし人々は立ち去らなかった。信徒、家族連れ、来場者たちは席に座ったまま祈った。すると誰かが「You Are My Sunshine」を歌い始めた。一つの声がやがて多くの声となり、まもなく群衆全体が一緒に歌っていた。

その場にいた一人は後にこう振り返った。
「強風が私たちの設営したものをすべて吹き飛ばした。集会は中止寸前だった。」しかし歌声が大きくなるにつれ、「暗雲はついに晴れた」。

約30分後、嵐は去り、スタジアムはフェスティバルの開始を待った。今日に至るまで、あの夜は奇跡として語り継がれている——信仰が天候さえも変えたという奇跡として
嵐が過ぎると、人々がさらに押し寄せた。教団の記録によれば、約4万人以上がスタジアムを埋め尽くし、フェスティバルは大成功を収めた。
アメリカへの愛から生まれた、帰還への呼びかけ
文総裁のスピーチの核心は、アメリカへの深い希望だった。彼は、かつて神に選ばれたこの国が、もう一度神のもとに立ち返ることを願う者として語った。
彼は率直な言葉でこの国の現状を描いた。世界はアメリカへの信頼を失い、ニューヨークは不道徳と堕落の密林と化した、と言った。
家族は崩壊し、教会は分裂し、国は共産主義の脅威にさらされていた。神は忘れられ、今にもこの地を去ろうとしている。そして彼は一つのシンプルな例えを用いた。
神はセメントである。神とともにあれば、アメリカはコンクリートのように一つにまとまる。しかし神なしには、砂のようになり、洪水が来れば、すべて流し去られてしまう。
アメリカが建国の真の精神に立ち返ることを、彼は願っていた。
「医師であり、消防士である」
では、なぜ韓国から来た一人のがここまでするのか？文総裁は一つの比喩で答えた。
あなたの家に病人がいるとき、外から医師を呼ぶ必要があるのではないか？家が火事になったとき、外から消防士を呼ぶ必要があるのではないか？神は私を医師として、消防士として、アメリカに遣わされた。

アメリカが背を向けたとしても、神は彼らを見捨てない、と彼は言った。
神の御心が世界を救うことにあり、アメリカがその先頭に立たなければならないことを、私は知っている。だからこそ、私はアメリカに来た。
アメリカから「神のもとに一つの世界」へ
この集会は単なる祝典ではなかった。
文・韓総裁にとって、それはアメリカにおける平和運動の出発点だった。
アメリカが神のもとに立ち返れば、他の国々もそれに続くと彼は信じた。文総裁は、自由を求めて共産主義から逃れてきた人々を一つにまとめることを呼びかけ、自由世界は今こそ共産主義に隷属する世界を解放しなければならないと訴えた。その先に彼が描いていたのが「神のもとに一つの世界」という姿だった。
他の国々もアメリカの模範に倣って自国の地に神の王国を築き、すべての人々が親なる神のもとで兄弟姉妹となる——それが彼のビジョンだった。
アメリカの新たな世紀への神の祝福を祈る言葉でスピーチを締めくくった。
五十年後
ヤンキースタジアムのあの夜に投げかけられた問いは、今も消えていない。
三ヶ月後、さらに大きな群衆——およそ30万人と言われる——がワシントン・モニュメントに集まった。
当時、この運動は支持だけでなく批判や論争も呼んだ。それでもこれらの集会が目指したものは、アメリカの刷新にとどまらなかった——人種や国籍の壁を越えて、世界が一つになることだった。

「神のもとのアメリカ」を語ったのは、文総裁だけではない。

1954年、アイゼンハワー大統領は忠誠の誓いに「神のもとに（under God）」という言葉を加える法律に署名し、1982年にはレーガン大統領がアメリカを「自由のために神に献身する国」と呼んだ。
しかし、これらの大統領が語ったのは一国の信仰だった。ヤンキースタジアムのビジョンははるかに大きかった——その信仰を、全世界を変えるための出発点として見ていたのである。
そして今、その問いが戻ってきた。

2026年、アメリカは建国250周年を迎える。トランプ大統領はこの節目を「リデディケート250（Rededicate 250）」と名付け、国を「神のもとに一つの国」として再献身することを呼びかけている。

アメリカが再び神に国を捧げようとする今、その行く先はどこか？
嵐の夜から五十年、あの問いは今も響き続けている。

title: "America, Turn Back to God!": A Vision of Renewal in a New York Once Called a Jungle of Depravity
previewText:

blocks.text: "America is a nation chosen by God—yet today they has turned away from Him." Fifty years ago, at America's 200th birthday, Rev. Moon carried this message across the country.
The journey reached its height before two great crowds—40,000 at Yankee Stadium, and 300,000 in Washington, D.C.

And today, President Trump is preparing to mark the nation's 250th birthday as a "rededication to God." The words Rev. Moon spoke before those crowds have not faded. They are needed now more than ever.
A "Nation Chosen by God"
Rev. Moon's speech began with one belief: that God had guided America into being.
On June 1, 1976, the Unification Church (today the Family Federation) held the "God Bless America Festival" for the nation's 200th birthday.

The rally was led by Rev. Moon and Dr. Hak Ja Han. Why would a Korean leader, not even an American citizen, lead a national celebration? Rev. Moon said it was his firm belief that the United States was conceived by God. People who came to this land seeking God, he explained, had built a nation centered on Him.
In a short 200 years, God raised this nation to be the mightiest on earth. But blessings come with responsibility, he said, and a nation that gives up that responsibility loses the blessing too.
Brooms in Hand: A City Astir Before the Rally
The Yankee Stadium rally was not a sudden idea. It was a major milestone in four years of work across America, ever since Rev. Moon and Dr. Hak Ja Han came to the United States in 1972.
The preparation began in the streets. Members put on uniforms that read "God Bless America," picked up brooms, and went out to sweep the streets of New York with their own hands.

Neil Salonen, then president of the Unification Church in the U.S., later remembered the scene. If everyone cleaned the street in front of their own house, there would be no problems on the streets—but each person has to do his part, and trust that others will do theirs. It was a belief shown not in words but in action. 

Even Salonen's two-year-old daughter put on a small uniform and joined the line. Before long, the sight was in the newspapers and on everyone's lips.
As the rally drew near, the excitement spread through the whole city. People called out for tickets to catch a glimpse of Rev. Moon, and signatures of support swelled into the hundreds of thousands.

Ten phone operators answered calls that never stopped, from morning until late at night. Posters bearing Rev. Moon's face lined the streets of Manhattan, full-page ads ran in the newspapers, and radio and television carried word of the rally.

Members stood at subway stops and on street corners, handing out flyers and telling passersby about the night of June 1. Events and gatherings filled the city, and several thousand people packed a rally on Wall Street.

Events and gatherings filled the city as part of the buildup. On Wall Street—the very heart of American commerce—several thousand people came together for one of the largest of these gatherings, carrying word of the festival into the center of the city.
And through it all, one belief held them together: that on the night of June 1, the whole nation would wake up to its responsibility.
The Miracle in the Storm
That night, the story began with disaster.

Just before the program started, a storm hit the stadium. Winds of about 60 miles per hour ripped apart the new decorations. Forecasters warned of a tornado, and heavy rain poured down. The event was close to being canceled.

But the people did not leave. Members, families, and guests stayed in their seats and prayed. Then someone started to sing "You Are My Sunshine." One voice became many, and soon the whole crowd was singing together.

One person there later remembered: "The strong wind blew away everything we had set up. The event was close to being called off." But as the singing grew, "the dark clouds finally lifted." About 30 minutes later, the storm was gone, and the stadium was cleaned up. To this day, that night is told as a miracle—faith that changed even the weather.
When the storm passed, the crowds came. According to church records, more than 45,000 people filled the stadium, and the festival was a great success.
A Call to Return, Born of Love for America
The heart of Rev. Moon's speech was his deep hope for America. He spoke as someone who wanted this nation, once chosen by God, to turn back to Him once more.
He described the country in plain words. The world had lost faith in America, he said, and New York had become a jungle of immorality and depravity.
Families were breaking apart, churches were dividing, and the country faced the threat of communism. God was being forgotten, he said, and was about to leave. Then he used a simple image:
God is the cement. With God, America stays together like concrete. But without Him, she becomes like sand, and when the flood comes, all is washed away.
America, he hoped, would return to the true spirit of its founding.
"A Doctor, a Firefighter"
So why would a man from Korea go this far? Rev. Moon answered with a comparison.
If there is illness in your home, don't you need a doctor from outside? If your home catches fire, don't you need firefighters from outside? God has sent me to America as a doctor, as a firefighter.
Even though America had turned away, he said, God would not give up on her. I know God's will is to save the world, and that America must lead the way. That is why I came to America.
From America to "One World Under God"
This rally was not just a celebration.
For Rev. Moon and Dr. Hak Ja Han, it was the start of a peace movement in America.

If America returned to God, he believed, other nations would follow. Rev. Moon called for uniting people who were fleeing communism for freedom, saying the free world must now liberate the enslaved communist world. Beyond that was his picture of "one world under God."
Other nations would follow America's example and build the kingdom of God on their own lands, and all would become brothers and sisters under Heavenly Parent, God.
He closed his speech by praying for God's blessing on America's new century.
Fifty Years Later
The question from that night at Yankee Stadium has not gone away.
Three months later, a much larger crowd—said to be around 300,000—gathered at the Washington Monument.

At the time, the movement drew not only support but also criticism and debate. Still, what these rallies aimed at was more than America's renewal: it was a world joined together as one, beyond the lines of race and nationality.

Rev. Moon was not the only one to speak of an "America under God." In 1954, President Eisenhower signed a law adding "under God" to the Pledge of Allegiance, and in 1982, President Reagan called America a nation dedicated under God to the cause of liberty.
But these presidents spoke of one nation's faith. The Yankee Stadium vision was far bigger—it saw that faith as the starting point for changing the whole world.
Now the question is back.

In 2026, America turns 250. President Trump has named the milestone "Rededicate 250," calling for the country to be rededicated as "one nation under God." As America again moves to dedicate itself to God, where is it heading? Fifty years on, the question from that stormy night still echoes.

title: Data Exposes the "Fake Public Opinion" Behind Japan's Runaway Reporting on the Family Federation
previewText:
