title: Unification Church Dissolution - What Exactly Happens When a Religious Corporation Loses Its Status?
previewText: Title:  【Unification Church Dissolution】 What Exactly Happens When a Religious Corporation Loses Its Corporate Status? The “Legal Absurdity” That Religions Targeted by the State Are Almost Certainly

blocks.text: Title:  【Unification Church Dissolution】 What Exactly Happens When a Religious Corporation Loses Its Corporate Status? The “Legal Absurdity” That Religions Targeted by the State Are Almost Certainly Crushed

Author: Masaki Nakamasa 
Publication Date: March 16, 2026 
Publication Link: https://www.kk-bestsellers.com/articles/-/4228931/
The Unification Church’s dissolution was processed as a “non-litigious case”

It is probably widely known that, following the Tokyo High Court’s decision on March 4, the Family Federation (Unification Church) lost its corporate status, immediate liquidation procedures began, and believers have already been expelled from the church facilities and can no longer gather to perform worship or prayers. Since it is also widely known that I, from the position of a former believer with some knowledge of the church’s affairs, have opposed the dissolution order, this time I would like to explain — through the Unification Church case — what it actually means for a religious organization to lose its corporate status and be dissolved. Is the commonly repeated claim true that it merely means losing tax benefits, with no hindrance whatsoever to believers conducting their faith life?

The dissolution of the Unification Church was handled as a “non-litigious case” under Article 81 of the Religious Corporations Act. There has been debate about the requirements for dissolution under this Article 81 — whether it is limited to cases where the founder or top executives receive guilty verdicts in major criminal cases, or whether it also includes civil torts (note: torts refer to any acts that can be subject to damages claims and are not crimes). This time, however, I want to question whether it is appropriate in the first place to treat the dissolution of a religious organization as a “non-litigious case.”

When ordinary people hear the difficult-sounding term “non-litigious case,” they may imagine a strict formal review, but it is exactly the opposite. It is a simple court format close to mediation, in which the court administratively intervenes to handle internal party matters such as adult guardianship, disappearance declarations, changes to land-lease conditions, or election of corporate officers. It is a type of civil procedure, but it is almost never covered in law-school classes or textbooks, and there are few specialized explanatory books.

“Non-litigious” means there is no contentiousness — i.e., no clear dispute between the parties regarding their mutual interests. Situations like adult guardianship or disappearance declarations involve no dispute but require legal clarification, yet leaving the decision to an administrative office window would be unreliable. This procedure exists for such cases. In English it is called a “non-contentious case”; in French, matière gracieuse (“gentle matter”).

Because these are cases that should have no room for internal disputes, the format allows the court to process them quickly. Unlike regular civil litigation (which is public in principle), it is non-public in principle. Evidence examination does not need to be as rigorous as in ordinary trials; the judge can handle it conveniently under their own authority and issue a rapid “decision.”

The Religious Corporations Act does indeed stipulate that dissolution of a religious corporation is to be treated as a non-litigious case. But is the Unification Church dissolution truly a case without disputes between parties? No one thinks so. Of course, there are situations where handling a religious corporation’s dissolution as non-litigious is appropriate — for example, a small shrine or temple facing successor shortages or a drastic drop in parishioners, where the believers as a whole agree it can no longer continue.

Cases like Aum Shinrikyo or Myōkaku-ji, where the founder and executives committed major criminal acts, might also fit. Even in those cases, remaining believers contested the dissolution all the way to the Supreme Court, so “contentiousness” cannot be denied outright; however, once the main executives were arrested and what had been treated as religious acts were judged as crimes, one could argue there was originally no room for dispute.

The Unification Church case, however, is completely different. In Japan, no executives have been arrested in criminal cases. All the issues raised are civil torts — primarily lawsuits from former believers over large donations. Most of the tens of thousands of active believers did not force high donations on anyone. Tens of thousands of believers (apart from minor traffic violations) have committed no crimes, and the clergy-equivalent staff are fully in place. Knowing full well that this would severely restrict their freedom of religion, the state nevertheless ordered the dissolution on its own responsibility from the viewpoint of public interest in preventing torts.
The flaw in the current Religious Corporations Act that does not allow public adversarial trials

When the state and the organization are in direct confrontation, is it acceptable to use the simple, in-principle non-public procedures of a “non-litigious case” advanced at the judge’s discretion? The church side pointed out that the Agency for Cultural Affairs had fabricated victims’ testimonies, but the judge ignored this under their authority. Active believers applied to participate as interested parties, but that too was rejected by the judge’s authority — even though the Non-Contentious Case Procedure Act allows those affected by the ruling to become “interested participants.”

In countries such as the United States there is lively debate, from a constitutionalist perspective, about exactly which cases may be handled as non-litigious. In Japan such discussions are rarely seen. Regarding the 1966 Supreme Court special-appeal decision on whether handling fine impositions as non-litigious cases violates Article 82, Paragraph 1 of the Constitution (“Trials and judgments shall be conducted in open court”), the majority rejected the unconstitutionality claim; however, dissenting opinions argued it is still unconstitutional to deny adversarial trials when the person objects, and supplementary opinions acknowledged that the law has flaws and the matter is not entirely unproblematic.

Is it a proper understanding of the rule of law simply to execute the procedure because the Religious Corporations Act says so, when the issue involves basic human rights guaranteed by the Constitution — namely, whether the religious corporation has committed civil torts warranting dissolution or whether there is fear of future ones?

Tens of thousands of people object because their freedom of religion may be restricted, yet the current Religious Corporations Act refuses to allow public adversarial trials — a clear flaw. It is strange to proceed to trial without first considering how to correct that flaw. Isn’t this legislative inaction by Agency for Cultural Affairs officials, the Religious Corporations Council (which includes lawyers and legal scholars), and the lawmakers (including former Prime Minister Kishida) who decided to exercise the right of inquiry? In other words, didn’t they fail to take legislative measures to fix the Religious Corporations Act?

Human-rights advocates or constitutional liberals are quick to loudly denounce legislative or administrative inaction on issues like the Hansen’s disease prevention law. Yet on this issue, lawyers, legal scholars, and intellectuals who style themselves as human-rights advocates have not discussed at all the pros and cons of dissolving religious corporations via non-litigious procedures. Is it because the target is their enemy — the hated “anti-communist cult”? Shouldn’t a true human-rights advocate or liberal insist that, precisely because it is a hated enemy, it must be judged openly and fairly in a public trial?
What exactly will happen to the Family Federation after losing its corporate status?

The problem is not limited to court procedure. In non-litigious cases, just as in ordinary civil lawsuits, liquidation begins the moment the appeal-court (High Court) decision is issued. As reported in the media, the Family Federation has lost its corporate status and can no longer act as a corporation. What does this mean concretely?

All 260 facilities nationwide owned or leased by the church have been seized by the liquidators. Believers are barred from entering, making worship and various rituals impossible. Weddings and funerals are no exception; they cannot hold funerals or use cemeteries. In some locations the responsible liquidator (agent) has even refused permission to remove personal belongings. They are also being asked to surrender believers’ personal information stored on PCs.

Normally, once liquidation is complete, remaining assets are transferred to a voluntary organization formed by former believers. But the Agency for Cultural Affairs and the liquidators say they must wait for years because it takes time for Unification Church victims to come forward courageously.

In ordinary corporate liquidation the creditor-claim period is two months. Waiting years is extraordinarily long. Moreover, the liquidators’ daily fees are paid from the church’s own assets. The Agency for Cultural Affairs, the liquidators, and the left-wing lawyer groups (such as the Japan Federation of Bar Associations) collaborating with them apparently do not want to hand over any facilities or assets to the believers. The president of the Japan Federation of Bar Associations has publicly argued that this is how it should be done.

Some may say believers can simply perform rituals outside the facilities, but that is not easy either. The staff who preach, provide pastoral care, and officiate rituals are church employees; their current superiors are the liquidators. Staff are prohibited from religious activities during working hours. Many have been ordered to remain on standby at home. Meeting other believers during standby time under business orders and discussing anything could be viewed as a religious gathering and thus a violation of business orders. On holidays it would technically be outside business hours, but that would fall outside the doctrinally fixed times for rituals; if working hours are not clearly defined, virtually everything risks being treated as a violation.

This creates a major obstacle for believers filing a special appeal to the Supreme Court. Without access to church facilities or assets, key figures cannot easily gather to plan countermeasures, prepare documents, or hire lawyers. The church website and communication equipment are unavailable, so they cannot appeal their legitimacy to the public — nor even send messages from leaders to ordinary believers. Any message sent risks being checked for the presence of staff members. The organization also cannot take legal action as a corporation against media defamation or privacy violations. I am currently assisting with the final survival struggle of the church in exactly this situation.
The “dissolution order” is a pitfall lurking in the current law

Is the current law reasonable when it stipulates that a dissolution order — which prevents believers from performing religious rituals, holding gatherings, or freely expressing opinions, and even makes preparation for the final hope of a special appeal impossible — is to be reviewed as a non-litigious case? Even if amending the current law is difficult, could the judge not have exercised discretion to open the review to the public, make it as adversarial as possible, and limit the scope of liquidation until the special appeal is concluded?

Did the Japan Federation of Bar Associations (obsessed with crushing the Unification Church), former Democratic Party and Communist Party lawmakers, the media, religious scholars, and journalists never anticipate that such problems would arise? It is now becoming concretely clear what mental suffering the dissolution is causing believers and how it is restricting their religious activities — yet the media and intellectuals pay no attention and merely repeat, like a broken record, “Victim relief as soon as possible…” Do they realize that they themselves are creating “victims” — not only by restricting faith activities but also by causing job losses, disadvantages in school admissions, discrimination, and bullying?

If such closed-door procedures via non-litigious cases are justified, no religion can feel safe. If organizations can be dissolved on the basis of vague speculation such as “In the past they committed △△ illegal acts based on ○○ doctrine, so even if they are quiet now, in the future…” in a court format that allows such reasoning, won’t this boomerang against those who denounce the Unification Church as the representative of evil religions?

title: Communism's One Consistent Enemy: The Family
previewText:
Communism has one enemy it cannot negotiate with, cannot co-opt, and cannot ignore. It is not a nation. It is not an army. It is not a political party.
It is the family.
Every communist regime in

blocks.text: Communism has one enemy it cannot negotiate with, cannot co-opt, and cannot ignore. It is not a nation. It is not an army. It is not a political party.
It is the family.

Every communist regime in history has understood this. The family is where loyalty forms before the state can claim it. It is where values are passed from parent to child before ideology can replace them. It is where a person learns to love something more than the collective — and that, to any totalitarian system, is the most dangerous thing in the world.
This is not an interpretation of communist theory. It is written plainly in the founding document. Marx and Engels declared:

"Abolition of the family! Even the most radical flare up at this infamous proposal of the Communists. On what foundation is the present family, the bourgeois family, based? On capital, on private gain... The bourgeois family will vanish as a matter of course when its complement vanishes, and both will vanish with the vanishing of capital."

Marx argued that communism would ensure children would be educated by the state, not by their parents. Communists, he wrote, would "rescue education from the influence of the ruling class." The making of the "New Man" was the priority, and the family was an obstacle.

Once the Bolsheviks took power in Russia, theory became policy. Soviet commissar Alexandra Kollontai put it plainly: "The old family, narrow and petty, where the parents quarrel and are only interested in their own offspring, is not capable of educating the 'new person.'"
So the family was not a casualty of communism. It was the target.
What Happens When They Win
If you want to see Marx's vision made concrete, look at what North Korea built.
Kim Il-Sung declared that any person with anti-government sentiments should be wiped out entirely, and that up to three generations of their family should be punished. These words became law.

A truck comes in the middle of the night and sweeps every family member away. They are taken to a prison camp without trial. Only after entering do they learn what "sin" their family member committed.
Children. Grandparents. Cousins. All imprisoned for a thought crime committed by one relative they may not even know.

Particularly horrifying is the incarceration of entire families — including children and grandparents — to isolate and punish them because of their relationship to someone accused of political crimes. Rooting out "class enemies for three generations" was specifically ordered by Kim Il-sung, which at times has led to comparisons with Nazi death camps.
From 1981 to 2013, an estimated 400,000 people out of 500,000 imprisoned in these labor camps were killed.
This is not a distortion of communism. This is communism operating exactly as designed — a system that sees the family as a threat, and treats it accordingly.
Two Children Who Survived It
Before Rev. Sun Myung Moon and Dr. Hak Ja Han built one of the most consequential anti-communist movements in modern history, they were both children fleeing the same regime.

Moon was arrested in 1948 and sentenced to five years at Hungnam labor camp. In 1950, he was liberated by United Nations troops. He emerged from those years as a staunch anti-communist, teaching that the Cold War between capitalism and communism was the final conflict between God and Satan, with divided Korea as its primary front line.

Dr. Hak Ja Han's story begins with the same enemy. Born in what is now North Korea in 1943, her mother and grandmother were arrested by Communist police when she was five years old and jailed for eleven days. After their release, Hak Ja Han, her mother, and her grandmother fled their village in the middle of the night.

A man who survived a communist labor camp. A woman who fled communist police as a child. They met, married, and spent the rest of their lives building the direct opposite of everything that had been done to them.

On April 11, 1960, the young Hak Ja Han married the church's founder, Rev. Sun Myung Moon. She stands as co-founder of the Unification Church, now known as the Family Federation for World Peace and Unification.
The heart and soul of their lifelong ministry was the re-establishment of God's ideal of the family as the foundation for harmonious societies and the cornerstone of world peace.
Two survivors of communism's war on the family. One marriage. One mission.
The Movement They Built

The Unification Church did not simply preach against communism from a pulpit. It built an international institutional campaign to defeat it — across three decades, four continents, and ultimately inside the Soviet Union itself.

In 1963, Rev. Moon initiated what became the International Federation for Victory over Communism (IFVOC). By the early 1970s, VOC theory had become one of the principal sources of anti-communist education in South Korea, training hundreds of thousands of civil servants, soldiers, and local officials annually.

On June 7, 1975, the campaign reached its most visible moment. The World Rally for Korean Freedom was held at Yoido, Seoul, directly confronting the increasing communist threat in Asia as the Indochina peninsula had just fallen.
Over one million demonstrators gathered. Representatives from sixty nations stood together.

Rev. Moon's address that day carried a prophecy he had already stated publicly: "Communism, begun in 1917, could maintain itself approximately 60 years and reach its peak. So 1978 is the borderline and afterward communism will decline; in the 70th year, it will be altogether ruined. This is true. Therefore, now is the time for people who are studying communism to abandon it."
The Soviet Union dissolved in 1991.

While Rev. Moon built the ideological infrastructure, Dr. Han was building a global movement of women. In 1992, she co-founded the Women's Federation for World Peace and delivered its inaugural speech in 113 cities, in 12 countries, in three languages, within eight months. Despite inclement weather, 150,000 women from 72 countries gathered at Seoul Olympic Stadium for its inaugural rally. That fall, she addressed 50,000 women in the Tokyo Dome.

Her 1993 American tour saw her welcomed by 35 governors, 131 mayors, and 25 U.S. senators. In dozens of states and cities, the day of her speech was declared "National Parents Day," the "Day of Women and World Peace," or "Hak Ja Han Moon Day." It culminated when she spoke before ambassadors from 67 nations at the United Nations.
In December 1991, she and her husband traveled to North Korea itself — putting her life on the line to meet with President Kim Il Sung for the purpose of pursuing Korean reunification.
The woman who had been driven from that country at night as a five-year-old walked back in as a peace envoy.

And then came the moment that shook the communist world to its foundation. Rev. Moon stood in Moscow and told Gorbachev directly: "The Soviet Union must know God. You have to go back. Otherwise, there is no way. You will suffer!"
More than 800 retired high-ranking U.S. military officials attended CAUSA presentations on VOC ideology, including a sizeable number of retired four-star generals and full admirals.
In 1984, The Washington Times was founded specifically to advance the peaceful fall of communism, a goal achieved in conjunction with the Reagan Administration.
When historians make a final analysis of why communism came to an end, they will recognize that no single person did more than Reverend Sun Myung Moon to bring about the peaceful end of communism.
Standing beside him throughout was Dr. Hak Ja Han.
The Counterattack — 70 Years and Counting

An ideology that has identified a movement as its primary enemy does not walk away. What has unfolded over the past seven decades is not a series of unrelated controversies. It is a coordinated, multi-country campaign to destroy the one organization that beat communism on every front where they met.

It started in Japan. The National Network of Lawyers Against Spiritual Sales was a pro-communist group formed in 1987 with the express purpose of destroying the Unification Church precisely because it was openly fighting communism.

For decades they pursued civil claims and pressured members who left to file lawsuits as proof of departure — a process one investigative journalist compared to the 17th-century practice of forcing Christians to trample icons to prove they had abandoned their faith.

In November 2022, Japan Communist Party Chairperson Kazuo Shii declared openly in a magazine interview: "This is a final war against the Unification Church for the Communist Party. This time we will never give up until we win."

They made good. On March 25, 2025, the Tokyo District Court ordered the dissolution of the Unification Church — the culmination of forty years of effort by politically motivated lawyers whose stated aim was to destroy the church because of its anti-communist activities.

The Chinese Communist Party celebrated publicly. The China Anti-Xie-Jiao Association released a statement expressing satisfaction that the church had been dissolved as "a tool of the anti-Communist ideology," praising the lawyers who made it happen.

In South Korea, the attack moved directly to Dr. Han herself. In the predawn hours of September 23, 2025, Dr. Hak Ja Han Moon — 82 years old — was arrested after hours of questioning at Seoul Central District Court.

She had arrived in a wheelchair. She denied all charges, stating she had no interest in politics and neither ordered nor permitted the acts attributed to her. She said the alleged bribery was carried out by a fired federation official acting on his own initiative.

She was indicted on charges of bribery, embezzlement, violating political funding laws, and instructing the destruction of evidence — part of an expanding probe into figures linked to imprisoned ex-President Yoon Suk Yeol.

The arrest is widely seen as part of a coordinated campaign between South Korea and Japan to simultaneously dismantle the Family Federation. The United Nations has formally warned Japan that its dissolution proceedings may violate international law.
The leader of the opposition People Power Party called South Korea's new government a "pro-China dictatorship."

The Rev. Demian Dunkley, president of the U.S. branch of the federation, stated: "This arrest is not just an attack on Holy Mother Han. It is an attack on freedom of religion itself. It is a warning shot to every church, mosque, temple, and synagogue in Korea — and beyond — that faith is not safe from the grasp of government overreach. If they can arrest the Mother of Peace, they can come for anyone."

Former House Speaker Newt Gingrich named the motive plainly: "It was an effort, frankly, by the communists to create an environment where there could be a closer relationship with China and a more distant relationship with the United States."

Secretary of State Mike Pompeo identified the geopolitical stakes: "If there is anything the Unification Church undermines, it is indeed communism. We should see the Japan Communist Party's attack for exactly what it is — an attempt to undermine and weaken the vital US-Japan alliance while encouraging better relations between Japan and the Chinese Communist Party."
The Only Question That Matters

The woman who fled North Korea at night as a five-year-old child was arrested again at 82 by a government her own country's opposition calls pro-China. The ideology that drove her family into exile as a child has pursued her across a lifetime and across borders.
Ask yourself why.

Communism does not hunt organizations that pose no threat. It does not spend seventy years orchestrating the legal, political, and judicial destruction of a movement unless that movement represents something it genuinely fears. Chinese Communist Party operatives are covertly supporting anti-cult campaigns in both Korea and Japan to destabilize anti-communist religious movements across the region.
This is not paranoia. This is documented, on the record, and confirmed by former U.S. secretaries of state and speakers of the House.

What does communism fear? A movement built entirely on the premise that the family — not the state — is the foundation of civilization. A church that has spent sixty years proving that men and women can build something together the state can never replace. Dr. Han is the mother of 14 children and the grandmother of more than 40 grandchildren — exemplary above all as a woman who has created a God-centered marriage and family of four generations.
Marx called for the abolition of the family in 1848. Rev. Moon and Dr. Hak Ja Han spent their lives building one — and calling the world to do the same.
That is why communism has never stopped trying to destroy them.
And that is why you should pay attention to what is happening to them right now.

title: Election Integrity, Media Capture, and Institutional Breakdown in South Korea
previewText:
A Review of Evidence Presented in "December 3, 2024 — The Hidden Truth" Jeon Han-gil News Documentary (2 hrs 21 min)
On December 3, 2024, South Korean President Yoon Suk-yeol declared emergency

blocks.text: A Review of Evidence Presented in "December 3, 2024 — The Hidden Truth" Jeon Han-gil News Documentary (2 hrs 21 min)

On December 3, 2024, South Korean President Yoon Suk-yeol declared emergency martial law. It was lifted six hours later. He was impeached within days and removed from office by the Constitutional Court. Opposition leader Lee Jae-myung — who was standing criminal trial for election law violations and fraud at the time — won the subsequent snap presidential election on June 3, 2025.

A widely viewed documentary by Jeon Han-gil News compiles evidence from government audits, court proceedings, National Assembly testimony, whistleblower accounts, and statistical analysis to raise questions about the integrity of South Korea's election system, the independence of its judiciary during the impeachment process, and the systematic use of legislative power to dismantle executive branch functions prior to the martial law declaration.

This report presents the key evidence from that documentary in a format intended for policymakers in allied democracies. South Korea hosts 28,500 U.S. troops, anchors America's Indo-Pacific alliance structure, and is home to the world's most critical semiconductor manufacturing infrastructure. The democratic legitimacy of its government is a matter of direct U.S. national security interest.
PART ONE: ELECTION DATA ANOMALIES

The documentary's central evidentiary pillar is statistical. It examines the relationship between early voting results and election-day results across multiple election cycles and identifies a pattern that begins in 2020 and has persisted in every subsequent election.
Baseline: 2016 General Election

In the 2016 (20th) general election — the last election before the anomalous pattern appeared — early voting and election-day results were statistically consistent. The difference between a candidate's early vote share and election-day vote share was small (1-6 percentage points), random in direction, and varied by district. This is the expected statistical behavior in any election where both voting methods draw from the same population.

2016 general election: Early voting (사전투표) vs. election-day voting (당일투표) by candidate and district. Differences are small, random in direction, and vary by location — consistent with expected statistical behavior.
2020 General Election: A Uniform Shift

In the 2020 (21st) general election, a different pattern emerged. Across Seoul, the Democratic Party's early voting share exceeded its election-day share by 12.79 percentage points. The conservative party's early voting share was 12.79 percentage points lower than its election-day share. The figures are symmetrical to three decimal places.

Comparison of 20th (2016) and 21st (2020) general elections in Seoul. In 2016, early and election-day results were nearly identical (difference of ~0.5%). In 2020, a 12.79% gap appeared — identical for both parties in opposite directions. Bottom text: "A match this precise cannot occur without design" (설계가 아니면 나올 수 없는 일치).

The Democratic Party's standard explanation is that its supporters prefer early voting. If true, higher early voting turnout should correlate with higher Democratic vote share. The documentary presents data showing the opposite: in districts with the highest early voting turnout, the Democratic Party's vote share was often lower. The explanatory framework offered by the party does not align with its own data.
The 2020 election produced an overwhelming Democratic supermajority:
2020 (21st) general election results. Democratic coalition: 155-178 seats. Conservative coalition: 107-130 seats.
Nationwide District Analysis

South Korea has 3,551 individual voting districts. In a statistically normal election, the direction of the early-vs-election-day difference should be approximately random — roughly half favoring each party. The documentary presents the actual distribution:

Of 3,551 voting districts: 3,347 (+) showed the Democratic Party performing better in early voting than on election day. 56 (0) showed no difference. The conservative People Power Party showed the inverse: 3,487 (-) districts with lower early vote share. Only 56 districts showed parity.

In 94.3% of districts, the Democratic Party's early voting share exceeded its election-day share. In 98.2% of districts, the conservative party's early voting share was lower. A uniform directional pattern across 3,551 geographically diverse districts is inconsistent with random voter behavior.
Individual District Charts: 52 Contested Results

The documentary identifies 52 Democratic Party members of the 22nd National Assembly (elected April 2024) whose district-level results display the early voting anomaly. Statistical analysis indicates that if these 52 results were reversed, the People Power Party would hold 142 seats — a governing majority.

52 members of the 22nd National Assembly whose election results show statistically anomalous early voting patterns. Title: "22nd National Assembly — Suspected Fraudulent Election Winners" (제22대 국회의원 부정 당선자(의혹)).
District-level charts illustrate the pattern:

Gyeonggi Hanam-Gap, 22nd General Election (2024). Blue = Democratic candidate. Red = conservative candidate. Left portion = early voting precincts. Right portion = election-day precincts. The Democratic candidate leads by 15-20 points in early voting; the margin collapses to near-parity on election day

Dongdaemun-Gap, 22nd General Election (2024). The conservative candidate (red, Kim Young-woo) overtook the Democratic candidate (blue, An Gyu-baek) on election day. An Gyu-baek won overall due to a 62.1% to 35.4% early voting margin that reversed to near-parity on election day.
The 2022 Presidential Election

Yoon Suk-yeol won the 2022 presidential election by 0.73% — approximately 247,000 votes — defeating Lee Jae-myung. The early voting data shows Lee outperforming his election-day numbers across every region of South Korea, consistent with the pattern observed in the general elections.

2022 presidential election: Early voting (사전, dark line) vs. election-day (당일, light line) by region. The Democratic candidate's early vote share consistently exceeds his election-day share across all regions.

The documentary's interpretation: the early voting manipulation was calibrated for a narrow Lee Jae-myung victory, but Yoon's election-day performance exceeded projections by a sufficient margin to overcome the advantage. This would explain the narrow result.
The June 3, 2025 Presidential Election

In the June 3, 2025 snap presidential election following Yoon's removal, conservative candidate Kim Moon-su won election-day voting by approximately 15 percentage points. He lost the election by 2.89 million votes. The early voting margin favoring Lee Jae-myung was approximately 40 percentage points — the largest early-vs-election-day gap in South Korean electoral history.
Z-Value Analysis

Z-value analysis measures how many standard deviations a result falls from the expected mean. It is a standard tool in inferential statistics for determining whether an observed result could have occurred by chance. The higher the Z-value, the less likely the result is natural.

Z-value reference table from the documentary. Everyday occurrence (coin flip): Z=0. Fairly rare (meeting someone over 190cm): Z=3. Miracle-level (lottery 2nd prize): Z=5. Both parents dying in separate accidents same day: Z=7.6. "Mathematically impossible" (red): Z=40 — "could not occur once in the history of the universe." Below: "Manipulation" (조작).
Z-values calculated for the early-vs-election-day voting differential:

21st General Election (2020): Z = 40
22nd General Election (2024): Z = 42
June 3, 2025 Presidential Election: Z = 1,500

For reference: a Z-value of 7.6 represents the probability of both parents dying in separate, unrelated traffic accidents on the same day. A Z-value of 40 represents an event that could not occur once in the history of the observable universe. No natural dataset in any field of science has produced a Z-value of 1,500.
Statistics expert interviewed in the documentary. Subtitle: "Phenomena that are probabilistically difficult to occur cannot all happen simultaneously" (확률적으로 일어나기 힘든 현상들이 동시에 일어날 수는 없다).

"In my classroom, I teach students that a Z-value above 2 means the samples come from different populations. That is a textbook exercise. A Z-value of 40 — I have never seen that in my career. It cannot come from the same population of voters."
— Statistics professor, interviewed in the documentary
PART TWO: INSTITUTIONAL VULNERABILITIES AND SUPPRESSED INVESTIGATION
National Election Commission: Security Audit Findings

From July to September 2023, the National Intelligence Service (NIS) conducted a penetration test of the NEC's election systems. The findings were reported to the National Assembly and are a matter of public record.

Key findings:
 
1. Vote sorting machines were vulnerable to manipulation via unauthorized USB devices. A hacking program installed via USB could cause ballots marked for Candidate A to be classified as votes for Candidate B.
 
2. The internal network, election network, and external internet — designed to be isolated — contained connection points that allowed cross-infiltration.
 
3. The integrated voter registry system was accessible from outside the NEC.
 
4. The system architecture permitted the creation of fraudulent voter records ("ghost voters") and mass printing of counterfeit ballot papers.

"It was worse than I expected. The level of vulnerability was significantly below adequate. If an attack on the election system occurred immediately after a ceasefire, it could cause social chaos. The vulnerabilities need to be addressed urgently."
— NIS official, National Assembly testimony
NEC Internal Whistleblower Testimony

NEC internal whistleblower, identity protected. Upper-left label: "NEC Internal Whistleblower" (선관위 내부제보자). Subtitle: "Without security monitoring, it could be done from China — from Yanbian" (그런데 관제를 안한 상태에서는 중국에서 연변에서 할 수도 있는거죠).

The NEC maintained publicly that its systems were under 24/7 security monitoring. An internal whistleblower, whose identity is protected in the documentary, provided a different account: security monitoring was not operational during election periods.

"Why didn't they include the security monitoring team during elections? If you include monitoring, they detect intrusions. But without monitoring — China could connect and do it. From Yanbian. Yes. It's possible."
— NEC internal whistleblower
NEC Secretary-General Testimony Before the National Assembly

Under questioning by legislators, the NEC's Secretary-General acknowledged that the internal and election networks were connected during early voting periods — directly contradicting the NEC's longstanding public position that its systems were completely isolated from external networks.

"The network separation issue involves the business network and the election network. This requires significant budget, so we are pursuing it as a medium-term project. The integrated voter system cannot operate without connection during early voting. During the test day before early voting and during the two early voting days — those are the only times it is connected."
— NEC Secretary-General, National Assembly testimony

A legislator responded: "You just said network separation is insecure. If a hacking organization targets the system during those connected days, we are breached. This is an urgent matter." The Secretary-General agreed that network separation was necessary. The budget was never allocated.
Why the NEC Has Never Been Independently Investigated

The NEC is constitutionally independent under Article 114 of the South Korean Constitution. No prosecutor, police force, or executive branch agency has jurisdiction to compel an investigation of its operations, subpoena its records, or seize its servers. Every election fraud lawsuit filed in South Korean courts has been dismissed. No court has issued a warrant to examine NEC servers or open ballot boxes for verification.

This institutional reality is central to understanding why martial law troops were deployed to the NEC on December 3 — and why they constituted a larger force (approximately 300) than those sent to the National Assembly (approximately 280), arriving 78 minutes earlier. The NEC was the primary operational objective.

CCTV footage: Martial law troops entering the NEC's Gwacheon headquarters at 22:34 on December 3, 2024 — 78 minutes before the National Assembly operation. The CCTV timestamp is visible at bottom: 2024-12-03 22:34:18.

Nineteen Defense Intelligence Command agents entered the NEC server room. A military truck arrived to transport servers for forensic analysis. Separately, 47 troops secured the Public Opinion Survey Review Committee facility in Gwanak — the body responsible for managing exit polls and election surveys. When martial law was lifted six hours later, all troops withdrew. No servers were seized. No forensic analysis was conducted. No ballots were examined.
The Druking Case: Adjudicated Opinion Manipulation

One case of organized election-era opinion manipulation in South Korea has been fully adjudicated. In 2018, Kim Dong-hun ("Druking") was convicted of operating a macro system called "King Crab" that could mass-manipulate online comments, trending topics, and approval polls. He worked with Kim Kyung-su, governor of South Gyeongsang Province and one of President Moon Jae-in's closest political allies.

Court records established that the operation manufactured online narratives during the 2017 presidential campaign. Druking's team claimed credit for shaping public perception of Moon Jae-in's TV debate performances and for "dominating online opinion" after the election. Kim Kyung-su was convicted and imprisoned.

First Lady Kim Jung-sook was documented participating in events organized by Druking's affiliated group during the campaign. This is the only proven, convicted case of organized election-era opinion manipulation in South Korean history — conducted by associates of the party that now controls all branches of government.
Additional Concern: NEC Staffing Patterns During Elections

Internal records cited in the documentary indicate that NEC staff took mass leave during election periods. In March 2022 — during both the presidential election and local elections — the number of staff on leave reached 209, a historical high. The NEC responded by conducting emergency hiring of 152 contract workers to fill gaps. The documentary raises questions about whether critical institutional knowledge and oversight were absent during the most sensitive operational periods.
PART THREE: INSTITUTIONAL PATTERN — LEGISLATIVE POWER AND EXECUTIVE REMOVAL
The documentary identifies a recurring sequence of events across two administrations that it characterizes as a repeatable methodology for regime change using legal and institutional mechanisms.
Use of National Tragedy as Political Catalyst

In 2014, the Sewol Ferry disaster killed 304 people, including 250 high school students. The national grief was channeled into a sustained political campaign targeting President Park Geun-hye personally, centered on allegations about her whereabouts during a seven-hour period on the day of the sinking.
2016 candlelight protests preceding Park Geun-hye's impeachment. Banner: "Park Geun-hye — Immediate and Complete Resignation" (박근혜 즉각 완전퇴진). These protests drew millions of participants.

In 2022, the Itaewon crowd crush killed 159 people. A similar mobilization pattern emerged: candlelight vigils converted to political protests, identical slogans deployed, marches directed at the presidential office.

2022 Itaewon disaster candlelight protests. Subtitle: "Memorializing the victims of the Itaewon disaster" (이태원 참사 희생자를 추모합니다). Protest signs demanded presidential resignation, using language identical to the 2014 Sewol-era protests.

The Itaewon mobilization was disrupted when South Korean intelligence agencies uncovered that a former Korean Confederation of Trade Unions (KCTU) official had received operational directives from North Korea instructing the weaponization of the disaster. The directives included specific protest slogans:

"Maximize the outpouring of rage. Combine the November-December struggle with candlelight protests. Use the slogans: "The people are dying," "Is this a country?," "Resignation is the memorial.""
— North Korean directive — agent convicted and sentenced to 15 years imprisonment
Evidence Fabrication Allegations in Both Impeachments

The Park Geun-hye impeachment (2016-2017) was precipitated by JTBC's report on a tablet allegedly belonging to presidential confidante Choi Soon-sil. Subsequent trial proceedings established that the device belonged to Blue House administrator Kim Han-su. Former Prime Minister Hwang Kyo-ahn confirmed publicly that the tablet was never admitted as evidence in court.

"The tablet — do you still believe it was fabricated? It wasn't admitted as court evidence. Look into it yourself. It was not admitted. If it were legitimate, it could not have been excluded."
— Hwang Kyo-ahn, former Prime Minister and Acting President

The Yoon Suk-yeol impeachment (2024-2025) relied heavily on a handwritten memo allegedly documenting presidential orders to arrest lawmakers, and on testimony from Special Warfare Commander Kwak Jong-geun regarding a phone call from the president.

Special Warfare Commander Kwak Jong-geun (right, in uniform) testifying at the National Defense Committee. His testimony regarding the president's phone call shifted on key details during questioning.

Issues identified with the evidence:
 
• Kwak's testimony shifted on the central question of whether the president used the word "legislators" (의원) or "personnel" (인원). He acknowledged that his recollection of specific details came not from his own memory but from subsequent conversations with others.
 
• The initial "handwritten" memo presented as evidence was sourced from the internet, not composed at the scene.
 
• A handwriting analysis commissioned by media figure Byun Hee-jae, conducted by a retired National Forensic Service examiner with over 30 years of experience, found that handwriting on the key memo was consistent with that of Democratic Party lawmaker Park Soon-won — whose office had been actively investigating martial law preparations for months prior to December 3.
 
• The Constitutional Court declined defense requests to call the witness who could verify the memo's provenance.
 
• The "insurrection" charge — the basis of the impeachment — was removed from the trial to expedite the ruling.

Formal impeachment charges against President Yoon: Insurrection (Criminal Code Article 87), Abuse of Power (Article 123), Obstruction of Official Duties (Article 144). The insurrection charge was subsequently removed from the trial.

The documentary notes a constitutional law point: in the history of constitutional governance, no head of state has been convicted of insurrection for exercising emergency powers granted by their own constitution.
Serial Impeachments: Executive Branch Paralysis

Prior to the December 3 martial law declaration, the Democratic Party — holding a legislative supermajority — filed 29 impeachment motions against executive branch officials. Thirteen were passed by the National Assembly. Targets included the Interior Minister, prosecutors handling cases against Lee Jae-myung, the Board of Audit chairman, and three successive chairs of the Broadcasting and Communications Commission.

Lee Jin-suk at her Broadcasting and Communications Commission confirmation hearing. She was impeached after one day in office. When the Constitutional Court dismissed the impeachment, the Democratic Party passed legislation abolishing the commission and replacing it with a new agency. She was subsequently arrested.

The Broadcasting Commission case illustrates the escalation pattern:
 
1. Chair Lee Dong-gwan: appointed, resigned under impeachment pressure after 95 days.
2. Chair Kim Hong-il: appointed, impeachment filed immediately, resigned.
3. Chair Lee Jin-suk: appointed, impeached after one day. Constitutional Court dismissed the impeachment. The Democratic Party then passed legislation abolishing the entire commission, created a functionally identical replacement agency, and arrested Lee Jin-suk.
 
Separately, the Democratic Party unilaterally cut the government budget by 4.1 trillion won — including elimination of the presidential office's special activity funds and reductions to youth and vulnerable population support programs. After Lee Jae-myung assumed the presidency, the same budget lines were restored.

JTBC report: Political broker Myung Tae-kyun threatened to release recordings and materials if arrested. The timing — days before December 3 — contributed to the pressure timeline preceding the martial law declaration.
The Democratic Party's Advance Knowledge

The documentary presents evidence that the Democratic Party had advance knowledge of martial law preparations months before December 3. According to testimony cited in the documentary, Lee Jae-myung directed lawmaker Park Seon-won to investigate military preparations for an emergency declaration. Park's office — which included staff with NIS and Ministry of National Defense backgrounds — conducted intelligence gathering through personal networks over a period of months.

"The party leader asked: "What could the Yoon administration do next?" I said: "In my assessment, it's martial law." He told me: "Investigate inside the military." So my staff — one from NIS, one from the Defense Ministry — went out drinking with their contacts every night until 1 or 2 a.m. Little by little, the information came out."
— Account of Rep. Park Seon-won's activities, as reported in the documentary

When the martial law declaration came, Democratic Party lawmakers moved with coordination that the documentary characterizes as pre-planned: a Telegram channel under the code name "Wol-loom" had been pre-established, communication protocols for a potential signal blackout were in place, and military veteran lawmaker Kim Byung-joo served as operational coordinator.

Kim Min-seok — now Prime Minister — had been publicly discussing the possibility of martial law since August 2024, four months before the declaration. The Democratic Party introduced the Martial Law Prevention Act in September 2024, which would have required prior National Assembly approval for any martial law declaration. The documentary frames this legislation as a strategic forcing mechanism: President Yoon would need to act before it passed or lose the option entirely.
IMPLICATIONS FOR THE U.S. ALLIANCE

South Korea is the cornerstone of the U.S. alliance structure in the Indo-Pacific. It hosts 28,500 American service members, manufactures the majority of the world's advanced semiconductors, and serves as the primary intelligence platform for monitoring North Korean and Chinese military activity.
The evidence compiled in this documentary raises questions in four areas that are directly relevant to U.S. strategic interests:

1. Election Infrastructure Security: The NIS audit confirmed that the NEC's systems were vulnerable to external hacking, including during early voting periods when networks were connected to the internet. An internal whistleblower testified that security monitoring was inactive during elections. These findings have not been addressed.
 
2. Judicial Independence During Impeachment: The Constitutional Court declined to call defense witnesses, removed the primary charge from the trial, and relied on testimony that shifted on key facts. The evidentiary basis for the impeachment — a memo whose provenance is disputed and a witness whose testimony was internally contradictory — has not been subjected to independent review.
 
3. Legislative Overreach: The use of serial impeachments to remove executive branch officials, the unilateral slashing of the government budget, and the abolition of a constitutional body through legislation to remove a single individual represent an exercise of legislative power that, regardless of legality, raises questions about institutional balance.
 
4. Foreign Interference Vectors: The NEC whistleblower's testimony that unmonitored election networks were accessible from external networks — combined with the NIS's confirmed finding that server networks were not properly separated — identifies a potential vector for foreign interference in the elections of a key U.S. ally.
A straightforward verification mechanism exists:
Select 10 early voting ballot boxes at random from districts identified as statistically anomalous.
Count the physical ballots in each box.
Compare the count to the NEC's published voter totals for those boxes.
Cross-reference each listed voter against registration records to confirm they voted.
This process would confirm or eliminate the statistical concerns identified in this report. To date, no such verification has been permitted.

This report is based on evidence presented in the documentary "[Official] 2024.12.3 That Day, The Manipulated Insurrection — Hidden Truth" by Jeon Han-gil News, supplemented by publicly available National Assembly testimony, NIS audit reports, and court records. All visual evidence is sourced from the publicly available documentary.

title: 日本で信教の自由が十字架に釘付けにされている＿自分が次の標的になるまで黙って見ているわけにはいかない
previewText: ランディ・エバンス大使（ワシントン・タイムズ掲載の意見記事より）

blocks.text: ランディ・エバンス大使（ワシントン・タイムズ掲載の意見記事より）
売り出し中：260の教会、礼拝堂の信者席、祭壇、説教壇、そして聖書、解説書、賛美歌集を含む様々な宗教文献。裁判所による解散・清算命令のもとで選任された清算人までご連絡ください。すべての資産は差し押さえられ、確保されており、必要に応じて清算人によって売却可能な状態にあります。
信仰や教会を解散・禁止の対象にする政府の行為は、信教の自由という概念に根本的に反するものだが、日本に倣う他の国々はさらに一歩踏み込んでいる。
マッシモ・イントロヴィーニェは2024年8月21日付の「ビター・ウィンター」誌への寄稿にてこう述べた。「ルワンダもケニアも、日本における旧統一教会（現・世界平和統一家庭連合）などの少数派への弾圧や、フランスの反カルト法を、自国の取り組みの手本として称えている。アフリカはこれまで多くのウイルスと闘ってきた。信教の自由を脅かすウイルスは、予想以上の速さで広がっているようだ。」
ルワンダはこの2年間で8,000以上の教会を閉鎖した。ナイジェリアではキリスト教徒が標的にされ殺害されている。イランはかつて聖書を禁書とした。歴史は、さまざまな理由から政府が信仰や宗教を標的にしてきた事例で満ちている。
上記の内容は衝撃的に見えるかもしれないが、すべて事実であり、すでに世界各地で他の国々が信仰を標的にする動きへとつながっている。
ソウルの朝鮮日報が報じた韓国の動向がその証拠だ。「李在明大統領は2日の閣議で、宗教法人による組織的な政治介入は憲法違反であると指摘し、『日本と同様に宗教法人への解散命令を可能にする制度的措置を検討すべきだ』と述べた。」
その1週間後、12月9日の閣議で李大統領はこう述べた。「（解散が）正当かどうかは訴訟によって判断できる。日本は裁判所に解散を申し立てているようだ。」
日本は解散命令を得るにあたり、刑事ではなく民事訴訟において、多数の不正行為とされる事項を列挙した。しかしその背景にあるのは、本質的には、2022年7月8日に安倍晋三首相を暗殺した山上徹也による主張である。
暗殺犯は、旧統一教会が自分の家族を経済的に破綻させたと主張した。奇妙なことに、暗殺犯は人気を誇った首相が教会と関係を持っていると信じていた。そして、安倍氏が関係を持っていたその教会が、今まさにその解散の根拠とされているのだ。
もちろん、一般的に教会に対する告発には、聖職者による性的虐待のような刑事的不正行為や、政治的不安定を招くといった民事的問題が含まれることもある。被害者への補償や再発防止のための監督といった改革には意義があるが、教会を禁止・解散させることに意義はない。

恐ろしいのは、日本では誰も声を上げていないことだ。これはマルティン・ニーメラー（ナチス政権による教会への国家統制に反対したとして自ら投獄された人物）の詩を想起させる。
「まず彼らは社会主義者のところへやってきた。しかし私は社会主義者ではなかったから、声を上げなかった。」
アメリカの役割、とりわけアメリカの宗教指導者や教会の役割は明確だ。私たちは宗教の自由と信仰の自由のために立ち上がらなければならない。特に、他に誰も立ち上がらないときに。他者が権利を失う場面で沈黙を守ることは、政府が集団を一つずつ標的にする力を与えるだけだ。

日本と韓国を自ら訪れたチャーリー・カークはそれを直接目撃した。

ガーディアン紙はこう伝えた。「カーク氏は尹錫悦前大統領と戒厳令に関する特別検察官捜査を批判し、韓国では『いくつかの不穏な事態が進行している』と述べた。『牧師たちが逮捕され』、『自宅が家宅捜索されている』とし、こう付け加えた。『韓国がこのような行動を続けるなら、正しいことのために立ち向かうのがアメリカの流儀だ。』」
今がその時だ。

日本の清算人は、すべての教会の扉にこの通知を貼り付けた。

「本施設およびその施設内の全資産は、清算人の管理下にある。清算人の許可なく、いかなる人物も（宗教法人の会員または職員であっても）施設内の物品を持ち出したり処分したりすることは許可されない。さらに、清算人の許可なく、いかなる人物も（宗教法人の会員または職員であっても）施設に立ち入ることは許可されない。」

日本では日曜日、数千人の信者が200以上の教会から締め出され、聖歌集にも聖礼典にもアクセスできず、礼拝する場所もなかった。

チャーリー・カークは正しかった。正しいことのために立ち向かうのはアメリカの流儀だ。宗教の自由のために。彼らが自分たちのところへやってくるまで待つことはできない。
ランディ・エバンスは2018年から2021年まで駐ルクセンブルク米国大使を務めた。

ワシントン・タイムズ掲載。2026年3月9日

blocks.text: When Reporting Creates "Facts"
One day, you lose your job.
The reason: because of your religion**.**
You try to rent an apartment.
The contract falls through at the last stage.
Same reason.
This is not a story from an authoritarian state.
It is happening in Japan, right now.
A second-generation believer of Family ****Federation ****working at an advertising agency in Fukuoka had landed two contracts in just two months.
His boss was so impressed he gave him five neckties as a gift.
But at an after-work drinking party, the young man declined alcohol for religious reasons.
When his faith came to light, the company president shouted at him.
He was terminated the next day.
He won the lawsuit that followed — but a court verdict cannot erase the scars carved into a 20-year-old's heart.
Why does this happen?
One answer lies in "media framing."
How the press selects, trims, and contextualizes facts fundamentally reshapes public perception.
And that perception carries enough force to destroy the life of the person sitting right next to you.
"Cult": A Label Too Convenient
The 1995 Tokyo subway sarin attack by Aum Shinrikyō left a deep wound in Japanese society.
But it also left the media with a kind of template.

As research by Professor Erica Baffelli at the University of Manchester demonstrates, Japanese media began using the word "cult" (karuto) freely when covering any new religious movement after the attack.
The word automatically carries connotations of brainwashing, violence, and fraud.
A single incident by one group came to define the public image of hundreds of unrelated religious organizations.
The problem is that this "cult" frame remains alive nearly three decades later.
In 2025, four United Nations Special Rapporteurs jointly raised concerns about Japan.
They pointed out that "Children's Human Rights SOS Mini-Letters" distributed in schools reinforced discriminatory stereotypes against religious minorities.

Practices as varied as Jehovah's Witnesses not celebrating birthdays and the dietary laws of Judaism, Islam, and Hinduism were all placed under the vague umbrella of "child abuse related to religious beliefs."
The UN experts stated:
Rather than protecting children who belong to religion or belief minorities, these materials risk contributing to their bullying and marginalization."
Materials designed to protect children end up hurting them.
Is this irony? Or is it the inevitable result of underestimating the power of framing?
Zainichi Koreans, Another Casualty of Framing
Prejudice against religious minorities is just one facet of the discrimination embedded in Japanese society.
In July 2022, immediately after the assassination of former Prime Minister Shinzo Abe, a false claim spread like wildfire across social media: that the suspect was a "Zainichi Korean."
It was entirely untrue, but the speed of the lie far outpaced any fact-check.
As TIME reported, Zainichi Koreans are the most targeted minority in Japan, subjected to relentless discriminatory speech online.
In 2021, a 22-year-old man set fire to and destroyed seven buildings in Utoro, an ethnic Korean neighborhood in Uji, Kyoto.
The court found that the perpetrator had been radicalized by consuming anti-Korean content online.
Or consider the case of Fuji Corporation, an Osaka-based homebuilder.
Management distributed flyers in the workplace that included screenshots of xenophobic YouTube videos. The materials featured online comments reading "Die Zainichi."
A third-generation Zainichi Korean woman employed there suffered psychological distress and filed a lawsuit.
What do these cases have in common?
Negative framing of specific groups, amplified repeatedly through media and online platforms, eventually crystallizes into real-world discrimination and violence.
The Story of "Pitiful Children"
The label attached to second-generation believers of the Family Federation (formerly the Unification Church) comes from a slightly different angle of framing.
The media portrays them as "pitiful children forced into faith by their parents."
But multiple second-generation believers who have spoken out on the streets challenge this one-dimensional depiction.
One believer stated plainly that among his four siblings, "not a single one was forced."
He remained in the church because he saw people, his family and church members, who truly "lived for the sake of others."
Another believer, Mr. Fukunaga, shared how his father, a church staff member, collapsed from a brain hemorrhage and was left with severe disabilities.
There was a time when he doubted God's existence and sank into despair, feeling "it would be fine if I disappeared."
But watching his mother accept his disabled father as "a precious person chosen by God" and devote herself to his care, he rediscovered the meaning of faith.
"My life cannot exist without this person," his mother declared. Those words became, for him, proof of what faith could mean.
But stories like these almost never make it into the media.
Why?
The reason is simple.
"Pitiful victims" get better ratings. Multifaceted reality doesn't fit into a 30-second news clip.
And what doesn't fit is treated as if it never existed.
The Irreversibility of Framing
The most dangerous property of media framing is its irreversibility.
Once a label like "cult," "dangerous," or "brainwashed" has been applied, removing it becomes nearly impossible.
No matter how much counter-evidence is presented, the cognitive framework formed in people's minds does not change easily.
What psychologists call "confirmation bias" takes over and only the information that fits the existing frame is selectively absorbed.

The U.S. State Department's 2023 Report on International Religious Freedom noted that Family Federation members were unable to openly express their faith following the Abe assassination, due to what they described as "biased" or "antagonistic" media coverage and pressure from the National Network of Lawyers Against Spiritual Sales.
Cases were documented in which members were denied participation in community cultural events and had monetary donations rejected.
Holding a religious belief, an inherently private choice, becomes directly linked to public disadvantage.
This is happening in a country where freedom of the press and freedom of religion are both constitutionally guaranteed.
Why Discrimination in Developed Nations Is Hard to See
Japan has ratified most major international human rights treaties.
Freedom of expression and freedom of religion are both enshrined in its constitution.
And yet, discrimination fueled by media framing persists.
It remains invisible because discrimination in developed nations operates not through the absence of law, but through "atmosphere."
The stated reason for a firing is never "religion."
A rental refusal is explained as "a comprehensive judgment."
Bullying at school is dismissed as "something between kids."
Everything takes an ambiguous form.
That is precisely why it is hard to denounce and even harder to make visible.
The vagueness of the concept of "public welfare" that UN Special Rapporteurs flagged strikes at the very heart of this issue.
What violates "public welfare"?
As long as that definition shifts with political and social currents, minorities will always stand on unstable ground.
Dialogue as a Prescription
The second-generation believer who gave a street speech in front of the Okinawa Prefectural Office chose to turn his wounds a starting point for dialogue rather than grounds for accusation.
When a Christian pastor asked him, "Couldn't you have had more dialogue with children who were hurt within the church?" — the words cut deep.
And that pain strengthened not his desire to criticize, but his resolve to pursue mutual understanding.
Is this beautiful idealism?
In reality, simply beginning a dialogue remains enormously difficult.
But what can ultimately counter framing is individual human voices and faces.
Not statistics or labels, but one person's experience changing another person's perception.
"Even in an era when religion tends to be disliked, I believe in a future where people will say, 'Religion really was necessary after all’”.
It would be easy to call these words optimistic.
But behind them lies a quiet conviction to continue fighting prejudice and stay true to their beliefs.
The Question Is Ours
It doesn't matter what faith the person sitting next to you holds.
It doesn't matter what ethnic background they come from.
The question is whether you are judging their life by a story the media created for you.
Japan is one of the safest countries in the world, proud of a culture that values courtesy and order.
In that same country, people lose their jobs and are denied housing because of their beliefs.
Ethnic neighborhoods are set on fire based on social media lies.
Government-distributed educational materials fuel the bullying of children from religious minorities.
These are not exceptional incidents.
They are the result of the quiet violence of “media framing” that has seeped into the fabric of everyday life.
Being a developed nation does not prove the absence of discrimination.
It may, in fact, prove that discrimination has been made invisible with greater sophistication.
There is a decisive line between reporting facts and using framing to push a specific group to the margins of society.
Guarding that line is not the responsibility of media alone.
It belongs to each of us. Whether it’s those who receive information or share it, that information shapes how we see the person sitting right beside us.

The second-generation believers featured in this article have shared their experiences publicly through street speeches and the N.A.B.I documentary. Their testimonies are both a rebuttal to biased reporting and an invitation to dialogue.

title: "Keep Politics and Religion Separate" — But Was That Ever Really the Right Answer?
previewText:
Trump's "Rededication to God" and the Movement That Asked the Same Question a Quarter Century Ago
 
February 5, 2026, at the 74th Annual National Prayer Breakfast. President Trump declared.
"On May

blocks.text: Trump's "Rededication to God" and the Movement That Asked the Same Question a Quarter Century Ago
February 5, 2026, at the 74th Annual National Prayer Breakfast. President Trump declared.
"On May 17, we're inviting Americans from all across the country to come together on our National Mall to pray, to give thanks. We are going to rededicate America as one nation under God."
A standing ovation lasting nearly a minute.
Trump declared, "You just can't have a great country if you don't have religion."
Meanwhile, church-state separation advocates immediately denounced it as "Christian Nationalist rhetoric."
Praise and outrage. Prayer and protest.
This scene forces us to confront a fundamental question.
"Politics and religion must be kept apart" — but was this conventional wisdom ever truly correct?
The Real Meaning of the "Wall"
The origin of church-state separation was, in fact, born from anger over religious persecution.

In 1636, Baptist minister Roger Williams was banished from Massachusetts and fled to Rhode Island. His call for a "wall between church and state" was a levee to protect faith from government corruption.
What he sought to protect was religion itself.
When Jefferson wrote of a "wall of separation" in 1802, the context was the same.
A religious minority feared persecution and appealed to the President. Jefferson promised that the government would not interfere with faith.
In other words, church-state separation at America's founding meant "the state must not impose a specific religion."
It never meant "purge religious values from politics."
Stanford professor Michael McConnell puts it this way:
"What the Framers intended was to prohibit the government from 'controlling' religion. There was nothing wrong with having religious elements in the culture."
Nineteenth-century historian Philip Schaff drew a sharp distinction.
"The American separation of church and state rests upon respect for the church. The European separation rests on indifference and hostility toward the church and religion itself."
The problem is that, somewhere along the way, the world adopted "hostility as separation" as the standard.
What Happened When Religion Was Removed
Since 1945, the United Nations has operated on a design that deliberately excluded the religious dimension.
Despite roughly 80% of the world's population holding religious beliefs, religious leaders have almost never been formally incorporated into conflict mediation.
Rwanda, Srebrenica, Sudan, Myanmar, Gaza — nearly every case the UN acknowledges as a failure involved conflicts intertwined with religion, ethnicity, and culture.
A table of politicians and diplomats alone cannot reach the spiritual dimensions at the root of these conflicts.
Security Council reform has stalled for 30 years, the budget has shrunk roughly 30%, and staff has been cut by 20%.
It is not just the international stage.

Domestically as well, as religion retreated from public life, family breakdown, epidemic loneliness, rising suicide rates, and a loss of meaning — a "crisis of the spirit" beyond the reach of policy — have been eroding societies from within.
Religion is, at its core, the backbone that supports the spiritual life of a nation.
Laws can regulate behavior, but they cannot sustain the human heart.
For thousands of years, that role has been fulfilled by religion and faith.
What happens when you remove that backbone — we are witnessing the answer in real time.
The 80-year experiment of excluding religion has, at least in terms of achieving peace, been difficult to call a success.
The Door Trump Opened
Against this backdrop, Trump shook conventional wisdom with two actions.
The first was the establishment of the Board of Peace in January 2026.
The second was his declaration to "rededicate America to God."

Marking the nation's 250th anniversary, he launched the "America Prays" initiative calling on Americans nationwide to pray weekly, and announced a major prayer gathering on the National Mall for May 17.
In an era when invoking "God" in politics had become taboo, the president of the world's most powerful nation declared publicly.
"You just can't have a great country if you don't have religion. You have to believe in something."
The concerns of those who criticize church-state entanglement — favoritism toward a specific religion, political exploitation of faith, exclusion of minorities — deserve serious consideration.
But here, one question must be posed.
"Has a politics that completely excluded religious values made the world a better place?"
A movement that has been squarely confronting this question existed a full quarter century before Trump.
The "Answer" from a Quarter Century Ago
In 2000, at the United Nations headquarters, Sun Myung Moon and Dr. Hak Ja Han founder of the Family Federation for World Peace and Unification, proposed.
"An interreligious council, composed of the world's religious leaders, should be established within the United Nations."
Them argument was clear.
Political leaders and religious leaders must work together for world peace.
Politics alone cannot reach the human heart; religion alone cannot move reality.
Only when both sit at the same table, respecting each other's roles, can peace be realized.
This was not a call for theocracy.
It was a "third way" — between the separation of church and state and the union of church and state.

The Universal Peace Federation (UPF), established in 2005, holds the highest-level General Consultative Status with the UN Economic and Social Council and facilitates interreligious dialogue in over 157 countries.
And at the heart of this movement lies a surprisingly simple conviction: Peace begins in the family.
Peacebuilding That Starts with the Family
In post-conflict societies, the family is the first thing to collapse — and broken families become the breeding ground for the next generation's violence.
The UN deploys troops.
The Board of Peace addresses infrastructure.
But no international framework squarely tackles the spiritual rebuilding of the families living in those very places.

The network cultivated by the Family Federation across more than 120 countries represents an attempt to approach  "inner peace" — the peace within human beings — starting from the smallest possible unit.
Similarly, the interreligious diplomacy of the UPF holds practical value.
History provides numerous examples where the mediation of religious leaders served as a breakthrough for peace, such as in Northern Ireland, Mozambique, and Colombia.

By monitoring and advocating for religious freedom through a network spanning 157 countries, this initiative can play a unique role in peacebuilding—driven not by military or formal diplomatic power, but by civil society.
Putting a "Door" in the Wall
The "wall" of church-state separation should not be torn down.
When a specific religion fuses with state power, persecution and corruption follow.
But raising the wall ever higher and excluding religion has also proven, over 80 years of experimentation, to be no answer.
What is needed is neither tearing down the wall nor raising it higher. It is putting a "door" in the wall.
A door through which political and religious leaders can sit at the same table when needed, without encroaching on each other's domains.
A door through which humanity's spiritual heritage can serve the international order without imposing any specific faith.
What the Family Federation has advocated for a quarter century is precisely the blueprint for this "door."
Now that Trump has launched the Board of Peace and declared America's rededication to God, that blueprint carries more relevance than ever before.
What lies beyond the door?
Perhaps those who will show us first are the people who have been building peace from the most universal place of all — the family.

This article does not promote any specific political position or religious doctrine. Its purpose is to examine the structural challenges of church-state separation and the international order from multiple perspectives.
