title: Allegations of Election Fraud: A 21-Year Global Timeline of Electronic Voting Systems
previewText:
A 21-Year Journey
Across the globe, electoral anomalies and unnatural late-night reversals have become a recurring theme.
These are not mere coincidences, but rather signs of a vast interconnected web

blocks.text: A 21-Year Journey
Across the globe, electoral anomalies and unnatural late-night reversals have become a recurring theme.

These are not mere coincidences, but rather signs of a vast interconnected web of technology, funding, and organization—a 21-year journey that began in Venezuela in 2004 and has now come full circle to the South Korean elections of 2025.
1. 2004: Venezuela, The Testing Ground for High-Tech Manipulation
The story begins with the 2004 presidential recall referendum under Hugo Chávez.
The Rise of Smartmatic: A then-obscure company, Smartmatic, emerged with voting machines that were more than simple tabulators; they possessed two-way network communication capabilities.

The "Miracle Reversal": Immediately following a mysterious late-night pause in counting, the results saw a dramatic shift from an opposition lead to a Chávez victory. Experts pointed to the potential existence of "backdoors" and algorithms designed to force results toward a specific percentage.
2. Technological Succession: Entering the U.S. via "Dominion" (2005–2010)
The technology refined in Venezuela was integrated into North American election infrastructure through a series of corporate acquisitions.

The Sequoia Acquisition: Smartmatic acquired the prominent U.S. firm Sequoia Voting Systems. Although later forced to divest by the U.S. government (CFIUS) due to foreign influence concerns, the assets and intellectual property were eventually absorbed by the Canadian-founded Dominion Voting Systems.

A Shared Bloodline: Allegations persist that the original Venezuelan source code or its core design philosophy was inherited by Dominion. This became a central flashpoint during the 2020 U.S. Presidential Election regarding "vote flips" and "data spikes."
3. The Global Distribution Hub: A-WEB and USAID (2013–2014)

In 2013, the Association of World Election Bodies (A-WEB) was established in Seoul, spearheaded by the South Korean National Election Commission (NEC), serving as a global gateway for "Standardizing Elections."

USAID Funding: In 2014, the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) signed an MOU with A-WEB. This meant U.S. taxpayer money was now backing the export of South Korean-made election systems to developing nations.
The Quadrilateral of Allegation: A powerful network was finalized: Smartmatic, Dominion, A-WEB, and USAID—all sharing technical roots or a common pipeline of funding.
4. Field Testing: Exporting "Failure" to Developing Nations (2014–2024)
Systems exported via A-WEB led to chaos rather than democratic stability in several regions.

The Congo and Iraq Crises: In the 2018 DRC elections, citizens denounced the touchscreen machines as "Cheating Machines," sparking mass protests. In Iraq (2018), identical systems faced such severe fraud allegations that polling stations were set on fire, and a manual recount eventually overturned the electronic results.
5. 2025: The Circle Closes in South Korea
After 21 years of global "field testing" and refinement, the system has returned to the very place that facilitated its global spread: South Korea.

The Return of the Master Algorithm: There is grave concern that the "seeds of manipulation" planted in Venezuela in 2004—polished through U.S. corporate shifts and global A-WEB deployments—will operate as a "perfected manipulation package" in the 2025 South Korean elections.
Common Signatures: Abnormal server access and unnatural statistical "spikes" seen worldwide are warned to be the "digital fingerprints" of a single, 21-year-old lineage of code.
Conclusion: Is Your Vote "Will" or "Data"?
This timeline illustrates a chilling risk: that beneath the guise of "efficiency," an opaque power now possesses the ability to design election results without the public’s knowledge.
Identical code, identical funding, and identical patterns of fraud. As we head into 2025, we must ask.
Is the vote you cast a "will" to be accurately counted, or is it merely "data" to be processed by a system perfected over two decades of shadow play?

title: "TM Special Report" Raises Suspicions of Intentional Alterations by Yun
previewText:
Overview and Emergence of Alteration Suspicions
At the end of 2025, the Korean media outlet Hankyoreh reported on the "TM (True Mother) Special Report," which attracted attention as an internal

blocks.text: Overview and Emergence of Alteration Suspicions

At the end of 2025, the Korean media outlet Hankyoreh reported on the "TM (True Mother) Special Report," which attracted attention as an internal document of the Family Federation for World Peace and Unification (former Unification Church).

This document is a report to President Han Hak-ja, covering 222 entries from 2018 to 2022. However, according to the Family Federation's official stance, its credibility is questioned. Reports from staff who worked under Yun Young-ho (Yun Yong-ho), the former world headquarters director, suggest intentional omissions, rewritings, and additions, raising issues with media misinterpretations.
Church's View: Creation Process and Lack of Credibility

The Family Federation's investigation committee is currently verifying the 3,200-page document. It is based on materials submitted by Yun to the Korean prosecution, but suspicions of alterations arise as follows:
Suspicion of Omissions: Initially explained by Yun himself as exceeding 5,000 pages, it was reduced to 3,200 pages. Staff testimonies confirm cases where parts unfavorable to Yun were deleted.

Suspicion of Rewritings/Additions: Date errors (e.g., January 2022 entries listed as January 2021, January 2023 as January 2022). This strongly suggests additions or corrections to make it appear as if Yun reported a meeting with Korean politician Kwon Seong-dong in advance. The Family Federation judges this as alterations to favor Yun's trial in Korea.
Specific Examples: Factual Discrepancies and Traces of Alterations
The document contains numerous errors, suggesting Yun's manipulation:
Related to Japanese Lawmaker Hagiuida Koichi: Description of presenting a Hermes necktie was clearly denied by Hagiuida on a program on January 18, 2026. Testimony states "I did not receive it."
Takai Sanae’s Place of Origin: Misrecorded as "Kanagawa" (actual is Nara).
Election Support Numbers: "290 LDP members" exceeds the total number of LDP candidates, showing inconsistency.

Abe Shooting Incident Report: No actual report from the Nara district leader exists; writing style differs and appears fabricated (e.g., description that Chairman Tanaka ordered deletion of suspect Yamagami Tetsuya's name, but deletion is impossible at the local church—only possible at the Korean headquarters under Yun's management. Mother's affiliated church is also incorrect). These suggest distortion under Yun's supervision.
Details of Yun's Alterations: Leak Process and Artificial Elements
There is a high possibility that Yun was directly involved in the leak; the 3,200-page version extracts only Japanese parts:
Traces of Deletions: All content unfavorable to Yun was removed.

Routine Supervision: Site reports were revised at the Korean headquarters, with exaggerations for faith-based considerations or to emphasize Yun's achievements, as per staff testimonies. Site leaders could not grasp differences between their reports and revisions made by Yun at headquarters. The Family Federation views this document not as the prosecution's seized evidence but as one strongly reflecting Yun's intentions. It points out the possibility that it was aimed at leading to favorable outcomes for Yun's trial in Korea through dissemination in Japanese media.
Media Issues: Lack of Fact-Checking
The reporting reflects the bashing after the 2022 Abe shooting incident. Ignoring the background of Yun's alterations, it treats "support for 290 LDP members" as fact:
Dangers: Promotes defamation and political confusion. Repeats past media rampages.
Rising Voices: Opinions calling for "media accountability" are increasing.
Importance of Clarifying Suspicions and Fair Reporting

The TM Special Report is a document with high possibility of intentional additions, deletions, and alterations by Yun, and its credibility is denied. With Yun's trial ongoing, clarifying these suspicions will be key to preventing social division.

title: Religion or Cult? The Growing Threat to Democracy in South Korea’s Campaign Against "Heresy.”
previewText: In January 2026, an agreement reached between South Korean President Lee Jae-myung and leaders of major established religions sparked international concern. Far from being a mere domestic religious

blocks.text: In January 2026, an agreement reached between South Korean President Lee Jae-myung and leaders of major established religions sparked international concern. Far from being a mere domestic religious issue, this development represents a significant challenge to the freedom of thought.
This article delves deeper into the warnings presented in the original report and explores the implications of this controversial move.
1. The Dangerous Collusion of Political Populism and Religious Authority

During a meeting on January 13, President Lee and leaders of prominent Buddhist and Christian denominations labeled groups such as the Family Federation for World Peace and Unification (formerly the Unification Church) and the Shincheonji Church of Jesus as "heretical."

A particularly striking aspect of this meeting was the use of "public support" as a justification to discuss the disbandment of specific groups and the seizure of their assets without following formal judicial procedures.

For politicians, attacking "easy targets" that lack broad public sympathy serves as a form of populism to boost approval ratings. For established religions, it offers an opportunity to eliminate emerging competitors using the power of the state. This "closed-door collusion" risks leading to extrajudicial measures that bypass the essential principle of due process.
2. Power, Not Theology, Distinguishes "Religion" from "Cult"
History shows that almost every religion considered "orthodox" today was once branded an "anti-social cult" during its infancy.

The Paradox of Christianity: Early Christians were persecuted by the Roman Empire for refusing to participate in emperor worship and holding secret meetings. They were targets of malicious rumors, accused of cannibalism and destroying the family unit.

Catholic Martyrdom in Korea: In the 18th and 19th centuries, tens of thousands of Korean Catholics were executed. Because they rejected the Confucian tradition of ancestral rites (jesa), their faith was condemned as a "wicked heterodoxy" that was unfilial and anti-national.

History proves that "what is labeled a cult in one era may become the state religion in the next." It is a profound historical irony that established religions, once the victims of persecution, are now mobilizing state power to suppress newcomers.
3. Double Standards: The "Dark Side" of Established Religions

The established religions that label new movements as "dangerous" often harbor their own severe historical or structural issues. The original article highlights the following examples to point out this hypocrisy:

Systemic Crimes of the Catholic Church: During the Middle Ages, the Inquisition justified torture and execution in the name of faith. In modern times, the systematic concealment of sexual abuse of children by thousands of clergy members worldwide—often by simply transferring perpetrators—demonstrates a grave institutional failure.

"Cult-like" Inner Circles: As Andre McNicoll argued in his 1982 book Catholic Cults, certain organizations within the Church, such as Opus Dei, have been criticized for using methods similar to those of "cults," including extreme secrecy and demands for absolute obedience to leaders.

Protestantism and Violence: Historically, various Protestant sects spearheaded "witch hunts." During the colonial era, they used the Bible to justify the destruction of indigenous cultures and the institution of slavery.

Modern Buddhism and Islam: From the persecution of the Rohingya by certain Buddhist factions in Myanmar to the atrocities committed by extremists claiming the mantle of Islam, history shows that "established" religions can cause greater social harm than new movements when tied to political ambition or exclusionism.
Critiques such as "destroying families" or "mind control" can, to varying degrees, be applied to almost any religious organization that demands fervent devotion.
4. The End of Religious Pluralism and the Risk of a "Negative Chain Reaction"

Currently, established religions in Korea face a crisis of rapidly declining memberships. As younger generations turn away from traditional faiths, turning to state power to stop the flow of believers to new religious movements is, in essence, a declaration of spiritual defeat.
Furthermore, if this "Korean Model"—where the state defines and eliminates heresy—becomes an international standard, it could trigger a terrifying global chain reaction:
In the Islamic World: Christians could have their assets seized as "heretics who incite social unrest."
In India: Under Hindu nationalism, Christianity or Buddhism could be banned as "foreign cults."
Granting the state the right to restrict the freedom of others will eventually result in the restriction of one's own.
Conclusion: Freedom of Religion as the Bastion of Democra
The essence of religious freedom is not protecting what society deems "correct." It is about upholding the right to exist for those things we believe are wrong or find uncomfortable.
If Korea’s established religions choose to collaborate with power to annihilate minorities, they are destroying the very democratic foundation they helped build.
When a state acquires the power to screen "correct" religions and disband "distasteful" groups, the freedom of thought for all citizens dies.
The events of January 13 serve as a stark warning: we are witnessing a moment where the most fundamental right—freedom of conscience—is being bartered for political expediency and populist gain.
Sources:

Ward, Thomas J. "When established religions turn to state power: Korea's dangerous precedent." The Korea Times, January 21, 2026. https://www.koreatimes.co.kr/opinion/20260121/when-established-religions-turn-to-state-power-koreas-dangerous-precedent

title: “Just for Being Alive”: The Untold Human Rights Crisis Behind Japan’s Religious Crackdown
previewText:
[英語記事 + 日本語訳あり]

"Treated as Criminals Just for Being Alive": A Second-Generation Believer’s Account of Unjust Discrimination and Human Rights Violations
“――There are even second-generation

blocks.text:
[英語記事 + 日本語訳あり]

"Treated as Criminals Just for Being Alive": A Second-Generation Believer’s Account of Unjust Discrimination and Human Rights Violations

“――There are even second-generation believers who have committed suicide due to bullying at work.” As the dissolution order for the Family Federation for World Peace and Unification (formerly the Unification Church) looms, the words of this second-generation youth pierce the heart. Since the shooting incident involving former Prime Minister Shinzo Abe, believers have been exposed to a storm of discrimination and exclusion under political pressure, media bias, and the shadow of the judiciary. Is this testimony a harbinger of the “collapse of human rights” that dissolution would bring? We uncover the reality through the raw experiences of Shin Nitta, a youth from N.A.B.I. (Second-Generation Believers’ Street Advocacy Team).
Is “Freedom of Religion” After Dissolution Just an Illusion?
He first questions the repeated media claim that “even if dissolved, religious activities can still be conducted freely.”

I have one thing I want to say to everyone. It is said on TV that even if the Family Federation is dissolved, religious activities can still be conducted freely and freedom of religion will be protected. However, as active believers, from the perspective of those of us who have been subjected to slander and defamation by society, the government, and the media since the shooting incident involving former Prime Minister Abe—and whose freedoms are increasingly restricted in our daily lives—it is impossible to believe that we will be able to conduct religious activities freely at all.

These words illustrate how the social backlash after the incident has severely constrained believers’ daily lives. He points out that if a dissolution order is issued, these freedoms are likely to be further stripped away. Believers are already subjected to “slander and defamation,” making free religious activity increasingly difficult.

The Volunteer Activity in Fukuoka and the Revocation of the Award: An Experience Where Pure Goodwill Was Denied

Mr. Nitta, the vice representative, speaks about the social contribution activities he undertook during his university years. He vividly describes how faith-based volunteer work came to be treated after the incident.

Let me share my personal experience. When I was attending university, as part of my social contribution activities, I wanted to help maintain order in society, so I wore a ranger costume and participated in trash collection and cleaning activities. This was part of my university club activities. That work was commended by the City of Fukuoka, and I received an Environmental Merit Award. I was thanked by the city, and I was happy to contribute to its citizens; based on my faith, I engaged in many such volunteer activities. However, after the assassination of former Prime Minister Abe and the subsequent declaration of severance of ties with the Family Federation, the Mayor of Fukuoka also announced a severance of ties with the Family Federation. Following that, the Environmental Merit Award I had received was revoked and treated as if it had never existed. I was truly shocked. This was simply an effort to make the city better, done for the sake of Fukuoka. I was not engaging in any proselytizing at all. Yet the fact that a university student who believes in the Family Federation had done volunteer work was treated as if it were a crime. It was so frustrating and so unjust that I cried.

This experience demonstrates the irrationality of denying acts of goodwill solely because of one’s faith. The revocation of the award is a symbolic act that discourages believers from participating in society. Volunteer work unrelated to proselytizing being “treated as a crime” is the product of prejudice and constitutes nothing short of a human rights violation.

The Flower-Planting Volunteers in Niigata and the Spread of Discrimination: Exclusion from Society

Furthermore, he cites victims in other regions. Volunteer activities in Niigata also changed drastically due to the post-incident atmosphere.

In Niigata, we were engaged in flower-planting volunteer activities. But after this uproar, we were told to pull out the flowers we had planted ourselves and go home. As Japanese citizens, do we not have the right to contribute to society and our country? We simply wanted to do volunteer work, yet we were unilaterally judged as doing something suspicious and had everything denied—just because we are believers in the Family Federation. We can’t even rent housing or use public facilities.

Here, it is clear that believers’ basic rights are being violated. The results of their volunteer work are denied, and even access to housing and facilities is restricted. Such exclusion is a manifestation of social pressure that infringes upon freedom of religion.
Bullying in Schools and Workplaces, and Severe Mental Harm: A Reality Where Suicides Occur

Mr. Nitta emphasizes the severity of the discrimination faced by second-generation believers through examples from schools and workplaces. These abuses cause deep psychological suffering and, in extreme cases, lead to tragic outcomes.

In schools, there are students from the Family Federation who have cried after teachers openly denied their faith. One teacher criticized blessing marriages by saying, “Your parents’ marriage is the same as a dog and a cat getting married,” and the student burst into tears. The repeated bullying is so painful that some second-generation believers become hikikomori (social recluses) and cannot leave their homes. There are also second-generation believers who have taken their own lives because the bullying at work was too severe. Even now, before any dissolution of the Family Federation has been officially decided, this situation is already so unfair, unequal, and devoid of human rights. People are being treated as if they were criminals simply for being alive.

These examples underscore the tragic consequences of discrimination. Insults in educational settings and harassment in workplaces lead to social withdrawal and, in the worst cases, suicide. If such harm is occurring even before any dissolution is finalized, there is grave concern that it will intensify further afterward.

Conclusion: A Social Reexamination to Protect Freedom of Religion and Human Rights

Mr. Nitta’s testimony powerfully conveys that the dissolution crisis facing the Family Federation threatens the dignity of believers. Under the combined influence of politics, the media, and the judiciary, believers are already being “treated as criminals,” and their freedoms are being restricted. This situation raises grave concerns from the perspective of freedom of religion and human rights as guaranteed by the Japanese Constitution.

Did the government or the judiciary ever imagine that, through their decisions, tens of thousands of citizens in Japan would come to be treated like criminals based on false accusations and be forced to live under such conditions? It is my hope that the sincere and passionate voices of these young people will reach society. When discussing the merits and drawbacks of dissolution, we must not ignore the lived experiences of believers and must maintain a fair and balanced perspective. Ultimately, a society that respects diverse faiths is what truly embodies democracy.

「生きているだけで犯罪者扱い」信教二世の青年が語る、理不尽な差別と人権侵害の現実
「――会社でのいじめが原因で自殺した信教二世もいるんです」

家庭連合（旧統一教会）の解散命令が迫る中、信教二世の青年が語る言葉は、胸をえぐる。安倍晋三元首相の銃撃事件以降、政治の圧力、メディアの偏向、司法の影で、信徒たちは差別と排除の嵐にさらされている。この証言は、解散がもたらす「人権崩壊」の予兆か？ N.A.B.I（信教二世遊説隊）の青年・新田さんの生々しい体験から、その現実を暴く。   解散後の「信教の自由」は幻想か？彼は、まずメディアで繰り返される「解散しても宗教活動は自由にできる」という主張に疑問を投げかける。
私から皆様に一つ申し上げたいことがあります。それは、もし家庭連合が解散になっても宗教活動は自由にできると、信教の自由は守られるとテレビで言われました。しかし、私達現役信者として今回の安部元首相の銃撃事件以降、社会から国からメディアから誹謗中傷をあげられていて自由をどんどん制限されながら今生活している当事者からしてみたら全く自由に宗教活動ができるとは到底思えないのです。

この言葉は、事件後の社会的なバッシングが、信徒の日常をどれほど制限しているかを物語る。解散命令が出れば、さらに自由が奪われる可能性が高いと彼は指摘する。信徒はすでに「誹謗中傷」にさらされ、自由な活動が難しくなっているのだ。   福岡でのボランティア活動と賞の剥奪：純粋な善意が否定された体験　新田副代表は、大学時代に取り組んだ社会貢献活動について語る。信仰に基づいたボランティアが、事件後どのように扱われたかを生々しく明かす。

私の体験談を話します。大学に通っていた時、社会貢献活動として、世の中の秩序を守りたいという理由で、レンジャーのコスチュームを着てゴミ拾いの清掃活動をしていた。大学のサークル活動として。その活動は、福岡市から表彰されて、環境功労賞というものをもらった。市からも感謝され、市民のために貢献できることが嬉しくて、信仰に基づいてそういうボランティア活動をたくさんしてきた。しかし、安部元首相暗殺事件以降、家庭連合との関係断絶宣言がされてから福岡市長も家庭連合との関係断絶を宣言した。その後、もらった環境功労賞が剥奪、なかったことにされた。本当にショックだった。ただ純粋に、この市をよくしたいと思って福岡のために活動したことだった。布教活動は一切していなかった。ただ家庭連合で信仰している大学生がボランティア活動したことが、まるで犯罪を犯したかのような扱いをされた。あまりにも悔しくてあまりにも不当で泣いた。
この体験は、信仰を理由に善意の活動が否定される理不尽さを示す。賞の剥奪は、信徒の社会参加を阻害する象徴的な出来事だ。布教とは無関係のボランティアが「犯罪扱い」されるのは、偏見の産物であり、人権侵害に他ならない。   新潟での花植えボランティアと広がる差別：社会からの排除　さらに、彼は他の地域での被害を挙げる。新潟でのボランティア活動も、事件後の風潮で一変した。

新潟では、花植えのボランティア活動をしていた。だが、この騒動以降、自分達で植えた花を抜いて帰れと言われた。私達は日本国民として、社会のために、国のために貢献する権利もないのでしょうか？ただ純粋にボランティア活動をしたいだけだったのに、何か怪しいことをしているのではないかと一方的に決めつけられて、全てを否定されてきたんです。（家庭連合の信者という理由で）家も借りれない、施設も借りれない。 ここでは、信徒の基本的な権利が侵害されていることがわかる。ボランティアの成果が否定され、住宅や施設の利用すら制限される。こうした排除は、信教の自由を侵す社会的な圧力の表れだ。
学校・職場でのいじめと深刻な精神的被害：自殺者も出る現実　彼は、信教二世が直面する差別の深刻さを、学校や職場での事例で強調する。これらの被害は、精神的苦痛を引き起こし、極端な結果を招いている。

学校では、先生が堂々と家庭連合の信仰を否定するようなことを言われて、涙を流した家庭連合の学生達がいる。ある先生からは、**「お前のお父さんお母さんは、犬と猫が結婚したのと同じなんだ」**と祝福結婚を批判されて、涙を流した学生がいました。あまりにも度重なるいじめは苦しすぎて引きこもりになって、家から出られなくなった信教２世がいる。また、会社内でいじめが酷すぎて、自ら命を絶ってしまった信教２世がいる。社会からのバッシングゆえに、自殺してしまった信教２世たちもいる。本当に今この状態で、家庭連合の解散が正式に決まっていないこの段階であっても、これほどに不公平で、不平等で、人権が全くない。生きているだけで犯罪者と言われているような、そんな気持ちになる扱いをされている人もいるんです！

これらの事例は、差別がもたらす悲劇を浮き彫りにする。教育現場での侮辱、職場でのいじめが、引きこもりや自殺につながる。解散が決まっていない段階でこれほどの被害が出ているなら、解散後はいっそう深刻化する恐れがある。   結論：信教の自由と人権を守るための社会的な再考を　彼の証言は、家庭連合の解散危機が、信徒の尊厳を脅かすものであることを強く訴える。政治・メディア・司法の影響下で、信徒はすでに「犯罪者扱い」され、自由を制限されている。この状況は、日本憲法が保障する信教の自由と人権の観点から、深刻な問題だ。 　政府が司法が決定によって、日本国内にいる数万人の国民が冤罪によって犯罪者のような扱いを受け、生活していくことになるなんて、予想しただろうか？こうした青年の純粋で熱情的な声が社会に届くことを期待したい。解散の是非を議論する際は、信徒の生の体験を無視せず、公平な視点を持つべきだ。最終的に、多様な信仰を尊重する社会こそが、真の民主主義を実現する。

title: Shock of Dissolution Order in Japan: Congressman Konishi’s Video Exposes State Overreach
previewText:
[英語記事 + 日本語訳あり]
“I am responsible for the request for the dissolution order against the Unification Church.” 
This bold declaration by Democratic Party for the People Congressman Hiroyuki

blocks.text: [英語記事 + 日本語訳あり]
“I am responsible for the request for the dissolution order against the Unification Church.”
This bold declaration by Democratic Party for the People Congressman Hiroyuki Konishi in a recent video has sent shockwaves through Japanese society.

His raw, boastful narrative has ignited public outrage. Admitting to tactics such as, “I threatened to keep calling Prime Minister Kishida the ‘Guardian Deity of the Unification Church’” and “I taught him the methods,” Konishi exposed a backstage where a politician seemingly coerced the Prime Minister into forcibly reversing long-standing legal interpretations.
The video documents an opposition lawmaker hounding the Prime Minister with derogatory labels to force a 180-degree shift in the interpretation of the Religious Corporations Law overnight.
During the October 2022 Diet session, Prime Minister Kishida initially testified that “civil law violations do not meet dissolution requirements.”

Yet, following Konishi’s aggressive pressure, the government revised its stance the very next day to include “civil law torts.” Konishi’s posture—claiming this as a personal “achievement”—symbolizes a dangerous privatization of state power.
If this dissolution order is finalized, Japan will set an abnormal precedent where the law changes based on political threats rather than judicial principle.
Why Is This a “Constitutional Violation”? Core Points by Professor Setsu Kobayashi
Preeminent constitutional scholar Professor Setsu Kobayashi condemns these actions as “the epitome of constitutional violation” and “a violent act that undermines the separation of church and state.”

Infringement on Administrative Independence: Legal interpretations must be judged independently by administrative agencies. However, Konishi’s admission that he “taught the methods” to force a change through threats distorts Article 41 (Diet as the highest organ) and Article 65 (Executive power) of the Constitution.

Infringement on Freedom of Religion (Article 20): For 70 years, “violation of laws” in the Religious Corporations Law was understood as criminal-level offenses (e.g., Aum Shinrikyo). Expanding this to “civil law torts” threatens the survival of all religious groups. As Professor Kobayashi warns, “Any religion could be targeted over past civil lawsuits, turning the law into a tool for state-led persecution.”

Collapse of Separation of Church and State: When the government moves under political pressure to crush a specific religion, the constitutional wall of separation collapses, violating the equality principle (Article 14).
Warnings from the International Community: A Threat to Global Freedom
This issue has drawn sharp international scrutiny.

In October 2025, four UN Special Rapporteurs sent a formal letter warning the Japanese government that the dissolution order and anti-religion propaganda in schools violate international human rights standards.
Former EU Special Envoy Ján Figeľ also expressed “serious concern,” warning that Japan’s actions could trigger a domino effect of religious persecution in other democratic nations.
The Spread to Korea: President Lee Jae-myung’s "Japan Model"

The most alarming development is the export of this precedent. In South Korea, President Lee Jae-myung (inaugurated June 2025) has instructed his cabinet to consider dissolution orders against religious groups, citing the "Japan model" as a justification.
This has put diverse faith communities—from minority Christian sects to Buddhist groups—at risk of political retaliation under the guise of "social stability."
The Path Forward: Protecting the Rule of Law
The dissolution order, as exposed by Konishi’s video, is the result of political maneuvering over legal integrity.

If finalized, it will lead to the destruction of organizations, mass unemployment, and the collapse of believers' lives. This is a cry for the survival of Japan as a nation governed by the rule of law. We must choose: protect the fundamental freedom of religion or allow the unchecked runaway of state power.
解散命令の衝撃：小西議員の「自慢動画」が暴く、国家権力の暴走と憲法の危機

「統一教会の解散命令請求は、私の手柄だ」——。立憲民主党の小西ひろゆき議員（小西洋之氏）が、最近の動画でこう高らかに宣言した瞬間、日本社会に衝撃が走りました。この動画では、小西議員が自慢げに語る内容があまりに生々しく、国民の怒りを爆発させています。「岸田首相を『統一教会の守護神』と言い続けるぞと脅した」「やり方方法を授けた」「その通りに首相は動いた」——こうした言葉が飛び出し、まるで政治家が首相を脅迫して法解釈を強引に変えさせたかのような舞台裏を披瀝しているのです。

動画は、野党議員が与党首相を「守護神」呼ばわりしながら追い込み、一夜にして宗教法人法の解釈を180度転換させたプロセスを、まるで自慢話のように語っています。2022年10月の国会質疑で岸田首相が当初「民法違反は解散要件に該当しない」と答弁した直後、小西議員の猛攻が始まり、翌日には政府が「民法の不法行為も含む」と修正。これが「私の手柄」と胸を張る姿は、単なる政治的成果ではなく、国家権力の私物化を象徴するものとして、世間から「憲法違反の極み」と非難されています。もしこの解散命令が確定したら、日本は「議員の脅しで法が変わる」異常な前例を残すことになるのです。
なぜこれが「憲法違反」なのか？ 小林節教授が指摘する核心
憲法学の権威である小林節教授は、この一連の動きを「憲法違反の極み」「政教分離の原則を根底から崩す暴挙」と断罪しています。理由を一つ一つ詳しく見ていきましょう。

行政解釈の変更が議員の圧力で起きたこと（行政の独立性侵害）政府の法解釈は、行政機関が憲法・法律に基づいて独自に判断するものでなければなりません。しかし、小西議員の動画で明らかになったように、野党議員が首相を「守護神」と脅し、具体的な「やり方」を授けて解釈を強制的に変えさせた。これは、立法府（国会）が行政府（政府）を直接支配する行為に等しく、憲法41条（国会の最高機関性）と65条（行政権の帰属）を歪めるものです。行政は政治的圧力から独立して法を運用すべきなのに、ここでは議員の「脅し」が法解釈を一変させたのです。

宗教法人法の解散要件を民法不法行為に拡大したこと（判例の無視と信教の自由侵害）宗教法人法81条は「法令に違反して、著しく公共の福祉を害する行為」が要件ですが、過去70年の判例では「法令違反」とは刑事罰レベルの犯罪行為（例: オウム真理教の殺人事件）を指していました。民法上の不法行為（民事トラブル）を理由に解散を認める新解釈は、判例をポイ捨てした異常事態です。これにより、信教の自由（憲法20条1項）が脅かされます。なぜなら、宗教活動は本質的に「信仰の自由」であり、民事レベルのトラブルで国家が法人を解散させるのは、信者の宗教実践を根こそぎ奪うからです。教授は「これが通れば、どんな宗教も過去の民事訴訟で狙われ、国家による宗教弾圧の道具になる」と警告しています。

政教分離原則の崩壊（憲法20条3項違反）憲法20条3項は「国及びその機関は、宗教教育その他いかなる宗教的活動もしてはならない」と定めています。政府が特定の宗教団体を標的に解散を請求・推進するのは、まさに国家による宗教的活動の制限・抑圧です。小西議員の圧力で政府が動いた場合、これは「政治家が特定の宗教を潰す」ための国家権力行使となり、政教分離の壁を完全に崩壊させます。平等原則（憲法14条）も侵害され、他の宗教団体が「自分たちも次に狙われる」と恐怖を感じる事態です。
小林教授は「裁判所がこの新解釈を容認すれば、憲法の骨格が揺らぐ」と強調。実際、東京地裁の決定（2025年3月）はこの新解釈を基にしていますが、抗告審で覆る可能性が高く、世間では「憲法違反の決定を司法が追認するのか？」という声が爆発しています。
国際社会と国連の警告：日本の解散命令が世界の宗教自由を脅かす

この問題は国内に留まらず、国際社会から厳しい視線が注がれています。国連の特別報告者4名は、2025年10月に日本政府に対して書簡を送り、家庭連合の解散命令と学校での反カルト宣伝が国際法に違反すると警告しました。具体的に、解散は信教の自由を侵害し、「公共の福祉」を口実に宗教少数派を差別するものだと指摘しています。 また、国連人権委員会は、日本が「公共の福祉」を理由に宗教自由を制限しないよう勧告を出しており、2025年3月の東京地裁判決を「恣意的」と批判しています。

さらに、EUの元特使であるヤン・フィゲル氏は、2025年9月の国連人権理事会サイドイベントで、日本の宗教弾圧を「深刻な懸念」と非難。解散命令が国際基準に反し、他の民主主義国家に悪影響を及ぼす可能性を警告しました。 ワシントンDCの宗教自由サミット（2025年2月）では、参加者から「重大な結果を生む」との声が上がり、家庭連合に対する政府のキャンペーンが宗教自由のグローバルスタンダードを崩す前例になるとの懸念が共有されました。 国連の専門家たちは、2025年10月に「宗教少数派へのスティグマ化が続いている」との声明を発表し、日本政府に即時是正を求めています。
これらの国際警告は、日本が国際人権基準を無視している証拠です。世間では「国連の声すら聞かないのか」「アジアの宗教自由が崩壊する」との危機感が広がっています。
韓国への波及：李在明大統領が日本を「参考」に解散を推進する恐怖
さらに恐ろしいのは、この悪しき前例が国境を越えて広がることです。韓国では、李在明大統領（2025年6月就任）が、2025年12月の閣議で「政教分離に反した宗教団体に対する解散命令」を検討するよう指示を出しました。2026年1月現在、宗教指導者たちからの要請に「深く共感し、解散の必要性を認める」と公言し、旧統一教会（家庭連合）を念頭に置いた動きを加速させています。

李大統領は「日本では宗教財団の解散命令を出した例がある」と明言し、日本式の解釈を参考に法的整備を進めています。これが特に警戒されるのは、韓国の家庭連合だけでなく、様々な宗教団体——新興宗教、少数派のキリスト教派、伝統的な仏教団体やシャーマニズム関連のグループ——を解散対象に検討している点です。尹錫悦前政権との癒着疑惑を口実に、政敵や批判勢力の宗教団体を標的にする動きが見られ、2026年1月の国会演説では「社会の安定を脅かすあらゆる宗教的過激主義を排除する」と広範な宗教規制を宣言しています。これにより、韓国国内の多様な信仰コミュニティが一斉に脅かされ、信者たちの礼拝所閉鎖や活動禁止が現実味を帯びています。韓国は教団の本拠地で、数百万人の信者がいますが、解散が実現すれば、日本同様に組織壊滅→職員大量失業→信者生活崩壊の連鎖が発生。政治的に利用した報復として進めば、信教の自由はアジア全体で危機に瀕します。

国際人権団体が警告するように、これは「民主主義国家の宗教弾圧」の輸出となり、世界の宗教少数派に冷たい風を吹きつけるのです。世間では「日本が火をつけたら、韓国で大火事になる」「アジアの宗教自由はどうなるんだ」という危機感が広がっています。特に、李大統領の政策が日本のモデルを基に拡大すれば、韓国社会の宗教多様性が失われ、少数派の信者たちが孤立する事態を招く可能性が高く、注意深く監視する必要があります。
解散が確定したら待ち受ける最悪の未来
この動画が象徴するように、解散命令は「一人の議員の自慢」で法が変わった結果です。確定すれば、信仰は続けられても組織は壊滅、数千人の職員が職を失い、生活が崩壊。韓国でも李在明大統領が日本を「参考」に解散を推進し、アジア全体の宗教自由が危機に陥ります。
世間の声はすでに沸騰中です。「脅しで法が変わるなんて民主主義の死」「憲法違反を放置するのか」——これは家庭連合だけの問題ではなく、日本という法治国家の存亡を問う叫びです。私たちは今、信教の自由を守るか、国家権力の暴走を許すかの選択を迫られています。歴史は、この決定を厳しく裁くでしょう。

title: THE FALL OF FREE KOREA - Pastors Jailed. Churches Raided. Chips Stolen. Beijing Embraced.
previewText:
THE FALL OF FREE KOREA
Pastors Jailed. Churches Raided. Chips Stolen. Beijing Embraced.
🚨 SOUTH KOREA CRISIS
America's Key Pacific Ally Is Undergoing a Dangerous Transformation Under President Lee

blocks.text: THE FALL OF FREE KOREA
Pastors Jailed. Churches Raided. Chips Stolen. Beijing Embraced.
🚨 SOUTH KOREA CRISIS
America's Key Pacific Ally Is Undergoing a Dangerous Transformation Under President Lee Jae-myung — And Most Americans Have No Idea
South Korea hosts 28,500 U.S. troops. It's America's strategic anchor against China and North Korea in the Indo-Pacific.
What's happening there now should concern every American who cares about freedom, religious liberty, and our national security interests.
Here's the full story. 🧵
1/ THE BACKSTORY: HOW WE GOT HERE

On December 3, 2024, President Yoon Suk-yeol declared martial law in a televised address, citing "anti-state forces" and political gridlock. Troops surrounded the National Assembly. The decree suspended political activities, imposed media controls, and authorized warrantless arrests.

Within hours, lawmakers voted 190-0 to lift it. Yoon was impeached on December 14, 2024, with 204 votes including 12 from his own People Power Party. U.S. Deputy Secretary of State Kurt Campbell condemned the move as "illegitimate."
The Constitutional Court unanimously upheld Yoon's removal on April 4, 2025.
2/ THE NEW PRESIDENT

A snap election was held June 3, 2025. Democratic Party candidate Lee Jae-myung won with 49.42% of the vote (17.29 million votes), defeating PPP nominee Kim Moon-soo (41.15%) and Reform Party nominee Lee Jun-seok (8.34%).
Turnout was 79.38%, the highest since 1997. Lee took office immediately on June 4, 2025, without a standard transition period. His party now holds a National Assembly majority.
U.S. conservatives, including Laura Loomer, labeled Lee a "communist," citing his past skepticism of U.S. troop presence and pragmatic diplomacy with China and North Korea.
3/ YOON NOW FACES THE DEATH PENALTY
Yoon was arrested on January 15, 2025, becoming the first sitting South Korean president detained in history. He was released briefly in March but re-detained in July.
On January 16, 2026, Yoon received a five-year sentence for obstructing his arrest, abuse of power, and falsifying documents related to the martial law decree.

Prosecutors sought the death penalty on January 13, 2026, for insurrection. A verdict is scheduled for February 19, 2026. If convicted, he would be only the second former president sentenced for insurrection, after Chun Doo-hwan in 1996.
Human rights groups criticized the death penalty request as regressive.
4/ RELIGIOUS PERSECUTION BEGINS

Pastor Son Hyun-bo of Busan Segyeoro Church, one of Korea's largest congregations with over 4,000 weekly attendees, was arrested on September 8, 2025, for allegedly violating election laws by mobilizing members to support the PPP during the 2025 primaries.
His son, Chance Son, told CBN: "The court's claim of flight risk makes no sense. I believe this is clearly political retaliation and religious oppression targeting Korean churches."
As of December 2025, Pastor Son remained in detention. His family and supporters call the charges minor and politically motivated.
5/ RAIDS ON MAJOR CHURCHES
The crackdown didn't stop with Pastor Son.

Authorities launched aggressive raids on Yoido Full Gospel Church, the world's largest Pentecostal congregation and a site visited by Donald Trump Jr. Police also raided the headquarters of Far East Broadcasting Company (FEBC), led by Pastor Billy Kim.

Warrants were issued for Pastor Jeon Kwang-hoon in December 2025. His home was "ransacked" by prosecutors, and he is forbidden from leaving South Korea pending investigations into allegations he instigated a court invasion.
Former Speaker Newt Gingrich compared the "all-out assault" on political and religious opponents to the FBI's raid on Mar-a-Lago.
6/ THE UNIFICATION CHURCH TARGETED

The Unification Church (Family Federation for World Peace and Unification) was blamed for bribing former First Lady Kim Keon-hee with luxury items, including Chanel bags, a Graff necklace, and ginseng, allegedly to influence policy.
Leader Hak Ja Han Moon, 82, a North Korean refugee who fled communist persecution in 1948, was arrested on September 22, 2025, after a warrant citing flight risk and evidence tampering.

She spent over 30 days confined in a 70-square-foot cell at Seoul Detention Center, where attorneys say she has endured multiple interrogations lasting 10 to 12 hours. Nearly blind and suffering from a heart condition, she is allowed only five visitors for a total of 10 minutes a day.
The church denied the allegations.
7/ TRUMP AND POMPEO RESPOND
On August 25, 2025, during President Lee's White House visit, President Trump decried the "vicious raids on churches" in South Korea.

Former Secretary of State Mike Pompeo wrote on X: "The lawfare being directed at religious leader Dr. Hak Ja Han in South Korea is deeply troubling. The intensifying assaults on religious liberty are a betrayal of the democratic principles that South Korea is meant to espouse."
Jan Figel, president of the Forum for Religious Freedom Europe, accused Lee's government of political vengeance: "This is not anti-corruption. It is a purge."
8/ THE UNIFICATION CHURCH DONATED TO BOTH PARTIES
Investigations revealed the Unification Church donated to both major parties, including $96,000 to Yoon's PPP in 2022 and funds to Democratic Party figures.
This embarrassed Lee's administration after initial claims targeted only conservatives.
Critics say this proves the crackdown is not about corruption but about targeting political opponents under the guise of law enforcement.
9/ LEE MEETS WITH RELIGIOUS LEADERS WHO WANT TO DISSOLVE CHURCHES
On January 12, 2026, President Lee met with religious leaders who urged dissolving the Unification Church and Shincheonji as "illegitimate cults" causing harm.
Lee agreed the issues were "neglected too long." His administration issued a December 2025 directive to explore disbandment based on Japan's model for groups involved in illegal funding or politics.
In January 2026, over 330 faith leaders urged protection of religious rights in South Korea.
10/ CRITICS WARN OF AUTHORITARIANISM
Michael Breen, writing in the Korea Times, called Lee's actions "an astonishing misreading of the basic values that underpin Korea's democracy."

Breen wrote: "That the president, who represents all Koreans, would pass judgment in this way, as if he were the nation's chief priest, and call for the organizational equivalent of the death penalty, is quite shocking."
He added: "Let's face it: He wants to crush these two religions for political reasons. They appeared to support his predecessor."
The Daily Caller warned: "By effectively claiming that organized political expression by religious groups is 'unconstitutional,' he is reversing the very purpose of religious freedom."
11/ U.S. COMMISSION ON INTERNATIONAL RELIGIOUS FREEDOM RESPONDS
By November 2025, the U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom highlighted eroding liberties in South Korea, including suppression of Christian activities in schools.

The Daily Caller called on the U.S. State Department and the Ambassador-at-Large for International Religious Freedom to publicly condemn any attempt to dissolve religious bodies based on their political speech.

They also called for Congress to direct the Administration to review South Korean officials involved in political persecution under the Global Magnitsky Act, which enables sanctions such as asset freezes and visa bans.
12/ NEW CENSORSHIP LAW TARGETS FREE SPEECH

On December 24, 2025, the National Assembly passed amendments to the Information and Communications Network Act, allowing punitive damages up to five times losses for "false or fabricated information" and fines up to 1 billion won.
The bill passed 170-3 with four abstentions after a 24-hour filibuster by the conservative PPP. The law takes effect July 2026.
PPP lawmaker Choi Soo-jin warned the bill could be broadly applied to content containing minor errors and used as a tool to silence critics with the threat of lawsuits.

The People's Solidarity for Participatory Democracy, one of South Korea's biggest civic groups, demanded Lee veto the bill, saying it could give excessive powers to remove content to private technology companies like YouTube.
13/ U.S. STATE DEPARTMENT CRITICIZES CENSORSHIP LAW

Under Secretary of State Sarah Rogers wrote on X: "South Korea's proposed amendment to its Network Act, ostensibly focused on redressing defamatory deepfakes, reaches much further — and endangers tech cooperation."
She added: "Deepfakes are understandably concerning, but it's better to give victims civil remedies than give regulators invasive license for viewpoint-based censorship."
The State Department expressed "significant concerns," warning the law undermines free expression and digital cooperation.
UNESCO, the primary U.N. agency promoting freedom of expression, also expressed concerns and noted "an increase in media self-censorship across the region."

Observers note the law could threaten U.S. tech business interests, as major platforms like Google, Meta, and X are likely to fall under the law's definition of "large platforms" and may face restrictions and penalties.
14/ CHINA STOLE SOUTH KOREA'S CROWN JEWEL TECHNOLOGY
While President Lee embraces Beijing, China has been systematically stealing South Korea's most valuable technology.
In December 2025, South Korean prosecutors indicted 10 former Samsung employees for leaking the company's most advanced semiconductor technology to China's ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT).

The stolen technology: Samsung's 10-nanometer DRAM process, the most advanced in the world at the time. Samsung spent 1.6 trillion won ($1.2 billion) over five years developing it. Prosecutors estimate the breach caused Samsung losses of approximately 5 trillion won ($3.57 billion) in 2024 alone.

CXMT, founded in 2016 with Chinese government backing, recruited a former Samsung executive as its head of technology development. He systematically poached South Korean engineering talent. To bypass Samsung's cybersecurity, one employee manually transcribed over 600 detailed process steps onto 12 sheets of paper. Suspects established shell companies, moved offices frequently, and used secret code words.
The result: CXMT achieved mass production of 10nm-class DRAM in 2023 — years ahead of projections. It now produces 280,000 wafers per month, approximately 15% of global DRAM production.

SK Hynix was also targeted. CXMT illegally obtained trade secrets through a subcontractor in 2020. A former SK Hynix engineer was arrested at an airport attempting to leak HBM technology to China. Another received 18 months for smuggling documents to Huawei.

This is part of a pattern. In February 2025, a former Samsung manager got 7 years for leaking 18nm DRAM tech. In September 2024, two executives were charged with stealing 4 trillion won worth of technology. Prosecutors describe this as theft of critical national infrastructure.
15/ COZYING UP TO CHINA
While China systematically steals South Korea's most valuable technology, President Lee met Xi Jinping twice in two months.
First at APEC in Gyeongju (November 2025), then during a state visit to Beijing (January 4-7, 2026), the first by a South Korean president since 2019.

Lee declared he wants to make 2026 "the first year of full-scale restoration of Korea-China relations." The two signed 15 agreements on supply chains, AI, intellectual property, and environmental cooperation.

Xi urged South Korea to make "correct strategic choices" in an "increasingly chaotic and complicated international situation." Analysts say this means Beijing wants Seoul to side with China rather than Washington on Taiwan.

After a state banquet at the Great Hall of the People, Lee snapped a selfie of the presidential couples using a Chinese-made Xiaomi smartphone that Xi had given him. Xi had jokingly urged Lee to "check if there's a backdoor."
Lee posted the photo on social media with a beaming face emoji, writing: "The image quality is certainly good, right? Thanks to you, I got the picture of a lifetime haha."
Critics viewed this as emblematic of Lee's overly friendly approach to Beijing — the same Beijing whose companies are systematically stealing South Korea's most valuable technology.
16/ NOTABLY ABSENT: DENUCLEARIZATION
South Korea and China "affirmed the importance of resuming dialogue with North Korea" but notably did not mention denuclearization.
Lee's North Korea stance includes halting propaganda and prioritizing stability over denuclearization, which concerns U.S. politicians focused on countering Chinese and North Korean threats.

Lee has criticized anti-Chinese sentiment in South Korea and those who spread conspiracy theories regarding China's involvement in election fraud, saying it "angered Chinese people and drove them to turn their backs on Korea."
17/ U.S.-SOUTH KOREA ALLIANCE UNDER STRAIN
In 2025, bilateral relations faced challenges from U.S. tariffs and demands for South Korean investments.
A July 30 agreement reduced U.S. tariffs on South Korean exports from 25% to 15% in exchange for $350 billion in investments, including $150 billion in shipbuilding and $100 billion in LNG.
However, negotiations stalled over U.S. insistence on cash payments. Lee warned it could trigger a financial crisis akin to 1997.
Reports in May 2025 suggested the U.S. considered withdrawing a brigade (about 3,500 troops) from South Korea to reorient toward deterring China, raising questions about the alliance's credibility.
18/ THE DATA CENTER DISASTER

A fire at the National Information Resources Service data center in Daejeon on September 26, 2025, caused by a lithium-ion battery explosion during maintenance, destroyed 858 terabytes of data and disrupted 647 government systems for nearly a week.
Five individuals, including a NIRS official and contractors, were charged with professional negligence on October 27, 2025, after revelations of illegal subcontracting and unqualified workers.
President Lee apologized, calling it "foreseeable," and ordered nationwide infrastructure audits. No further accountability measures were reported by year-end.
19/ THE COUPANG DATA BREACH
Coupang, one of South Korea's largest companies, faced a massive data breach starting June 24, 2025, affecting 33.7 million users' personal information. It went undetected until November.
CEO Park Dae-jun resigned on December 10, 2025. Police raids followed, along with a 1.69 trillion won ($1.18 billion) compensation plan.
Parliamentary hearings criticized founder Bom Kim's absence. The Korea Fair Trade Commission considered suspending operations.
20/ EXPERTS WARN: COMMUNISM IS TAKING HOLD
Former Speaker Newt Gingrich wrote in the Washington Times that South Korea is "heading toward a pro-Chinese communist dictatorship."
Suzanne Scholte noted the administration's tolerance of pro-North Korean elements, potentially eroding anti-communist safeguards.

Tony Perkins of the Family Research Council said on "Washington Watch": "I think the decline that we're seeing can be stopped. But at some point, if things continue in a downward slide in South Korea, it's going to be very, very difficult."
Professor Chester Tan, an expert in international criminal and human rights law, warned "a dictatorship could take hold in South Korea in the near future."
21/ THE SPIRITUAL DIMENSION
Tony Perkins of the Family Research Council stated: "There is a spiritual war going on. If you think about the kingdom significance, it's very profound."
"Across the demilitarized zone, you have the most unjust regime and the worst persecutor of Christians on planet Earth. Pyongyang was once the Jerusalem of the East."
"I believe the enemy fears a unified Korea, where South Korea has six out of the 10 biggest Christian churches in the world."
South Korea is the second-largest sender of missionaries worldwide after the United States.
22/ A BALANCED VIEW EXISTS
It should be noted that some observers disagree with the alarm.
Eric Foley of Voice of the Martyrs Korea said: "We still enjoy good, solid, strong religious freedoms here in South Korea."

He argued the four ongoing cases are best understood as involving the application of election laws to churches rather than a general crackdown, noting that "anytime there is a change in government, politically vocal pastors or ministry leaders become subjects of investigations."
Lee has pledged to strengthen ties with the United States without antagonizing China, and he maintained commitments to the U.S. alliance during his August meeting with Trump.
23/ WHY THIS MATTERS TO EVERY AMERICAN
South Korea is not just an ally. It's a strategic anchor holding the line against Chinese and North Korean expansion in the Pacific.

America sacrificed 36,574 lives and 103,284 wounded in the Korean War to keep South Korea free. We still have more than 28,000 American military troops serving there, and our commitment has been consistent for 75 years.

If Seoul pivots away from Washington, if religious freedom erodes, if censorship becomes the norm, if China continues to steal critical technology while Lee embraces Beijing, the entire balance of power in Asia shifts.
Americans need to pay attention before it's too late.
24/ WHAT CAN BE DONE
The Daily Caller has called for:
The U.S. State Department and Ambassador-at-Large for International Religious Freedom to publicly condemn any attempt to dissolve religious bodies based on their political speech.
Congress to direct the Administration to review South Korean officials involved in political persecution under the Global Magnitsky Act for possible sanctions.

Tony Perkins urged: "The church needs to exercise its spiritual authority and seek God's hand, blessing, and favor on Korea and really call out, cry out to God on behalf of their country as we need to do in the United States."
25/ THE BOTTOM LINE
South Korea stands at a crossroads.

It can either uphold the values that shaped its democratic identity — freedom of conscience, rule of law, and fairness — or it can slip back into a pattern of politically motivated suppression dressed in legal garments.
The signs are troubling:
☑️ Religious leaders imprisoned without conviction
☑️ Churches raided by police
☑️ A censorship law threatening free speech
☑️ $3.57 billion in chip technology stolen by China
☑️ A president cozying up to Beijing while tensions grow with Washington
This is happening to America's closest ally in Asia.
The time to act is now.
🔁 REPOST to raise awareness.

blocks.text: —— The Global Initiative of Rev. Sun Myung Moon and Dr. Hak Ja Han Moon to Overcome UN Stagnation

“Is the United Nations No Longer Functional?”

In 2026, the world faces this brutal question. Amid the relentless fires of conflict in Gaza, Ukraine, and Sudan, the UN Security Council—the supposed guardian of international order—has fallen silent, paralyzed by the wall of “veto” power held by major nations. As funding cuts, withdrawals from key agencies, and the erosion of multilateralism cripple humanitarian aid, the world is confronted with the stark “limits of politics.” 

Yet, as if foreseeing this dysfunction, Rev. Sun Myung Moon and Dr. Hak Ja Han Moon identified the coming limitations of the UN decades ago. They consistently offered a prescription for peace that goes beyond “visible powers” such as politics and economics.

What they proposed was not mere political compromise. By transcending national interests, breaking down religious barriers, and embracing humanity with maternal love, they launched a global peace implementation project rooted in the firm backbone of “Godism.” Now, we uncover the true value of this “other key to peace,” which complements the stagnating UN and seeks to transform the destiny of the global village.

Rev. Sun Myung Moon’s Address to the UN: Spiritual Renewal Through Interreligious Dialogue

Rev. Sun Myung Moon clearly identified the functional failures of the United Nations and advocated fundamental reform. In the landscape of 2026—marked by Security Council paralysis and the withdrawal of major powers from agencies such as UNESCO and the WHO—the credibility of multilateralism has been severely damaged. To address these limits, Rev. Moon proposed the establishment of an “Interreligious Council” at the Millennium World Peace Summit in 2000, calling for religious leaders to participate directly in international conflict resolution. 

He criticized the UN for failing to hold the “key to peace” due to bureaucratic obstacles and the competing interests of powerful nations, stating: “However, I submit that serious consideration should be given to forming a religious assembly, or council of religious representatives, within the structure of the United Nations.” He called for a “renewed UN” that would utilize the spiritual power of religion, grounded in the conviction of “Godism”—that interreligious harmony is a prerequisite for world peace.

Following the 9/11 attacks in 2001, he convened the “Islam and a Future World of Peace” conference in Jakarta. Working with former Indonesian President Abdurrahman Wahid, he identified religious misunderstanding as a root cause of terrorism and emphasized, “Islam is not bad… the true Islam must be known.” This presented a roadmap for conflict resolution through spiritual integration rather than bureaucracy alone.

Dr. Hak Ja Han Moon’s Address to the UN: The “Mother of Peace” Who Knows Heavenly Sorrow

Dr. Hak Ja Han Moon’s commitment to peace is rooted in personal suffering and a profound love for humanity, which she understands as cherished by Heaven. As a young girl during the Korean War, she narrowly escaped death as a refugee. The question, “Why do people wage war, and why must so many precious lives be lost?” became a lifelong inquiry, leading her to deeply resonate with the “sorrow of the Heavenly Parent” witnessing human suffering. This became the driving force of her global peace movement. Her survival of war formed the emotional foundation of her desire to embrace the world with a mother’s love.

In the 1990s, amid post–Cold War instability, male-centered ideologies still dominated, limiting women’s voices and social participation. At the 1992 inauguration of the Women’s Federation for World Peace (WFWP) at the UN, Dr. Han declared: “As women, we reject the ideologies of the past that have oppressed humanity. We are united in our desire to banish war, oppression, and exploitation from this earth.” She called for a new era of peace leadership led by women. 

Transforming personal and Heavenly sorrow into “True Mother’s Love,” she redefined women as “Mothers of Peace,” stating: “The true workers who will bring an end to the world of war and violence… are the women of the 21st century.” Through the concept of the “Abel Women’s UN” since 2012, she has emphasized that family stability is the foundation of national and global peace.

Impact and Achievements: From Vision to Implementation

The defining feature of the Moons’ work is that it does not remain theoretical but moves directly into action. The Universal Peace Federation (UPF), founded in 2005, holds General Consultative Status with UN ECOSOC and has appointed over 100,000 Ambassadors for Peace worldwide. Projects such as the International Peace Highway and reconciliation efforts through the Marriage Blessing have demonstrated practical, grassroots peacebuilding.

While the UN struggles with budget constraints and geopolitical deadlock, Rev Moon and Dr. Han’s global network spanning 143 countries enables rapid, flexible humanitarian and reconciliation efforts beyond bureaucratic limits. Their vision of one human family under God has functioned as a living “bulwark of peace” from the post–Cold War era to the present.

Their mission was not organizational expansion, but a lifelong struggle to wipe away the tears of God and end humanity’s suffering. In 2026, as international order fractures and nations retreat into self-interest, their peace model stands not as outdated idealism, but as a resilient and realistic framework for a world in crisis. The flame they lit continues to burn, illuminating the path toward true harmony.

title: Yamagami on Trial: How Media Narratives Diverged from the Defendant’s Own Testimony
previewText: In the trial of Tetsuya Yamagami, the defendant in the 2022 shooting of former Prime Minister Shinzo Abe, details previously unreported came to light during the defendant questioning

blocks.text:
In the trial of Tetsuya Yamagami, the defendant in the 2022 shooting of former Prime Minister Shinzo Abe, details previously unreported came to light during the defendant questioning (November-December 2025). Yamagami himself pointed out inaccuracies in media reports.

Following the incident, media outlets reported that "Yamagami, who led a difficult life due to the impact of donations, attended one of the top preparatory schools in the prefecture but gave up on university due to financial circumstances." However, this was not due to economic reasons. In his testimony, Yamagami described his childhood up to middle school as "smooth," noting that his maternal grandfather ran a business, allowing them to live comfortably. All three siblings attended cram schools and went to private schools. Yamagami's decision to forgo university was his own choice because "the universities had low deviation scores."

The financial troubles with the Unification Church were settled by 2014 with a repayment of 50 million yen, agreed upon by his mother and three siblings, and Yamagami himself recognized it as "resolved," so he had no intention of consulting a lawyer.
Yamagami testified that he supported former Prime Minister Abe's policies and repeatedly denied feeling "anger" toward Abe.

Just before the incident, he had poured money into making homemade guns and other preparations, causing his debt to swell to over 2 million yen. He quit his job in early June, and with no financial prospects in sight, he stated that he felt "compelled to cause some kind of incident or be cornered."

Triggered by journalist Eito Suzuki's reporting, it was revealed that just five days before the incident, he targeted former Prime Minister Abe due to his connection with the Unification Church, and aimed to deal a blow to the church by drawing public attention.

After the incident, large amounts of support funds were sent to Yamagami from across the country. However, Yamagami stated that there were inaccuracies in the reports about him, and once the trial ends, people will realize he is quite different from the image portrayed, so he believes the money should be returned.
This became a testimony from the defendant himself that overturned the media's initial reports on the motives and background of the incident.
2022年安倍晋三元首相銃撃事件の山上徹也被告裁判で、被告人質問（2025年11-12月）でこれまで報じられなかった詳細が明らかになった。山上被告自身、メディアの報道には不正確なものがあったと指摘した。

事件発生後、メディアでは「献金の影響で苦しい生活をしていた山上被告は県内屈指の進学校に通っていたが、経済的な事情から大学への進学を断念した。」と報じていた。しかし経済的理由で断念したものではなかった。山上被告の証言では、中学まで幼少期を「順調」と話し、母方の祖父が経営を営み不自由なく過ごしていた。兄弟3人全員が塾に通い私立校進学。山上被告の大学進学断念は「偏差値が低い大学だから」と自ら選択したものだった。
統一教会金銭トラブルは2014年までに5000万円返済で母と兄弟３人の同意のもと「解決済み」であり、山上被告自身も解決の認識でいたため弁護士相談の考えは無かった。
山上被告は、安倍元首相の政策を支持していたと証言し、安倍元首相への「怒り」の感情は何度も否定した。
そして事件直前は、手製銃の自作などのため金を注ぎ込み、借金は200万円以上に膨らんでいた。6月初めに仕事を辞め、経済的な見通しが立たなくなったため「何らか事件を起こさないと追い詰められていた」と語った。
ジャーナリストの鈴木エイト氏の報道をきっかけに、事件のわずか５日前に統一教会との関係を理由に安倍元首相を標的としたこと、そして世間の注目を集めることで統一教会に打撃を与えようとしたことを明らかにした。
事件後、山上のもとには全国から多額の支援金が差し入れられた。だが、山上被告は、自分に関する報道に不正確なものがあり、裁判が終わればイメージとかなりと違った人間とわかるはずなので、返すべきだと思っていると語った。
事件当初メディアが報じた動機や背景に関する報道内容を裏返す被告人本人の証言となった。

title: Persecuting Purity: South Korea's Bold Betrayal of Dr. Hak Ja Han and Religious Freedom
previewText: The detainment of Dr. Hak Ja Han, the 82-year-old leader of the Unification Church, has lasted 111 days as of January 11, 2026, since her arrest on September 23, 2025. This treatment contrasts sharply

blocks.text: The detainment of Dr. Hak Ja Han, the 82-year-old leader of the Unification Church, has lasted 111 days as of January 11, 2026, since her arrest on September 23, 2025. This treatment contrasts sharply with numerous historical cases where individuals accused of similar financial crimes received suspended sentences, fines, or pardons, avoiding prolonged incarceration. This analysis examines these disparities through factual comparisons to argue that Dr. Han's detainment is disproportionate and unjust, amounting to selective application of the law and religious persecution.
Background on Dr. Hak Ja Han's Case

Dr. Han was indicted on October 10, 2025, for bribery, embezzlement, and destruction of evidence. Despite denying the charges and cooperating with investigations, she has been subjected to extended pretrial detention, including a return to jail after temporary release for medical treatment. This approach deviates from South Korea's legal norms, where pretrial detention is intended for flight risks or evidence tampering threats, neither of which has been substantiated in her case given her age and public profile. Prosecutors have presented hardly any clear evidence to justify such concerns, yet Dr. Han endures inhumane conditions that endanger her health, highlighting a lack of proportionality in her treatment.
Comparative Analysis: Precedents in Religious Financial Crime Cases

South Korean courts have historically imposed lenient punishments on religious leaders convicted of financial crimes, often opting for suspended sentences or fines rather than incarceration. These precedents demonstrate a pattern of proportionality that is absent in Dr. Han's detainment.
Lee Man-hee (Shincheonji Church): In 2021, convicted of embezzlement involving church funds. He received a three-year suspended sentence, avoiding jail time.

David Yonggi Cho (Yoido Full Gospel Church): In 2014, convicted of embezzlement of 13 billion won ($12 million) and tax evasion. He was sentenced to three years in prison, suspended for five years, and fined 5 billion won, serving no time.
Huh Kyung-young (Spiritual Leader): Investigated in 2025 for embezzling funds to support political activities. The case resulted in fines and restitution, with no prolonged pretrial detention.
These cases illustrate that convictions for financial misconduct in religious contexts typically result in non-custodial penalties.
Comparative Analysis: Precedents in Non-Religious Financial Crime Cases

The leniency extends to high-profile business and political figures accused of bribery and embezzlement, where suspended sentences, reductions, or pardons are common. These examples highlight severe crimes with minimal consequences, underscoring inconsistencies in judicial outcomes.

Jay Y. Lee (Samsung Heir): Convicted in 2017 of bribery involving 43 billion won ($38 million) to influence government decisions, embezzlement, and perjury. Initial five-year sentence was suspended on appeal; he served one year before being pardoned in 2022.
Chung Mong-koo (Hyundai Chairman): Convicted in 2007 of embezzlement of 100 billion won ($90 million) and bribery. Received a three-year suspended sentence, avoiding jail.
Shin Dong-bin (Lotte Chairman): Convicted in 2018 of bribery in the Park Geun-hye scandal, involving billions in won. Sentenced to 2.5 years, suspended for four years.
Lee Kun-hee (Former Samsung Chairman): Convicted twice—in 1996 for bribery and in 2009 for tax evasion involving slush funds. Received suspended sentences both times, serving no jail time.

Kim Seung-youn (Hanwha Chairman): Multiple convictions, including 2012 embezzlement of 300 billion won ($270 million) and assault. Received suspended sentences or short terms, resuming business leadership.
These cases involve large-scale corruption yet result in limited incarceration, contrasting with Dr. Han's extended detention for lesser amounts.
Contributions of Dr. Hak Ja Han and the Unification Church to South Korea and Global Peace

In evaluating judicial leniency, courts have considered societal contributions, as in the case of David Yonggi Cho, where the court explicitly cited his extensive religious activities and long-term contributions to social welfare—such as founding and leading the world's largest Pentecostal church, promoting spiritual growth for millions, and engaging in charitable works—as mitigating factors for his suspended sentence. Similarly, Dr. Han and the Unification Church have made profound contributions to South Korea's development and global peace efforts, particularly during critical historical periods like the Cold War and South Korea's rapid industrialization. These efforts, which addressed urgent national and international needs, warrant comparable consideration and make her prolonged detainment illogical and unjust.
Defense Production and Economic Growth

Through Tongil Heavy Industries, part of the Tongil Group founded in 1963, the Unification Church played a key role in South Korea's defense manufacturing during the 1970s under President Park Chung-hee's Heavy and Chemical Industry Drive.

At a time when South Korea faced existential threats from North Korea following the Korean War, with limited industrial capacity and reliance on foreign aid, this initiative transferred advanced technologies and skills to produce military equipment, bolstering national security and fueling the "Miracle on the Han River." The defense sector's growth created jobs, spurred technological innovation, and integrated into broader economic policies that transformed South Korea from a war-torn agrarian economy into an industrial powerhouse, addressing the severe poverty and instability of the post-war era.
Inspiration for the Saemaul Undong Movement

The Unification Church's community development efforts in the 1960s, emphasizing self-reliance and cooperative projects, aligned with and influenced the government's Saemaul Undong (New Village Movement) launched in 1970. During South Korea's rural crisis in the 1960s-1970s, with urban migration depleting villages and exacerbating poverty, this movement mobilized local communities for infrastructure improvements like roads and housing. Adopted nationally, it revitalized rural areas, reduced inequality, and supported economic modernization. The program continues today, adapted for urban and international development, highlighting its enduring impact on South Korea's social cohesion and growth.
Little Angels Children's Folk Ballet

Founded in 1962, this troupe has performed over 7,000 shows in more than 50 countries, serving as a cultural ambassador during the Cold War. Amid ideological divisions, with South Korea on the front lines of anti-communism, the Little Angels bridged democratic and communist worlds through arts, performing in the Soviet Union and other bloc countries to foster dialogue and humanize relations. Their tours promoted Korean heritage globally, countering propaganda and building goodwill at a time when cultural exchanges were vital to easing tensions and preventing escalation.
Universal Ballet

Established in 1984, this company has toured internationally, advancing cultural diplomacy during the late Cold War. As ballet became a tool for soft power—evident in U.S.-Soviet exchanges—the Universal Ballet performed classical works to audiences in divided regions, symbolizing unity and peace. In an era of nuclear standoffs, such initiatives humanized adversaries, reduced mistrust, and supported detente efforts, aligning with global needs for non-violent conflict resolution.
Cultural Exchange Programs for Russians

In 1990, following a historic meeting with Mikhail Gorbachev, the Unification Church sponsored programs sending over 3,000 Soviet students to study in the United States, fostering cross-cultural understanding at the Cold War's end. As the Soviet Union collapsed amid economic turmoil and ideological shifts, these exchanges promoted peace by exposing youth to democratic values, building personal ties, and aiding Russia's transition—critical for global stability and preventing post-Cold War conflicts.
Broader Peace Initiatives

Dr. Han co-founded the Universal Peace Federation in 2005 and the Women's Federation for World Peace in 1992, organizing interfaith dialogues, international marriage blessings aimed at building families that transcend race, culture, and nationality to cultivate a world of peace through strong, intercultural families, and North-South Korean ventures like Pyeonghwa Motors. During ongoing Korean Peninsula tensions, these efforts advanced reunification and women's roles in peacebuilding, addressing historical divisions from the Korean War and Cold War.

Given these contributions—directly supporting South Korea's security, economy, and global standing during existential threats—it defies logic for the government to subject Dr. Han to prolonged detention over financial allegations, especially when similar cases received leniency based on comparable societal impacts.
Evidence of Selective Application of the Law and Religious Persecution

The disparities in treatment between Dr. Han's case and the precedents outlined above point to a clear selective application of the law, targeting the Unification Church in a manner that suggests religious persecution. While high-profile figures in business and politics face minimal consequences for far graver financial crimes, Dr. Han—an elderly religious leader with no prior convictions—endures extended detention on charges involving relatively small sums. This selective enforcement aligns with broader criticisms of South Korea's justice system being weaponized against minority faiths, as evidenced by international outcry.

Prominent religious leaders from around the world have traveled to South Korea to protest this injustice. For instance, Pastor Mark Burns, a spiritual advisor to U.S. President Donald Trump, visited the Seoul Detention Center multiple times in November and December 2025, meeting with Dr. Han and publicly condemning her detention as a violation of religious freedom. Imboni Dr. uZwi-Lezwe Radebe, founder of The Revelation Spiritual Home in South Africa and a 2025 Sunhak Peace Prize laureate, also visited in November 2025 to meet Dr. Han and advocate for her release. In December 2025, a delegation of American Christian leaders including Dr. Magna Faith Krimis, Pastor Nia Nkrumah from Philadelphia, and Dr. Antonio Bowen traveled to Korea to participate in interfaith discussions and express solidarity with Dr. Han. Additionally, over 50 global faith leaders from diverse traditions—such as Orthodox patriarchs, American gospel icons, Buddhist monks, and Islamic scholars—gathered in Seoul at Gwanghwamun in November 2025 to demand her immediate release, describing her detention as an assault on religious freedom and global spiritual unity. This global response underscores that Dr. Han's case is not merely a legal matter but a targeted attack on a religious movement, echoing historical patterns of persecution against non-mainstream faiths in South Korea.
Conclusion

Dr. Hak Ja Han's detainment is unjust when compared to precedents of lenient punishments for similar or graver offenses. Her and the Unification Church's contributions, which addressed critical historical needs, merit consideration akin to others, yet are disregarded in favor of harsh measures that smack of religious persecution. The selective application of the law, as highlighted by international religious leaders like Pastor Mark Burns, Imboni Dr. uZwi-Lezwe Radebe, Dr. Magna Faith Krimis, Pastor Nia Nkrumah, Dr. Antonio Bowen, and over 50 others who have protested in Korea, demands immediate rectification. Aligning her case with established norms—through release on bail or proportionate penalties—would restore judicial equity and uphold South Korea's commitment to religious freedom.
