title: South Korea's Drift from American-Inspired Ideals: Church-State Separation Under Siege
previewText: In the shadow of a proposed bill that could empower the South Korean government to investigate and dissolve religious organizations for alleged political interference, a deeper malaise in the nation's

blocks.text: In the shadow of a proposed bill that could empower the South Korean government to investigate and dissolve religious organizations for alleged political interference, a deeper malaise in the nation's democracy comes into focus. Targeting groups like the Family Federation for World Peace and Unification (Unification Church) and Shincheonji Church of Jesus, this legislation — currently in its pre-announcement phase until January 16, 2026 — is framed by President Lee Jae-myung's administration as a defense of church-state separation.

Yet, critics contend it exemplifies "revenge politics," where rival factions weaponize scandals to settle scores, using these churches as convenient scapegoats while ignoring systemic corruption that permeates South Korean society. Adding to the irony, President Lee himself faces multiple ongoing corruption investigations from his time as Seongnam mayor and Gyeonggi governor, involving allegations of bribery, breach of trust, and favoritism in development projects — probes he is accused of trying to thwart through sweeping prosecutorial reforms.

This not only highlights divergences in how the U.S. and South Korea interpret separation of church and state but also reveals how Seoul's actions may violate its own constitutional principles, rooted in American ideals, by inverting the doctrine to justify state overreach.
Historical Roots: A Constitution Born from American Influence, Now Strained by Revenge

South Korea's 1948 Constitution, drafted amid U.S. military administration post-World War II, mirrors American democratic frameworks with its emphasis on individual rights, judicial review, and a presidential system. Article 20 explicitly mandates freedom of religion and separation of church and state, echoing the U.S. First Amendment's protections against establishment and for free exercise.

This American imprint was intended to foster a stable, tolerant society after decades of Japanese colonial rule. However, South Korea's political evolution has been marred by a cycle of "revenge politics," where incoming administrations prosecute predecessors, often on corruption charges, perpetuating instability.A stark illustration: Every South Korean president in the last two decades has faced arrest, indictment, impeachment, or worse.
Roh Moo-hyun (2003-2008) committed suicide in 2009 amid a bribery probe.
Lee Myung-bak (2008-2013) was sentenced to 15 years for corruption.
Park Geun-hye (2013-2017) was impeached and jailed for 24 years on bribery and abuse of power.
Moon Jae-in (2017-2022) faced investigations post-tenure. Yoon Suk Yeol (2022-2024) was impeached and faced arrest attempts in 2025.
This pattern underscores a facade of democracy, where "vindictive political culture" trumps rule of law, turning governance into a zero-sum game of retribution.

President Lee Jae-myung, who assumed office in June 2025 after Yoon's impeachment, is no exception to this cycle. Even as he accuses religious groups and political opponents of corruption, Lee faces his own trials stemming from pre-presidency scandals, including a combined case on bribery and corruption related to property developments.

Critics argue his administration's aggressive reforms — such as dismantling the powerful Prosecutors' Office and separating investigation from indictment powers — are designed to limit probes into his own affairs, effectively shielding him while pursuing rivals. These moves, finalized in late 2025, have been labeled as efforts to curb "retaliatory" prosecutions, but they raise questions about impartiality in a system already plagued by selective enforcement.
Divergent Views on Church-State Separation: Accommodation vs. Overreach

The U.S. interprets separation through a balanced lens, with the Supreme Court allowing non-coercive religious expression (e.g., Kennedy v. Bremerton, 2022) while prohibiting endorsement. South Korea's "Jeonggyo bunri" under Article 20 demands stricter neutrality, as seen in Constitutional Court rulings on military worship and conscientious objection. But the current bill inverts this: While religions are barred from state interference, the state can probe and dissolve them for alleged meddling, potentially violating religious freedom.
Scapegoating Churches in a Culture of Widespread Corruption

The bill's focus on churches like the Unification Church and Shincheonji smacks of selective enforcement, using them as scapegoats in revenge politics. Politicians from both sides — the ruling Democratic Party and opposition People's Power Party — have been accused of accepting church funds, yet the crackdown targets faiths amid partisan battles. This "about-face" hypocrisy is endemic: South Korea pretends political gifts and special treatment are anomalies, but they are historical norms.
Chaebols like Samsung and Hyundai exemplify this. Samsung's Lee Jae-yong was convicted in 2017 for bribing President Park Geun-hye, funneling millions to scandal-linked foundations.
Hyundai and other conglomerates donated similarly, fostering a "culture of corruption" through embezzlement and influence-peddling.
Everyone does it — from tycoons to politicians — yet churches are singled out, perhaps because they lack chaebol economic clout.
Intra-Religious Persecution: Christians Targeting Marginal Groups

Compounding the state's actions is persecution by mainstream Christian groups against the Unification Church and Shincheonji. Protestant organizations, including the United Christian Churches of Korea, have opposed these "marginal" faiths, accusing them of heresy and fueling deprogramming efforts — coercive conversions involving kidnapping and confinement.

The Unification Church reports over 4,000 deprogramming victims, often orchestrated by anti-cult Christian activists. Shincheonji, blamed for COVID-19 spread in 2020, faces raids and opposition from Protestants fearing its growth, with leaked chats revealing political influence concerns. This intra-faith hostility, amid a "religious liberty crisis," amplifies state crackdowns, turning separation into suppression.
Lee's Concerning Ties to Communist China: A Pro-CCP Lean Amid Geopolitical Tensions

Further complicating Lee's push for domestic control is his administration's warming relations with Communist China, raising alarms in Washington about South Korea's alignment in the U.S.-China rivalry. Just days ago, on January 5, 2026, President Lee met with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Beijing, marking his second summit with Xi in two months and the first state visit by a South Korean leader to China since 2019.

During the talks, Lee emphasized elevating Korea-China ties to a "new stage," citing shared history and the need to minimize misunderstandings, while Xi referenced recent Communist Party plenary sessions. Lee also met with Shanghai's Communist Party Secretary Chen Jining, seeking a "public sentiment reset" in bilateral relations.

Critics view these engagements as part of Lee's broader "pragmatic diplomacy," which aims to balance U.S. alliances with closer economic and political ties to Beijing, but many fear it masks a pro-CCP tilt that could undermine South Korea's security partnerships.

Lee's past comments, such as his 2023 "xie xie" (Mandarin for "thanks") remark dismissing involvement in Taiwan Strait tensions as none of Korea's business, have fueled accusations of pro-China leanings, with opponents warning it echoes subservience to Beijing.

U.S. analysts express concern that Lee's perceived pro-China image could complicate negotiations on troop deployments or nuclear cooperation, potentially weakening the U.S.-Korea alliance amid escalating tensions with North Korea and China.
In online forums and conservative circles, Lee's CCP engagements are lambasted as risking South Korea's sovereignty, with some drawing parallels to Hong Kong's subjugation.
This foreign policy shift, critics argue, dovetails with his domestic crackdowns, prioritizing alliances with authoritarian regimes over democratic principles inherited from U.S. influence.
Persecution or Protection? A Call for Realignment

President Lee's push frames the bill as upholding Article 20, but it risks misapplying separation by enabling state aggression against faiths — all while he maneuvers to blunt investigations into his own alleged misconduct and deepens ties with the CCP. In a multi-faith society, this could alienate Christians (30% of the population) and erode U.S.-inspired liberties. As an ally, South Korea's trajectory demands U.S. scrutiny to preserve true democracy over revenge.

title: FABRICATED EVIDENCE: Japan Ministry Officials Face Criminal Charges Over Church Documents
previewText:
🚨 Japan’s Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology Suspected of Fabricating Evidence in Unification Church Dissolution Order. Witnesses state, "This Is Not What I Wrote"
In

blocks.text: 🚨 Japan’s Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology Suspected of Fabricating Evidence in Unification Church Dissolution Order. Witnesses state, "This Is Not What I Wrote"

In February 2025, the legal team for the Family Federation for World Peace and Unification (formerly known as the Unification Church) released a shocking report. It alleged that Japan's Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology (MEXT) intentionally inserted false content into statements from former and current members to justify the church’s dissolution.  These falsifications were revealed during witness examinations in court in December 2024. The church side argued that fabricating evidence undermines judicial fairness and threatens freedom of religion, and in September 2025, they filed criminal complaints against six MEXT officials for forgery.
【Main Examples of Alleged Fabrication】

Statement from Mr. C (65-year-old male): MEXT described current member Mr. C as being coerced into large donations and participation in a mass wedding through threats such as "ancestral misfortune" or "falling into hell." However, Mr. C denied this, testifying, "This is not what I wrote." He stated that he voluntarily visited the church for marriage and inquired on his own, "How can I participate in a mass wedding?" MEXT officials listened to Mr. C's story without disclosing their intent in creating the statement, and submitted the altered version on September 20, 2023. Mr. C later requested corrections.

Statement from Ms. D (91-year-old female): In a 34-page statement regarding Ms. D, false claims were included, such as attributing her husband's 1959 depression (which recovered in two months) to ancestral karma and coercing purchases of items like vases. Ms. D testified that she never created this document or sought refunds from the church. She left the church after the assassination of former Prime Minister Abe due to strong opposition from her sons, but she maintains her faith to this day.

Additionally, it was pointed out that, of 294 statements mostly from former members, 33 were in the names of members' relatives, MEXT officials, or lawyers opposing the church. Can these truly be considered statements from believers?

In response to the church's complaints, MEXT refused to comment, citing non-public proceedings. Nearly four mounth has passed since the complaints, with no progress reported. This case highlights issues of judicial fairness and independence from governmental power in Japan, exposed through one religious organization. Can the Japanese government and judiciary overlook such allegations of forgery? Can the Japanese courts be called "fair" in this matter? Internationally, the response of the Japanese government, courts, and media toward this religious group has drawn criticism, and failing to address these forgery suspicions will further erode trust in judicial independence and reliability.
🚨文部科学省が統一教会解散命令請求で証拠捏造の疑い。「これは私が書いたものではない」

2025年2月、世界平和統一家庭連合（旧統一教会）の弁護団は衝撃的な報告書を発表した。文部科学省は、当宗教団体の解散を正当化するため、現信者・元信者の陳述書に意図的に虚偽の内容を挿入し提出したとのことだ。これらの虚偽情報は、2024年12月に行われた法廷での証人尋問で明らかになった。教団側は、証拠の捏造は司法の公正さを損ない、信教の自由を脅かすものだと主張し、2025年9月に文部科学省職員6人を偽造罪で告発した。 【主な捏造事例】

C氏（65歳男性）の陳述書：文部科学省は、現信者C氏が「先祖の不幸」や「地獄に堕ちる」といった脅迫によって、多額の献金や合同結婚式への参加を強要されたと記述した。しかし、C氏はこれに対し、「私が書いたものではない」と否定。結婚のために自ら教会を訪れ、「合同結婚式を受けるにはどうすればいいのか」と自ら教会に尋ねたと証言した。文部科学省職員は陳述書作成の意図を明かさずにC氏の話を聞き、2023年9月20日に改ざんされた陳述書を提出した。C氏は後に訂正を求めた。
D氏（91歳女性）の陳述書：D氏に関する34ページにわたる陳述書には、夫の1959年のうつ病（2ヶ月で回復）が先祖の因縁によるものとされ、壺などの購入を強要されたと虚偽の記載があった。D氏は、この文書を作成したことも、教会に返金を求めたこともないと証言。D氏は安倍元首相暗殺後、息子たちの強い反対により教会を離れたが、信仰は現在も維持している。
また、元信者を名義とする陳述書など294人分のうち、33人分が信者の親族や文科省職員、教団反対派の弁護士らの名義であったと指摘。これは、信者の陳述書と言えるのだろうか。

教団からの告発に対して、文科省は非公開審理を理由にコメント拒否。そして告発から4カ月が経過しようとしているが、その後の進展報告はなし。この一件は、国内における司法公正や権力からの独立が問われている中、一宗教団体を通してその問題があらわになった。日本政府や司法はこのような偽造の罪を、そのままにしておくことができるのか？この件に関して、日本の裁判所は「公正」といえるのだろうか。国際的にも当宗教団体に対する日本の政府や裁判所、メディアの対応が問題視されているが、このまま偽造疑惑を放置すれば、司法信頼と権力の独立性がされに揺らいでいくであろう。

title: Strategic Analysis: The "Shadow Directorship" and Individual Deviance
previewText: The controversies surrounding the Unification Church and the alleged political lobbying of 2018–2020 are increasingly being defined not as an organizational mission, but as a "rogue operation" led by

blocks.text: The controversies surrounding the Unification Church and the alleged political lobbying of 2018–2020 are increasingly being defined not as an organizational mission, but as a "rogue operation" led by former Director General Yoon Young-ho. The synthesized evidence reveals a pattern of administrative bypassing, financial fraud, and inconsistent testimony that isolates Yoon and his wife, Ms. Lee, as the sole architects of the scandal.
1. The Administrative "State within a State"

The primary mechanism for this deviance was Yoon Young-ho's consolidation of unprecedented authority. By 2019, Yoon held four concurrent high-ranking positions: World Headquarters Director General, Chief of Staff to the Leader's Office, UPF Headquarters Director, and Head of the Hyojeong Cultural Center.¹ This concentration of power allowed him to operate a "Shadow Headquarters." Administrative records show that Yoon held the "final decision-making authority" (jeon-gyeol-gwon) over the execution of church funds.² Using this authority, Yoon bypassed the official General Affairs department, leaving the church's chief accountant with "no memory" of any budgets allocated for political figures.³
2. The Financial "Slush Fund Reservoir"

The lobbying was not an official church expenditure but was funded through a systematic financial crime against the denomination. Yoon's wife, Ms. Lee, utilized her role as Finance Director to create a "slush fund reservoir" by using personal credit cards for luxury purchases and then fabricating 225 instances of fake vouchers to receive "reimbursement" from church cash.⁴ This "Voucher-to-Cash" pipeline provided the liquidity for the high-profile gifts at the center of the scandal, including a 60-million-KRW Graff necklace and Chanel bags for the First Lady.⁵ The total embezzlement identified by the church—totaling nearly 2 billion KRW—positions the organization as a financial victim of the Yoon couple's private enterprise rather than a participant.⁶
3. The Structural Impossibility of Oversight

The narrative of "organizational intent" is further undermined by the physical and logical impossibility of leadership oversight. Leader Hak Ja Han has testified that she is "virtually blind," making it impossible for her to have reviewed the "special reports" Yoon claims to have submitted.⁷ Furthermore, Yoon's legal testimony contains objective chronological anomalies. For example, Yoon claimed to have delivered "election funds" to Rep. Kim Kyu-hwan in April 2020, even though Kim had been officially disqualified from the race and declared his non-candidacy in March 2020.⁸ Such inconsistencies support the view that Yoon's claims are a "kamikaze tactic" (mulgwishin) intended to drag the organization down to mitigate his own personal liability.⁹
4. The Evidentiary Collapse: Hearsay, Alibis, and Self-Incrimination

Independent analysis further exposes the fragility of the prosecution's reliance on Yoon Young-ho as its primary witness. A comprehensive review published by The Monarch Report consolidates three critical vulnerabilities in the case against Dr. Hak Ja Han:

A. The Legal Vacuum of HearsayProminent opposition figure Rep. Park Jie-won publicly criticized the investigation's evidentiary basis, stating: "There is no physical evidence like the two watches... no concrete events have emerged." He further noted that Yoon's statements amount to nothing more than "hearsay evidence [that] is not recognized even in court".¹² Reports confirm that police are struggling to establish "quid pro quo"—the essential element of bribery—due to the lack of specifics regarding time, amount, or delivery method.

B. The Alibi That Breaks the TimelineYoon's testimony contains spatially impossible claims. He alleged that Rep. Jeon Jae-su attended a Unification Church event at Busan BEXCO on May 27, 2018. However, photographic evidence with a visible timestamp of 12:13 PM places Rep. Jeon at a 60th-anniversary mass at Gupo Catholic Church—approximately 15km away—at the exact same time.¹³ This objective contradiction fundamentally compromises Yoon's reliability as a witness on any claim.
C. The "Smoking Gun" RecordingMost critically, a transcript from April 2022 captures Yoon admitting to unauthorized action in his own words:
"I couldn't even report to Mother [President Han] that I was going to do this." "I should probably report on inter-country projects after I have created and executed them."

He further acknowledged that Dr. Han was "surprised" upon learning of his private meeting with then-President-elect Yoon Suk-yeol.¹⁰ This self-incriminating admission directly corroborates Dr. Han's denial of knowledge and the characterization of Yoon's behavior as a "water ghost tactic" (mulgwishin)—a strategy to implicate others and dilute personal responsibility.
Read the full analysis: The Monarch Report — The Unjust Detention of Dr. Hak Ja Han — A Case Built on Hearsay and Contradiction https://x.com/monarchreport25/status/2001319446879891492¹⁴
5. Conclusion: A Narrative of Hijacking

When synthesized, the evidence paints a clear picture: Yoon Young-ho constructed an autonomous power base that kept the central leadership in the dark. By operating a "report after execution" policy and funding his activities through embezzlement, Yoon effectively hijacked the institution's resources for his own personal political ambitions.¹⁰ With objective alibis disproving Yoon's timeline, prominent politicians dismissing his claims as inadmissible hearsay, and his own voice recordings proving he acted without Dr. Han's knowledge, the narrative of "instruction" collapses under scrutiny. The church's subsequent expulsion of Yoon and its criminal complaints against him serve as the final institutional confirmation of this individual deviance.

title: A Legacy of Peace Under Siege: The Unjust Persecution of Dr. Hak Ja Han

blocks.text: In the heart of South Korea's turbulent political landscape, a humanitarian crisis is unfolding—one that questions the very foundations of justice and due process. Dr. Hak Ja Han, an 82-year-old great-grandmother and the revered leader of the Unification Church, has been detained for over 90 days without what many argue is concrete evidence. This prolonged confinement of a global peace advocate, who has dedicated her life to interfaith dialogue and family values, is not merely a legal matter; it is a stark symbol of prosecutorial overreach by a Special Prosecution (SP) team plagued by its own scandals. As the January 28, 2026, verdict approaches for related cases, the narrative emerging from multiple investigations and reports paints a picture of systemic failure: a prosecution built on fabricated timelines, coercive tactics, and selective justice, rendering Dr. Han's detention profoundly unjust.
I. The Humanitarian Crisis: 90 Days of Coercive Detention

At 82 years old, Dr. Hak Ja Han is not just a religious figure; she is a great-grandmother whose health and well-being should be paramount in any humane legal system. Yet, she has endured over three months in detention, a period that critics describe as psychological torture rather than necessary pre-trial restraint. The SP, led by Min Joong-gi, requested an arrest warrant after Dr. Han submitted reasons for non-attendance, citing her age and offering alternative cooperation through written or visit-based investigations. The Unification Church has decried this as "unjust suppression," arguing that forcing an elderly leader into direct confrontation ignores basic human rights principles (Nocut News, 2025).

This case echoes a disturbing pattern in the SP's methods. Just months prior, a 57-year-old Yangpyeong County official took his own life after a grueling 15-hour interrogation, leaving a 21-page suicide note detailing "scripted" depositions and coercive pressure to implicate political figures.² The National Human Rights Commission of Korea (NHRC) has already filed complaints against SP investigators for abuse of power in related cases, underscoring a systemic disregard for human dignity.⁹
II. The Factual Collapse: A Case Built on "Time-Travel" Documents

The SP's case against Dr. Han hinges on shaky foundations, most notably a "Special Report" document central to allegations of political fund transfers. The prosecution insists this report was authored on January 3, 2022. However, independent reviews, including by the Seoul Southern District Prosecutors' Office, confirm the document was actually created on January 3, 2023—complete with "2023 New Year's Greetings" and attachments of news articles from November 2022.¹

This chronological impossibility—dubbed a mere "typo" by the SP—exposes the prosecution's willingness to bend reality. Without this fabricated timeline, the "concrete evidence" evaporates, leaving Dr. Han's detention as an overreach based on speculation rather than facts.
III. The Pattern of Coercion and the "Poisoned Fruit"

The Special Prosecution’s unreliability is further proven by its history of "target-fixed" investigations. The Yangpyeong official’s 21-page suicide note describes a culture where interrogation is weaponized and narratives are pre-scripted.² Compounding this is the "poisoned fruit" issue: much of the evidence was seized under warrants for unrelated cases and then illegally repurposed for political fund charges. Under South Korean law, such tainted evidence should be inadmissible.¹¹
IV. The Selective Justice of a "Political Subcontractor"

No narrative of injustice is complete without examining the accuser. Special Prosecutor Min Joong-gi is himself entangled in scandals. Min profited over 100 million KRW from Neo Semitech, a fraudulent company—coincidentally, the same firm in which the SP's primary target, First Lady Kim Keon-hee, invested.³

Further, the Corruption Investigation Office for High-Ranking Officials (CIO) has launched a probe into Min for neglect of duty, accusing him of ignoring evidence of Unification Church funds flowing to Democratic Party (DP) politicians.⁴ Testimony revealed 80 million KRW and luxury watches given to DP figures, yet no action was taken—while Dr. Han and PPP members face relentless pursuit.⁶ Critics label Min a "DP subcontractor," turning the SP into a tool of selective justice.⁷
V. Conclusion: The Call for Justice – Release Dr. Han Now

The credibility of the Special Prosecution has vanished. A team that is ethically bankrupt, factually incompetent, and politically biased has no right to deprive Dr. Hak Ja Han of her liberty. The 90-day detention of an elderly woman based on fabricated timelines and suppressed evidence is not an act of justice—it is a violation of the soul of the law.
To restore faith in justice and human dignity, South Korea’s judiciary must choose law over politicized prosecution—beginning with the immediate release of Dr. Hak Ja Han.

title: The Skewed Lens: How South Korea's Legacy Media Shapes a Biased Perception of America
previewText: In an increasingly interconnected world, media plays a pivotal role in shaping public perceptions of foreign nations. In South Korea, legacy media outlets—such as *Chosun Ilbo*, *Hankyoreh*, *Yonhap

blocks.text:
In an increasingly interconnected world, media plays a pivotal role in shaping public perceptions of foreign nations. In South Korea, legacy media outlets—such as *Chosun Ilbo*, *Hankyoreh*, *Yonhap News Agency*, and others—wield significant influence over how Koreans view the United States. However, under the current administration of President Lee Jae-myung and the Democratic Party (DP), which assumed power in June 2025 following political turmoil and the ouster of former President Yoon Suk-yeol[1][2][3], this influence appears increasingly skewed. 

Positive U.S. initiatives, particularly those combating communism and promoting global democracy, are often underreported or framed neutrally at best, while negative aspects receive amplified coverage. This imbalance not only distorts Koreans' understanding of America but also aligns with broader shifts under the DP, including proposals to lift bans on North Korean websites, potentially normalizing communist propaganda[4][5][6]. Drawing on recent polls, media analyses, and public discourse, this article argues that such biases erode pro-U.S. sentiments, threaten the U.S.-ROK alliance, and serve a left-leaning agenda that downplays anti-communist efforts.
The Korean Media Landscape: Partisan Divides and Overall Bias

South Korea's media is deeply polarized along ideological lines, with conservative outlets like *Chosun Ilbo* and *Dong-A Ilbo* often advocating stronger U.S. ties, while progressive ones like *Hankyoreh* and *Kyunghyang Shinmun* emphasize autonomy and critique U.S. policies[7][8][9]. Despite this, overall coverage of the U.S. leans negative, with sentiment analyses showing a -0.77 score for alliance-related stories, indicating pessimism or criticism[10]. Public trust in media remains low at around 31%, exacerbating perceptions of bias[11].

This bias manifests in selective reporting: Positive U.S. stories, such as economic investments or cultural exchanges, receive coverage but are often overshadowed by critiques of U.S. politics or foreign interventions[12]. For instance, while U.S.-ROK summits in 2025 were highlighted for $350 billion in investments, media focused more on tensions over trade and Trump's "unpredictability"[13]. Experts and commentators have echoed this, noting how left-leaning media like MBC praises Chinese events while criticizing Korean pro-U.S. displays[14], and how outlets show anti-US, pro-CCP positions[15]. Such framing contributes to a narrative where America is seen as a powerful but unreliable partner, despite polls showing 85% of Koreans value the alliance[16].
Underreporting U.S. Anti-Communism: The Venezuela Case Study

A stark example of this bias is the minimal coverage of the U.S.'s 2025 initiatives against communism in Venezuela. Under President Trump, the U.S. has escalated efforts to oust Nicolás Maduro's regime, including military operations and support for opposition figures like Nobel laureate María Corina Machado[17][18].

Yet, in major Korean outlets, coverage of the 2025 US actions in Venezuela is sparse and predominantly neutral or critical, with searches yielding only about 5-10 relevant articles across outlets like Chosun Ilbo, Hankyoreh, Korea Times, and JoongAng Daily (no results from Yonhap or Dong-A Ilbo English sites). These pieces focus more on military escalations, risks, and potential negatives rather than emphasizing US efforts to promote democracy or support for opposition figures.

For instance, the Korea Times article "Trump orders 'blockade' of sanctioned oil tankers leaving, entering Venezuela" (Dec 17, 2025) highlights the blockade and over two dozen military strikes, noting they "have killed at least 90 people," with quotes like US Representative Joaquin Castro calling it "unquestionably an act of war" and expert David Goldwyn warning of "inflation to skyrocket, and massive and immediate migration from Venezuela to neighboring countries."[19]

Similarly, Hankyoreh's opinion column "[Column] Trump should win Nobel War Prize" (Nov 10, 2025) criticizes the actions as aggressive, stating Trump has "ratcheted up the pressure on Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro by conducting naval attacks near his border, authorizing CIA action inside the country, and considering a plan to seize the country’s oil fields," without any positive framing of democratic promotion.[20]

Chosun Ilbo's "Trump Orders Full Blockade of Venezuela Oil" (Dec 17, 2025) reports on the "full and complete blockade" and designation of Maduro as a terrorist, emphasizing heightened "military tensions in the Caribbean Sea to their highest level" and concerns of potential conflict, but no celebration of US democratic goals.[21]

JoongAng Daily's column "Maduro’s ouster and 'our hemisphere': First test of Trump’s national security strategy in Latin America" (Dec 17, 2025) discusses airstrikes, tanker seizures, and CIA operations, quoting expert Phil Gunson on risks of "civil war" and opposition leader María Corina Machado on a "peaceful transition," but frames the efforts as potentially "dangerous" without strong emphasis on democracy; it mentions Machado's Nobel attendance in Norway but not her escape or US regrets over casualties.[22] Overall, these articles prioritize the confrontational aspects, with little to no spotlight on US initiatives as advancing freedom or democracy.

North Korea's support for Maduro is noted tangentially, but Trump's role in countering communism—relevant to Korea's own history—is rarely framed positively[23]. This omission contrasts with Korea's anti-communist heritage, where the U.S. alliance was forged against North Korean threats[24][25]. As Asia expert Gordon G. Chang has highlighted, Korean media's erosion by Chinese capital leads to left-leaning distortions in such reporting[26].
Amplified Negatives: A Pattern of Selective Emphasis

In contrast, negative U.S. stories receive extensive airtime. The 2024 U.S. election was covered with biases, such as selective polling favoring Democrats, leading to "misjudgment" accusations[27]. Trump's policies are often labeled "transactional" or "unpredictable," especially in progressive media[28]. During COVID-19 (2020-2023), outlets contrasted Korea's successes with U.S. "failures," using blame attribution in 50-70% of editorials[29]. Commentators like Korean conservative podcaster Paul Sungwon Kim have pointed out how far-left outlets like JTBC smear Korean and American patriots as "far-right," fueling division and distorting U.S. alliances[30].
This pattern suggests an agenda: By downplaying U.S. anti-communism, media aligns with narratives that soften views on authoritarian regimes, potentially weakening public support for the alliance.
Government Influence: The Role of President Lee Jae-myung and the DP

Elected in June 2025 amid scandals and Yoon's impeachment, Lee Jae-myung is portrayed as a pragmatic liberal, but critics argue his administration exerts undue influence on media[31][32][33]. Lee has criticized broadcasts as "one-sided" and pushed probes into opponents, fueling bias claims[34]. Experts like Dr. Tara O, author on North Korea, accuse legacy media of being DP propaganda organs with a Chinese style, showing anti-US positions[15].

This influence is evident in coverage: Post-election, left-leaning outlets smeared pro-U.S. patriots as "far-right"[35]. Critics warn this setup distorts U.S. perceptions, aligning with pro-China elements[36].
The North Korean Websites Bill: A Step Toward Normalizing Communism?
In December 2025, the DP proposed revising the Information and Communications Network Act to lift bans on North Korean websites, framed as "freedom of information."[4][5][6][37][38][39][40].

Critics fear this exposes Koreans to Pyongyang's propaganda, potentially shifting views on communism[41][42][43]. Amid North Korea's anti-U.S. vows, this could erode anti-communist values, especially as media underreports U.S. counter-efforts[44]. As Gordon G. Chang noted, this legislative move weakens defenses against North Korean information warfare, opening gateways for propaganda under civil liberties rhetoric[45].
Impact on Public Perception: Polls and Shifting Sentiments

Polls reveal the consequences: While 70-90% hold positive U.S. views, anti-China sentiment has surged since 2016, with some young demographics softening on communism—a potential media influence[46][47]. Favorability dipped during COVID but rebounded, yet growing mistrust—fueled by events like the ICE debacle—aligns with media biases[48]. Younger generations, as noted by groups like Freedom-University, call for resisting leftist censorship that protects China's image while suppressing anti-communist voices[49].
Conclusion

South Korea's legacy media, under the DP's influence, perpetuates a biased view of America by underreporting anti-communist initiatives like those in Venezuela while amplifying negatives. The proposed North Korean websites bill risks further normalizing communism, threatening the U.S.-ROK alliance and Korea's democratic values. To counter this, Koreans must demand balanced coverage and support independent voices. As polls show enduring pro-U.S. sentiment, awareness of these biases can preserve the alliance forged in shared anti-communist history[50][51].

title: The Unjust Detention of Dr. Hak Ja Han — A Case Built on Hearsay and Contradiction
previewText: The recent detention of Unification Church Dr. Hak Ja Han, known as the Mother of Peace, has sparked significant controversy, not merely due to the high profile of the figures involved, but because of

blocks.text: The recent detention of Unification Church Dr. Hak Ja Han, known as the Mother of Peace, has sparked significant controversy, not merely due to the high profile of the figures involved, but because of the fragile evidentiary foundation upon which the investigation rests.

A forensic analysis of recent developments reveals that the allegations of political lobbying are driven almost exclusively by the testimony of one individual: former World Headquarters Director Yoon Young-ho.

When scrutinized against objective timelines, independent political commentary, and internal records, Yoon’s testimony collapses, revealing a case built on uncorroborated hearsay and self-serving fabrication.
I. The Legal Vacuum: Hearsay Disguised as Evidence

The core of the prosecution's case relies on Yoon Young-ho’s assertions that he delivered funds under instruction. However, legal experts and veteran politicians have pointed out the glaring lack of physical evidence to support these claims.
Representative Park Jie-won, a prominent opposition figure, publicly defended one of the accused recipients, Rep. Jeon Jae-su, stating,
"There is no physical evidence like the two watches... no concrete events have emerged."
He further critiqued the investigation's reliance on Yoon, noting that
"statements coming out from former Director Yoon waging his glib tongue are only that ‘I heard someone gave it’," emphasizing that such "hearsay evidence is not recognized even in court"
([Breaking] Park Jie-won “Jeon Jae-su, A Reflection of Me 25 Years Ago...", Munhwa Ilbo, 2025).

This legal fragility is compounded by the police's own admission of difficulty. Reports indicate that despite search and seizures, the authorities are struggling to prove the core element of bribery—"quid pro quo"—and are relying on statements that lack specifics regarding time, amount, or delivery method (Doubts Over Credibility of Yoon Young-ho’s Statement..., Mindle News, 2025).
II. Factual Impossibilities: The Alibi that Breaks the Timeline

The credibility of Yoon’s testimony is further eroded by demonstrable factual errors. Yoon claimed that Rep. Jeon Jae-su attended a Unification Church event at the Busan BEXCO on May 27, 2018. However, objective evidence contradicts this entirely.

Photographic records confirm that at the exact time of the Unification Church event, Rep. Jeon was attending a 60th-anniversary mass at Gupo Catholic Church, approximately 15km away. The clock in the photograph points to 12:13 PM, providing an ironclad alibi that renders Yoon’s account physically impossible (Doubts Over Credibility of Yoon Young-ho’s Statement..., Mindle News, 2025).

If the primary witness constructs a narrative that is spatially and temporally impossible regarding one target, the reliability of his entire testimony regarding President Han’s involvement is fundamentally compromised.
III. The "Smoking Gun" of Rogue Behavior

Perhaps the most damning evidence against the theory of President Han’s "instruction" comes from Yoon Young-ho himself. A recently released transcript from April 2022 captures Yoon admitting to a private meeting with then-President-elect Yoon Suk-yeol.
In his own words, Yoon stated,

"I couldn't even report to Mother [President Han] that I was going to do this," and later noted that President Han was "surprised" when she found out. He further admitted, "I should probably report on inter-country projects *after* I have created and executed them"

(Yoon Young-ho "Met with Yoon Alone Without Reporting...", News1, 2025).

Listen to his own words: https://x.com/monarchreport25/status/1998976878690849143

This admission aligns perfectly with Dr. Han’s statements to police, where she denied knowledge of the bribery and attributed the issues to incidents that "occurred as Yoon Young-ho... wielded significant authority" ([Exclusive] Han Hak-ja "Unaware of Bribery Suspicions...", MBN, 2025).

It corroborates the testimony of former Vice President Lee, who characterized Yoon’s actions as a "water ghost tactic"—a strategy to drag others down to dilute his own responsibility—and noted that Yoon used the President's trust to pursue his own political desires outside the church ([Exclusive] “If Yoon Young-ho Hadn’t Prepared It...", Kukmin Ilbo, 2025).
Conclusion
The detention of Dr. Hak Ja Han appears to be a miscarriage of justice driven by the "water ghost" tactics of a former executive seeking to evade sole responsibility for his unauthorized actions.

With objective alibis disproving Yoon’s timeline, prominent politicians dismissing his claims as inadmissible hearsay, and his own voice recordings proving he acted without Dr. Han’s knowledge, the narrative of "instruction" falls apart. The investigation must pivot to the objective facts, which increasingly exonerate Dr. Han.

title: Religious freedom is not a reward for the theologically correct
previewText: Not long ago, Pastor Joshua Holmes — a young American unificationist — visited a large evangelical church in Seoul. He arrived in a spirit of goodwill, hoping for understanding at a moment when

blocks.text: Not long ago, Pastor Joshua Holmes — a young American unificationist — visited a large evangelical church in Seoul. He arrived in a spirit of goodwill, hoping for understanding at a moment when several Korean religious leaders, including Pastor Son Hyun Bo and Unification leader Han Hak-ja, also known as Holy Mother Han, faced investigation and even pretrial detention. But after Pastor Holmes spoke about the universal value of religious freedom, a church elder cut him off with a chilling statement: “Religious freedom is precious — but your church does not deserve religious freedom.”

That sentence has echoed in my mind ever since. It reflects a dangerous misconception. Religious liberty is not a reward bestowed on the theologically correct. It is a safeguard for all of us — especially for those whose beliefs others may find unacceptable. The moment we decide that one faith is unworthy of protection, we begin dismantling the very principle that keeps every faith safe.

History offers stark warnings. The pilgrims crossed the Atlantic to escape persecution by the Church of England, only to replicate intolerance in the New World. Puritans executed Quakers. Catholics and other dissenters were barred from certain colonies. And yet, through painful trial and error, Americans learned that no single church can set the terms of belonging in a diverse society.

The First Amendment emerged from this hard-won insight. It rejected the old habit of using government power to enforce religious “correctness.” It declared, instead, that faith must stand on the strength of its own persuasion.

Benjamin Franklin embodied that spirit. Near the end of his life, he wrote to Yale President Ezra Stiles that he found the essence of “sound religion” in any sect that honored God, did good to others and recognized moral accountability. Franklin refused to police doctrinal boundaries. He cared about conscience, compassion and character — things that unite, not divide.

Reverend Sun Myung Moon, the late spouse of Han Hak-ja, lived out this same ethic. In the early days of his ministry in Korea, a pastor falsely accused him. Some followers urged him to sue. But Reverend Moon recalled Joseph in Genesis forgiving the brothers who had betrayed him. Just as Joseph chose gratitude over vengeance, Reverend Moon chose reconciliation. He remembered that Christians had carried Jesus’ message for 2,000 years, often at the cost of their lives. He felt indebted to that legacy, not entitled to retaliate against it.

My own life was shaped by this perspective. In 1971, disillusioned by U.S. foreign and defense policy, I moved to France. There, after encountering Father and Mother Moon, I came to appreciate their profound love for the United States — not because it is flawless, but because its ideals have inspired the constitutions of other nations far beyond its borders. The Moons honored the courage of early settlers who risked everything to practice the face of their choice. They revered the spirit of Nathan Hale, who declared before his execution that his only regret was having but one life to give for his country.
After Reverend Moon’s passing in 2012, Holy Mother Han continued to return to the U.S. — even though the country had once imprisoned her husband. She, too, chose forgiveness and reconciliation.

Reverend Moon and Holy Mother Han have expressed deep love for Korea and great pride in the beauty of Korean Christianity — its dawn prayers, its martyrs, its spiritual devotion. That is why it is so painful today to hear some within that same tradition argue that Unificationists do not “deserve” religious freedom. Such thinking contradicts the very democratic values and Christian legacy that helped shape modern Korea.
Pastor Martin Niemöller’s warning still rings with urgency:
“…they came for the Jews,
And I did not speak out —
Because I was not a Jew…
Then they came for me —
And there was no one left to speak out for me.”

Religious freedom is not reliant on doctrinal agreement and the erosion of such liberty never begins with the majority. It begins with a small, disfavored group that people find easy to dismiss. When society decides that some believers don’t deserve freedom, it sets a precedent to deny it to everyone else as well

By Thomas J. Ward
Published Dec 3, 2025 5:13 pm KST

Thomas J. Ward is professor of peace and development at HJ International Graduate School for Peace and Development in New York City. A Fulbright alum, Ward’s articles have been published by Cambridge University Press, East Asia Quarterly, E-International Relations, the Journal of CESNUR, and Bitter Winter, among other publications.
